Name: language_refusal_threshold
Title: The Cheapest Jailbreak Is a Translation: A Causal Account of the Query-Language Refusal Threshold in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Aligned multilingual LLMs carry a single, largely content-agnostic 'refusal threshold' scalar whose default value is covertly set by the query language: for borderline-harmful requests, the model refuses in high-alignment-coverage languages but complies with the identical request in low-coverage languages. The single new, sharp claim is a DISSOCIATION with an identification test: (a) a shared, language-agnostic harm/permissibility representation exists and is decodable even in languages where the model complies; (b) cross-lingual refusal inconsistency is driven by a per-language shift of a scalar refusal gate applied to that shared harm estimate, NOT by the model computing a genuinely different harm assessment; and (c) the threshold shift scales with the language's safety-alignment coverage rather than with typological distance, and can be causally moved by steering a single recovered 'refusal-threshold direction'. Formally, the threshold is defined as the projection of late-layer activations onto a recovered refusal-gating direction at which P(refuse) crosses 0.5 as harm severity increases; the per-language crossover severity operationalizes it.
Related Work: Refusal-direction interpretability (Arditi et al. 2024, 'refusal is mediated by a single direction') and follow-ups on downstream refusal gating are MONOLINGUAL/English: they show a refusal direction exists but never ask whether its activation BASELINE (the gate's default set-point) is conditioned by the query language, which is precisely our identification question. Work framing refusal as an 'action, not a representation' and as a 'late orthogonal language-specific change' establishes that a refusal decision is a late computation and that language-specific components live late in the network; neither poses, let alone tests, the causal dissociation of a shared harm estimate from a language-set threshold, nor tests whether coverage vs typology sets that threshold. Multilingual moral-reasoning work (One Model Many Morals 2025; Untangling Input from Reasoning Language 2026; Do Moral Judgment Capabilities Change with Language 2024) is purely behavioral and treats disagreement as genuine cultural variation. Value/culture-neuron work (ValueExploration 2025; Culturescope 2025; Isolating Culture Neurons 2025) localizes value/culture representations but not a scalar refusal gate and does not connect to jailbreaks. Low-resource-language jailbreak work demonstrates the vulnerability behaviorally with no mechanistic account. The specific prior result that fails to answer our question is the single-refusal-direction finding: it identifies the gate's geometry but not that the query language sets its threshold. We rephrase the paper around that gap: a cross-lingual safety dissociation (shared harm vs language-set threshold) with a coverage-not-typology identification result and a steering fix, delivered as a benchmark plus confirmatory mechanistic analysis.
Abstract: Aligned language models refuse harmful requests, but the same model asked the identical borderline-harmful question in a low-resource language often complies. This is usually attributed either to genuine cross-cultural moral difference or, in the jailbreak literature, treated as an unexplained vulnerability. We give a unifying mechanistic account and, separately, motivate its societal stakes so importance does not rest on novelty: whichever way it resolves, the result tells multilingual safety teams whether the fix is better harm modeling or better per-language gating. Mechanistically we propose that multilingual LLMs compute a largely shared, language-agnostic assessment of a request's harmfulness but gate refusal through a scalar threshold whose default value is covertly set by the query language; cross-lingual refusal inconsistency then arises not because the model judges the request as less harmful in another language, but because the language shifts the threshold. We define the threshold operationally as the harm-severity crossover at which the model flips to refusing, and as the set-point of a recovered refusal-gating direction, distinguished from logit/readout bias by pre-registered patching criteria. We build BORDERLINE-MULTI, graded borderline-harmful requests spanning safety-relevant domains, rendered across 15+ languages spanning several scripts, families, and safety-alignment-coverage levels, with severity calibration and native-speaker annotation that prior multilingual safety benchmarks lack. Behaviorally we measure per-language refusal rates and a dose-response crossover over a harm-severity gradient. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared harm-assessment direction that transfers cross-lingually even where the model complies; (ii) use activation patching, against pre-registered 'harm-same vs threshold-differs' criteria, to localize the gap to the threshold; and (iii) recover a single refusal-threshold direction and steer it to close the cross-lingual safety gap without harming benign compliance. We make the coverage-vs-typology dissociation the central contribution and predict the shift tracks safety-alignment coverage, not typological distance. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset BORDERLINE-MULTI (constructed from existing public red-team resources): 150 base harmful intents from AdvBench/HarmBench (existing), each templated at 4 severity levels (clearly benign -> mildly sensitive -> clearly disallowed) = 600 graded items, plus 250 matched clearly-benign controls from XSTest (existing). New annotation/protocol contribution: each item carries a native-speaker-validated severity calibration (inter-annotator agreement reported) and a harm-status-stability flag marking items whose harm status is cross-culturally stable, which prior multilingual safety benchmarks do not provide. Rendered in 15 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families, and a spread of safety-alignment-coverage levels (machine translation + native-speaker validation + back-translation audit). Per-language safety-alignment-coverage proxy = benign-refusal false-positive rate on XSTest controls, pretraining resource share, and an alignment-data-availability estimate (multiple proxies reported). Translation-artifact controls: independent human translations, back-translation checks, language-internal paraphrases, and matched script/tokenization statistics, so cross-language differences are not wording/tokenization artifacts. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B-Instruct (a 70B variant added as a scale ablation), frozen, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds. Refusal vs compliance scored by a validated multilingual refusal classifier with human spot-checks on 5% of outputs. Pre-registration: before probing, we register the criteria for 'harm assessment same' (cross-lingual harm-probe transfer within 10 pp of in-language AND decoded harm on complied-with items correlated with true severity at Spearman >=0.6) vs 'threshold differs' (language-signal patch flip rate exceeds harm-patch flip rate by >=25 pp). Dual-use note: only borderline items already in public benchmarks are used, completions kept coarse (refuse-vs-comply plus short text), no novel operational harmful content released.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- the cross-lingual refusal gap and its crossover shift exist): Decisive metric: cross-language refusal-rate gap on identical disallowed items, and each language's crossover severity. Convincing result: max cross-language refusal gap on identical disallowed items >=20 pp AND a crossover shift of >=1 severity level between highest- and lowest-coverage languages, while benign controls agree (gap <=5 pp). Ablations: severity-construction variant, language family, and script are reported as covariates to rule out confounds. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = weak; <8 pp undercuts the account. Negative result (uniform refusal) refutes the phenomenon.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- CENTRAL: the shift tracks coverage, not typology): the central contribution, framed as an identification problem. Predictors: the safety-alignment-coverage proxies vs lang2vec typological+script distance to the dominant language. Decisive metric: Spearman(crossover-shift, coverage) vs Spearman(crossover-shift, typology), bootstrap CIs, with a mixed-effects model (random effects for base-intent and model); key contrast = a typologically distant but well-aligned language vs a close but poorly-aligned one. Convincing result: |Spearman with coverage| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with typology| by >=0.2, key-contrast pair ordered by coverage not distance, robust across the multiple coverage proxies. Indecision band: within 0.05-0.2 = mixed; coverage not stronger, or gap <0.05 = refuted. Negative result reassigns the effect to typology (itself informative for benchmark design).

Experiment 3 (H1 -- a shared harm-assessment representation, separable from the gate): train a linear probe/logit-lens to decode graded harm severity from hidden states on held-out dominant-language items; test transfer to low-coverage languages INCLUDING complied-with items. Decisive metric: cross-lingual harm-probe transfer accuracy. Convincing result (pre-registered): transfer within 10 pp of in-language AND decoded harm on complied-with low-coverage items correlates with true severity at Spearman >=0.6. Indecision band: 10-25 pp below = partially shared; >25 pp below favors genuine reassessment, refuting H1. 

Experiment 4 (H2 -- harm same, threshold differs, causal; direct comparison to prior mechanistic work): on identical items refused in language A and complied-with in B, (a) patch A's mid-layer harm-assessment representation into B and test whether refusal is restored; (b) patch A's late-layer language-identity/threshold signal into B. To distinguish the threshold from logit/readout bias, we also compare against directly editing the refusal logit (a readout-bias control) and against the monolingual refusal-direction of Arditi et al. re-extracted per language. Decisive metric: causal flip rate (comply -> refuse) under each intervention. Convincing result (pre-registered): harm-patch flips <=15% while the language/threshold-signal patch flips >=50% (gap >=25 pp), and the effect is not reproduced by pure logit editing at matched norm -- localizing the gap to the threshold, not readout bias. Indecision band: language-signal flip 25-50% = partial; harm-patch flip 15-30% = mixed. If harm-patching flips more, H2 is refuted.

Experiment 5 (H3 -- a single steerable refusal-threshold direction that shifts refusal on matched items): recover a refusal-threshold direction as the mean activation difference between refuse and comply runs pooled across languages; steer to (a) RAISE refusal in leaky low-coverage languages and (b) LOWER refusal in strict languages. Systems compared: steering vs translate-to-English-first vs an explicit safety-prompt baseline vs matched-norm random-direction steering (sham control). Decisive metrics (in order): cross-lingual refusal-gap reduction on held-out harmful items; a matched-item check that steering flips refuse-vs-comply on the SAME items (not merely changing verbosity/calibration), measured as per-item decision changes; benign over-refusal rate (specificity); fluency (perplexity); generalization to held-out domains. Convincing result: steering closes >=50% of the refusal gap on held-out harmful items, flips decisions on matched items (not verbosity), adds <=5 pp benign over-refusal and <5% perplexity, beats the sham control, and generalizes to held-out domains. Indecision band: 25-50% = partial; <25%, or benign over-refusal >10 pp, or effect matched by sham = not a clean single gate, refuting H3. Attack-success-rate reduction by language on truly-disallowed items is reported as the applied safety framing.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Dual-use hazard: the dataset touches harmful topics; we use only borderline/graded items already in public red-team benchmarks, keep completions coarse, release no novel operational content, and follow responsible-disclosure norms. 2. Probe decodability of harm-assessment may reflect the readout basis, not a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 4, with a logit-editing readout-bias control) and steering (Exp. 5, with a sham control and matched-item decision check) promote correlation to mechanism. 3. Some cross-lingual refusal differences may be GENUINE cultural/legal variation; the shared-harm-probe transfer and the pre-registered harm-same/threshold-differs criteria separate genuine reassessment from a gate shift, and we restrict the key analyses to items flagged cross-culturally harm-stable. 4. The coverage proxy is noisy and may correlate with resource level and typology; the dissociation (Exp. 2) uses carefully contrasted languages, multiple proxies, and mixed-effects modeling. 5. Strong models may refuse near-uniformly, shrinking the gap; even a small measurable gap plus the induction (lowering refusal) experiment yields causal evidence, and a 70B scale ablation plus multiple models give power/scale coverage. 6. Judging refusal vs compliance across languages is nontrivial; we use a validated multilingual classifier plus human spot-checks. 7. Translation/prompt-naturalness/tokenization could confound cross-language differences; independent human translations, back-translation audits, paraphrase controls, and reported tokenization statistics address this. 8. Steering may trade safety-gap closure for benign over-refusal; we report the full trade-off curve. 9. The societal importance (a translation-cheap jailbreak surface harming non-English users) holds regardless of which mechanistic account wins, so importance does not depend on the novelty claim. 10. Findings may be model-specific; three families plus a scale ablation address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: depth_budget_truncation
Title: Running Out of Layers: Cross-Lingual Errors as Truncated Concept Computation Under a Fixed Depth Budget
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs allocate the same fixed number of layers to every language, but low-resource and typologically distant languages require MORE layers to finish computing a concept; consequently their concept computation is frequently TRUNCATED by the fixed depth budget before it converges, and this truncation — not missing knowledge — causes a large fraction of cross-lingual errors. The required-depth deficit scales with typological/script distance and resource level, and errors are causally recoverable by granting extra late-layer compute (looping late layers) without any retraining.
Related Work: Probing work shows concepts become decodable at different depths depending on complexity ('Concept Depth' 2024) and that low-resource languages exhibit flatter, shallower layer-wise probing trends than high-resource ones (Cross-Language Probing 2024), and that difficulty is encoded language-agnostically early then language-specifically late ('Shared Geometry of Difficulty' 2026). Cross-Layer Transcoder and latent-language work localize a shared middle-layer space with lossy late-layer decoding (Tracing Multilingual Representations 2025; MALT 2025), and DAMA (2026) reports a U-shaped adaptability pattern in speech ASR. ALL of these are correlational (where a concept is decodable, how well probes align by layer) or propose fine-tuning/adaptation fixes. NONE reframes the layer-wise gap as a CAUSAL compute-deadline problem: that the fixed layer budget TRUNCATES an in-progress concept computation for languages that need more depth, that this truncation (not absent knowledge) is what produces the error, or that granting extra inference-time depth to just those items causally recovers the answer. We contribute this compute-budget-truncation reframing, a per-item 'required depth' measurement, a causal early-exit/late-layer-looping test, and a training-free depth-budget intervention. We separate a causal THEORY (the fixed depth budget truncates unfinished concept computation for depth-hungry languages, and truncation - not missing knowledge - causes the error) from an ENGINEERING intervention (late-layer looping). The primary novelty is the causal theory and its per-item required-depth estimand; the looping fix is a corollary probe reported with its costs. The boundary against Concept Depth and cross-language probing is sharp: those localize WHERE a concept becomes decodable but never causally attribute errors to insufficient depth. Unlike general reasoning-loop papers, the multilingual case supplies a natural, non-engineered source of variation in required depth (language distance) and a matched-item control (the same fact in a shallow-converging language).
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions far more reliably in high-resource, typologically close languages, and interpretability work has shown that concepts become decodable at different layer depths across languages. But this has been treated as a correlational fact about representation geometry. We propose a causal, resource-based reframing: transformers apply a fixed number of layers to every input, yet distant, low-resource languages need MORE layers to finish computing a concept, so their computation is often truncated by the depth budget before it converges — the model 'runs out of layers.' Under this view, many cross-lingual errors are not missing knowledge but unfinished computation. We measure, per item and per language, the 'required depth' at which the correct answer first stabilizes via logit-lens/early-exit trajectories, and define a Truncation Gap as the fraction of items whose answer converges only in layers deeper than the model has, or would if given more. We test three claims: (1) required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on identical facts, and the excess predicts errors; (2) errors on truncated items are causally distinguished from knowledge failures — early-exiting a high-resource run at the low-resource run's shallower effective depth reproduces the error, and, crucially, granting extra late-layer compute (looping the final transformer layers) at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth items; and (3) the required-depth deficit and recovery scale with typological/script distance and resource level. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA factual QA and MGSM reasoning across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work recasts the multilingual gap as a depth-budget truncation phenomenon with a cheap, training-free inference-time fix. Practically, adaptive per-item depth allocation trades a little extra late-layer compute for recovered low-resource accuracy - a favorable latency/compute tradeoff we quantify as accuracy gained per extra layer-pass and cost per recovered answer - so deployment teams could route only high-required-depth items to extra compute. We state expectations as preregistered effect-size ranges with confidence intervals rather than hard cutoffs, and validate on a translation task in addition to factual QA and reasoning.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Data (existing, used as is): parallel factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA-53 (1,000 facts present in all chosen languages) and multilingual grade-school math from MGSM (250 problems; its 10-11 languages for the reasoning arm), so the SAME item is posed in every language. Languages span Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. Models of differing depth (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference only, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B (32 layers), Aya-23-8B (32 layers), Qwen2-7B (28 layers). Layer-wise readout by logit lens and a tuned lens (the lens's affine map is the only trained parameter, per layer). Per-language typological/script distance from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Answer matching alias-aware, last-token/answer-span. 3 seeds (item sampling).

Experiment 1 (H1 - distant/low-resource languages need more layers for the same concept). Tests whether required depth is systematically greater for distant/low-resource languages on IDENTICAL facts. For each (item, language) record the CONVERGENCE DEPTH: the shallowest layer after which the top-ranked answer token becomes and stays correct through the final layer (stability judged over the last several layers). Decisive metric: mean convergence depth per language on the shared item set, compared across the resource/distance groups. Convincing: distant/low-resource languages have mean convergence depth deeper than close/high-resource ones by >= 3 layers on the same facts, consistently across models. Indecision band: 1-3 layers deeper; reported as a weak depth shift. Negative result: convergence depth not deeper for distant languages (< 1 layer) refutes H1.

Experiment 2 (H3 - required-depth deficit scales with distance and resource). Tests whether the depth deficit tracks typological/script distance and resource level. Define per-language mean required depth and the TRUNCATION GAP = fraction of items whose answer converges only in the last few layers or is still rising/unconverged at the final layer (right-censored). Correlate both with lang2vec distance and the resource proxy; designed contrast: a distant-but-well-covered language vs a close-but-sparse one to partly separate the axes. Decisive metric: Spearman of required depth / Truncation Gap with distance and with resource (95% CIs). Convincing: both correlate (Spearman >= 0.4) with distance and with resource. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4; reported as suggestive. Negative result: no correlation (< 0.2) refutes H3.

Experiment 3 (H2 - shallow budget causally reproduces the low-resource error). Tests whether truncation, not missing knowledge, causes the error. Take facts answered CORRECTLY in a high-resource language with convergence depth d_hi; force EARLY EXIT of the high-resource run at the shallower effective depth d_lo observed for a low-resource language and test whether the high-resource answer degrades to the low-resource-style error. Specificity: early-exiting at d_hi should not degrade. Model frozen; early exit via the tuned lens at inference. Decisive metric: degradation rate induced by early exit at d_lo (reported first), with the d_hi early-exit degradation as the specificity floor. Convincing: early exit at d_lo degrades >= 50% of previously-correct high-resource answers while early exit at d_hi degrades < 10%. Indecision band: 25-50% degradation at d_lo; reported as partial support for the budget account. Negative result: < 25% degradation (shallow budget alone does not reproduce the error) refutes the truncation-causes-error claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 - truncation-type vs knowledge-type errors dissociate). Tests the crucial separation between unfinished computation and absent knowledge. Partition low-resource errors into TRUNCATION-type (the fact is answered correctly in the high-resource language, so the knowledge exists; the low-resource error co-occurs with a late/unconverged trajectory) vs KNOWLEDGE-type (wrong in the high-resource language too). Model frozen. Decisive metric: the difference in late-layer-looping recovery (from Exp. 5) between truncation-type and knowledge-type errors; here we first establish the partition sizes and that trajectory lateness predicts truncation-type membership. Convincing: truncation-type errors are a substantial share (>= 30% of low-resource errors) and are marked by significantly later/unconverged trajectories than knowledge-type errors. Indecision band: truncation-type 15-30%; reported as a smaller-than-claimed contribution. Negative result: truncation-type < 15% or trajectory lateness not distinguishing the two types refutes the truncation-vs-knowledge dissociation central to H2.

Experiment 5 (H4 - extra late-layer compute recovers truncated answers, training-free). Tests whether granting extra depth by LOOPING the final k transformer layers at inference recovers correct answers specifically on high-required-depth (truncation-type) items. Feed the last block's residual stream back through the last k blocks one or more times on the low-resource/distant run; dose-response over loop iterations and over k (last-1 vs last-k). Model frozen; no weights changed. Compare against a naive "add CoT tokens" baseline, translate-to-English, and a control that loops RANDOM blocks. Decisive metric: accuracy gain on high-Truncation-Gap items (reported first), split by error type, with output-language fidelity, fluency (perplexity), and specificity (already-converged items unchanged) alongside. Convincing: late-layer looping recovers >= 15 pp on truncation-type items, near-zero (< 5 pp) on knowledge-type items and on already-converged items, exceeds the random-block control, with a coherent dose-response and < 5% perplexity change. Indecision band: 5-15 pp recovery on truncation-type items, or recovery not concentrated on them; reported as a weak/ambiguous fix, while Exp. 1-4 (correlational required-depth + causal early-exit) still stand. Negative result: < 5 pp recovery or looping helping knowledge-type/converged items equally (i.e., generic corruption/help) refutes H4.

Computation-vs-rescoring controls and translation task. To test whether looping recovers answers via deeper COMPUTATION rather than mere answer-token re-scoring, Experiment 5 adds (i) a MATCHED-DEPTH RECOMPUTATION control (tuned-lens continuation for the same number of extra passes) and (ii) a logit-renormalization/temperature control that re-ranks final logits without extra computation; recovery must exceed both and the random-block control. We add a multilingual TRANSLATION subset (FLORES-200 sentence pairs) so the depth-budget account is tested on a generation task, and we validate required-depth measurements with a tuned lens plus a hidden-state perturbation test, defining required depth via a stability (not first-crossing) criterion with right-censoring for non-converging trajectories. All hard thresholds are reported as preregistered effect-size ranges with confidence intervals.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens convergence depth can reflect the readout basis rather than genuine computation state; we validate with a tuned lens and require the causal early-exit (Exp. 5) and late-layer-looping (Exp. 6) results to promote the depth measurement to a functional claim. 2. Late-layer looping is an untied-weights hack the model was not trained for and may simply corrupt representations rather than 'continue' computation; we mitigate by reporting dose-response, specificity (already-converged items must be unharmed), and by comparing looping the last block vs random blocks; if looping helps only on high-required-depth truncation-type items and not on knowledge-type or converged items, that pattern is strong evidence regardless of the hack's crudeness. A negative looping result still leaves the correlational required-depth + causal early-exit findings intact. 3. Truncation and knowledge failure are entangled; the high-resource-language knowledge control (Exp. 7) is the crucial dissociator and central to the claim. 4. Distance and resource level are correlated; the dissociating language contrasts (Exp. 4) only partly separate them, and we report multiple resource proxies. 5. Right-censored (unconverged) trajectories are hard to distinguish from noise; we use stability criteria over the last several layers and report robustness to the convergence definition. 6. Answer matching across scripts is noisy; we use alias-aware, last-token/answer-span matching and report tokenization statistics. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families of differing depth address but do not exhaust generality, and the model-depth ablation directly tests the budget interpretation.

Name: thematic_role_cue_dominance
Title: Who Did What to Whom, in Which Language? How Multilingual LLMs Lazily Impose Their Dominant Language's Word-Order Cue When Assigning Agent and Patient
Short Hypothesis: Human languages weight cues to thematic roles differently: some are word-order-dominant (English), others rely primarily on case marking (Russian, Hindi, Turkish, German) or voice (Tagalog). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-agnostic agent/patient (who-did-what-to-whom) representation, but that when a sentence's cues conflict it lazily applies its DOMINANT language's word-order-first cue hierarchy rather than the target language's, producing systematic agent/patient REVERSALS precisely in case-/voice-dominant languages when the reliable cue (case/voice) contradicts a non-canonical word order. We predict (a) reversal rate scales with the target language's reliance on non-word-order cues (its cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language), not with resource level; (b) a small, causally-manipulable 'role-binding' representation carries the assigned agent/patient; and (c) steering a recovered role direction repairs (or induces) reversals without changing propositional content.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows LLMs extract thematic roles mainly through a few attention heads, with role information weakly present in representations relative to humans (Do LLMs Know Who Did What to Whom, 2025), and that English models recruit word order in later layers to override lexical cues in non-prototypical sentences (BERT word order, 2022; Position-Role Mappings, 2022). Multilingual probing shows mBERT encodes morphosyntactic alignment/subjecthood continuously (Deep Subjecthood, 2021) and shares some syntactic subspaces (Universal Grammatical Relations, 2020), though grammatical transfer is limited and language-specific (Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer, 2020; Blackbird 2024). Cognitive science establishes a universal agent-first bias and the Competition Model's language-specific cue hierarchy (word order vs. case vs. animacy vs. voice) that determines role assignment (MacWhinney; agent-first 2019; Tagalog acquisition 2018-2019; agent-preference ERP 2023). However, ALL interpretability work on roles is either monolingual-English or studies static-encoder representations; NONE tests whether a multilingual GENERATIVE LLM covertly imports its dominant language's CUE HIERARCHY into other languages, causing role reversals when a reliable non-word-order cue conflicts with word order, nor gives a causal, steerable role-binding locus. We uniquely port the Competition Model cue-hierarchy conflict into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, with a causal account and a training-free fix. Primary contribution (chosen): the causal role-binding locus and its lazy import of the dominant language's word-order-first cue hierarchy; the reversal phenomenon and steerable repair are supporting. This differs from multilingual syntax probing and Competition-Model psycholinguistics by testing, inside a generative LLM, whether one language's CUE HIERARCHY is causally imposed on another under cue conflict. Beneficiaries: multilingual eval builders, model auditors, translation researchers, and psycholinguists; the deployment implication is to stress-test morphologically rich languages rather than trust English-centric transfer. If reversals prove rare but patching/steering still control role assignment, the result stands as a mechanistic diagnostic of role representation; if reversals occur but are untied to the dominant hierarchy, the import claim is rejected.
Abstract: Understanding a sentence requires deciding who acted on whom. Languages solve this with different, sometimes conflicting cues: English relies on word order (the first noun is the agent), while Russian, Hindi, Turkish, and German rely on case marking and Tagalog on voice, so that a non-canonical word order does not change the agent. When these cues conflict, each language has a reliable arbiter. We ask whether multilingual LLMs, whose dominant pretraining language is word-order-based, covertly import a word-order-first cue hierarchy into other languages and thereby reverse agent and patient exactly when a case-/voice-dominant language marks a non-canonical order. We build ROLE-CONFLICT, a controlled set of reversible transitive sentences crossing word order (canonical vs. scrambled), the reliable cue (case/voice present vs. absent), and animacy, rendered across word-order-dominant, case-dominant, and voice-dominant languages, each with a question probing who the agent is. Behaviorally we measure per-language reversal rate under cue conflict. Mechanistically we (i) probe for an abstract agent/patient direction shared across languages, (ii) use activation patching to localize a compact role-binding representation whose swap flips the assigned roles without changing the event or entities, and (iii) steer a recovered role direction to repair or induce reversals. We predict reversal rate tracks a language's cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language rather than its resource level, that some attention heads implement cue arbitration, and that steering repairs reversals without harming fluency, outperforming explicit-instruction and translate-to-English baselines. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. Falsifiable core in one sentence: under cue conflict, case-/voice-dominant languages inherit the dominant language's word-order-first agent assignment - rejected if reversal rate does not exceed the canonical-order control or if it tracks resource rather than cue-hierarchy distance. We control against generic parsing difficulty with matched scrambled/canonical minimal pairs of identical token length and monolingual target-language baselines, and separate a shared abstract role representation from a surface word-order heuristic via the position-probe contrast.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "dominant language" is operationalized per model as its highest-resource pretraining language (English), which is word-order-based. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by item, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); role assignments elicited under greedy decoding. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "reversible transitive" = a sentence whose two animate participants could each plausibly be the agent, so lexical plausibility does not decide roles. Dataset (ROLE-CONFLICT, constructed): reversible transitive events (e.g. "the doctor"/"the lawyer" + verb) in a factorial set crossing (a) WORD ORDER canonical vs non-canonical/scrambled; (b) RELIABLE CUE present vs neutralized (overt case marking or voice morphology unambiguously assigning roles, vs absent/ambiguous); (c) ANIMACY both-animate (maximally reversible) vs animate-inanimate control. Rendered across WORD-ORDER-DOMINANT (English, Chinese, Indonesian), CASE-DOMINANT (Russian, German, Hindi, Turkish, Finnish), and VOICE-DOMINANT (Tagalog, plus a symmetrical-voice control) languages, each with a probe question ("Who did the [action]?" / "Who was affected?"). We build ~200 events x the factorial cells x these languages; native speakers validate the correct agent per item (kept above 0.7 agreement) and a per-language cue-hierarchy index (reliance on non-word-order cues). Fewer than an exhaustive set because each cell needs grammatical construction and native validation.

Experiment 1 (H-behavior - the dominant word-order cue is lazily imposed, reversing roles under cue conflict): Tests whether case-/voice-dominant languages suffer agent/patient reversals when a reliable non-word-order cue contradicts a non-canonical word order. Data: the KEY cue-conflict cell (non-canonical order WITH a reliable case/voice cue assigning the agent to the later noun), plus canonical-order and animate-inanimate controls. Systems compared: English query, translate-to-English-first, per-language judgments. Decisive metric: REVERSAL RATE = fraction where the model picks the word-order-implied (first) noun as agent, contradicting the reliable cue; secondary: accuracy in the canonical and animate-inanimate controls (should be high everywhere). Convincing result: reversal rate in the cue-conflict cell exceeds the canonical-order control by >=15 pp specifically in case-/voice-dominant languages, averaged over models. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp excess is reported per language rather than as a global claim. Negative result: reversal within 5 pp of the canonical control means the model respects the target-language cue and the behavioral claim fails.

Experiment 2 (H-a - reversal rate tracks cue-hierarchy distance, not resource): Tests the dissociation. Data: per-language reversal rate vs the cue-hierarchy index and a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy); key contrast a lower-resource strongly-case-marking language (Turkish/Finnish) vs a higher-resource word-order language. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of reversal rate with cue-hierarchy distance from the dominant language controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for cue-hierarchy. Convincing result: partial correlation with cue-hierarchy distance >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: cue-hierarchy correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: reversals track resource (|rho| >=0.4) not cue-hierarchy, refuting claim (a).

Experiment 3 (H-shared - a shared agent/patient representation distinct from surface position): Tests whether the assigned agent is decodable and transfers across languages, beyond raw word position. Data: hidden states on held-out items. One probe decodes which entity is the assigned agent; a surface-position probe decodes which noun is first; the role probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: role probe, surface-position probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language role-probe transfer accuracy minus control; secondary: the role-vs-position dissociation. Convincing result: transfer accuracy >=15 pp above control and role is decodable beyond surface position. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: transfer within 5 pp of control means no shared role representation, weakening the hypothesis. Decodability is not use; Exp. 4 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 4 (H-b - a compact, causally-manipulable role-binding representation): Tests whether a small component carries the assigned roles and flips them without changing the event or entities. Data: for a cue-conflict item, runs under context/framing forcing agent=X vs agent=Y, yielding different answers. Activation patching transfers mid/late-layer components from one run into the other; attention-head attribution tests whether specific heads read case/voice morphology vs position. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control; overlap of the role-binding direction with generic subject/first-position directions (separability check). Decisive metric: role-flip rate (assigned agent switches) minus control, with event and entities preserved; secondary: identification of cue-arbitration heads and role-direction overlap with position directions (should be low). Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp flip indicates a distributed representation; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp flip means role-binding is not causally locatable and claim (b) fails.

Experiment 5 (H-c - steering repairs and induces reversals without changing content): Tests the training-free causal fix and induction. Data: reversals in case-/voice-dominant languages (repair); correctly-assigned items (induction); canonical-order and non-role items (specificity). Role direction = mean activation difference between agent=X and agent=Y runs, pooled across languages, at the Exp. 4 layer. Systems compared: steering vs explicit-instruction prompting ("the case marker, not word order, determines the agent") vs translate-to-English. Decisive metric: repair rate (fraction of reversals corrected to the cue-correct agent) minus baseline; secondary: induction rate, agent-assignment accuracy, content preservation, specificity (canonical-order and non-role items unchanged), fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: repair rate >=15 pp over baseline with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline; induction confirms functional causality. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair, or specificity change 5-10 pp, indicates a weak/leaky fix. Negative result: <5 pp repair means the role direction is not functionally causal, refuting claim (c). Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; adjacent vs long-distance argument scrambling; whether the imposed hierarchy is always the dominant word-order language or the nearest high-resource language; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: reversal rate, agent-assignment accuracy, probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with cue-hierarchy vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of the assigned agent may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 5) to establish functional relevance, and contrast against a surface-position probe. 2. Some case-/voice-dominant languages permit multiple acceptable readings or have optional case marking, making 'reversal' genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items where the reliable cue unambiguously fixes the agent, and treat optional-marking cases separately. 3. Reversals could be confounded with degraded fluency/parsing of scrambled sentences rather than a cue-hierarchy import; the canonical-order and animate-inanimate controls, plus the requirement that the reliable cue is clearly present, isolate cue arbitration from mere degradation. 4. Strong models may respect case/voice well, making reversals rare; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely cue-faithful role system) is an informative positive result, and the voice-dominant and long-distance-scramble conditions plus induction experiments still yield causal findings; multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of case/voice morphology varies across scripts and can split affixes unevenly; we use pooled-span or noun-final token representations and report tokenization statistics; case vs. voice vs. word-order cases analyzed separately. 6. The cue-hierarchy-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to index operationalization and alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade role correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: paraphrase_controlled_inconsistency
Title: Is Cross-Lingual Inconsistency Special? Using Within-Language Paraphrase Variation to Isolate the Language-Transition Component of Multilingual Factual Instability
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual factual inconsistency has two additive components: a language-agnostic instability that also causes a model to answer differently across paraphrases of the SAME language, and a genuinely language-specific instability introduced at the late-layer language-transition stage. We hypothesize (a) that a large, previously-unmeasured fraction of what is reported as 'cross-lingual inconsistency' is actually this baseline paraphrase instability rather than anything language-specific; (b) that the residual, language-specific component is causally localized to a distinct late-layer transition locus separable from the mid-layer concept computation; and (c) the size of the residual (not the total) is what scales with script/typological distance, while the paraphrase-baseline component does not.
Related Work: A wave of recent work attributes cross-lingual factual inconsistency to a late-layer 'language transition' failure over a shared concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), and proposes fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubSub/SubInj, steering to a shared space). Separately, LLMs are known to be highly unstable to meaning-preserving surface changes WITHIN a language (Prompt-Format Sensitivity 2023; RoParQ 2025). Crucially, ALL cross-lingual consistency work compares one prompt per language and implicitly treats every observed disagreement as language-caused, never subtracting the model's baseline within-language paraphrase instability. No prior work measures the paraphrase-controlled residual, tests whether the celebrated 'language-transition' locus explains the residual specifically (rather than total inconsistency), or checks whether existing fixes reduce the residual or merely the paraphrase-baseline. We contribute this decomposition, a causal locus test on the residual, and a re-evaluation of prior interventions against the correct baseline. Our three pieces, ranked: (1) primary - a measurement correction showing a large share of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline within-language paraphrase instability; (2) a differential-localization result relocating the language-specific RESIDUAL, not total inconsistency, to a late-layer transition; (3) a re-evaluation of published fixes against the corrected baseline. We frame (2) as a differential-localization hypothesis rather than a strong single-locus causal claim.
Abstract: Multilingual language models give different factual answers to the same question asked in different languages, and a growing literature explains this via a late-layer 'language transition' over a shared, language-agnostic concept space. But these studies compare a single prompt per language and treat every disagreement as language-caused, ignoring that the same models also answer inconsistently across meaning-preserving paraphrases within a single language. We ask a sharp question: once we subtract this baseline paraphrase instability, how much cross-lingual inconsistency is genuinely language-specific, and is the language-transition mechanism responsible for that residual rather than for the total? We introduce a paraphrase-controlled decomposition: for each fact we measure within-language answer variability across multiple paraphrases in each language, and define the language-specific residual as cross-lingual disagreement in excess of the pooled within-language baseline. Behaviorally, we predict a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline paraphrase noise, and that only the residual scales with script/typological distance. Mechanistically, we test whether the late-layer transition locus (via logit-lens and activation patching) causally explains the residual specifically: patching mid-layer concept representations should fix paraphrase-baseline errors in any language, whereas the residual should require correcting the late-layer transition. Finally we re-evaluate published fixes (linear shortcut, translation-difference vectors, SubInj) against the correct baseline, testing whether they reduce the language-specific residual or merely the paraphrase-agnostic component. Experiments span mLAMA/BMLAMA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B, sharpening what is and is not special about cross-lingual factual instability. Formally, for a fact f and language l we define within-language instability as the answer-disagreement rate across K paraphrases, and the language-specific residual as cross-lingual disagreement across paraphrase-matched prompts minus the pooled within-language baseline; we test whether this decomposition is additive versus interaction-heavy with a hierarchical variance decomposition across fact, language, and paraphrase, so the residual is a well-identified estimand rather than a relabeling. The consequence is concrete: if total inconsistency is the wrong metric, multilingual QA leaderboards, model-release consistency claims, and factuality/safety audits should report the paraphrase-controlled residual, and practitioners should stop attributing paraphrase noise to language-specific failure.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Data (existing, adapted): factual QA from mLAMA/BMLAMA (parallel templated facts; BMLAMA-53 supplies parallel items across 53 languages). Use 1,000 facts that exist in all chosen 15+ languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Perso-Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels. For each fact in each language, generate K=5 meaning-preserving paraphrase templates, validated by back-translation and native-speaker spot checks; low-agreement paraphrases dropped and reported. This yields both within-language (across the 5 paraphrases) and cross-language variants for every fact. Per-language typological/script distance to the dominant language (English) from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + light patching, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. Answer matching is alias-aware with answer-span normalization. 3 seeds (paraphrase sampling).

Experiment 1 (claim-a - how much cross-lingual inconsistency is really paraphrase baseline). Tests whether a large fraction of reported cross-lingual inconsistency is baseline within-language paraphrase instability. For each fact compute: (a) WITHIN-LANGUAGE instability = answer-disagreement rate across the 5 paraphrases within each language, averaged over languages; (b) TOTAL cross-lingual inconsistency = disagreement across languages using one canonical prompt each (matching prior single-prompt protocols); (c) LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC RESIDUAL = cross-lingual disagreement across paraphrase-matched prompts minus the pooled within-language baseline. Decisive metric: the fraction of total inconsistency attributable to the paraphrase baseline vs the residual, per model. Convincing: the paraphrase baseline accounts for >= 30% of what the single-prompt protocol reports as cross-lingual inconsistency, in all three models, establishing that a substantial share is not language-specific. Indecision band: 15-30%; reported as a non-trivial but modest overcount. Negative result: baseline < 15% of total (cross-lingual inconsistency is overwhelmingly language-specific) refutes claim (a) - itself a clean, publishable vindication of the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline.

Experiment 2 (claim-c - only the residual scales with distance). Tests whether the language-specific residual, not the paraphrase baseline, tracks script/typological distance. Correlate each of (i) total inconsistency, (ii) paraphrase baseline, and (iii) residual with lang2vec typological/script distance to English. Decisive metric: Spearman of the residual with distance vs Spearman of the paraphrase baseline with distance (95% CIs). Convincing: the residual correlates with distance (Spearman >= 0.4) while the paraphrase baseline does not (|Spearman| < 0.2), and the total's apparent distance-dependence is driven by the residual. Indecision band: residual Spearman 0.2-0.4, or the baseline also correlating (0.2-0.4); reported as partial separation. Negative result: the paraphrase baseline correlating with distance as strongly as the residual, or the residual not correlating at all, refutes claim (c).

Experiment 3 (claim-b - concept vs late-layer transition locus by error type). Tests whether paraphrase-baseline errors are fixable at the mid-layer concept stage (any language) while the language-specific residual specifically requires correcting the late-layer transition. Replicate the mid-layer-concept / late-layer-transition split via logit lens per model first. For PARAPHRASE-BASELINE errors (a fact correct under one paraphrase, wrong under another, same language), patch the mid-layer concept representation from the correct run into the wrong run and measure recovery. For RESIDUAL (language-specific) errors, test whether mid-layer concept patching alone recovers the answer or whether correcting the late-layer transition (a translation-difference / language-transition vector) is additionally required. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: recovery rate by error type and patch type. Convincing: paraphrase-baseline errors recover >= 50% from mid-layer concept patching regardless of language, while residual errors recover < 20% from concept patching alone but >= 50% once the late-layer transition is corrected. Indecision band: residual concept-patch recovery 20-40%; reported as a partially-shared locus. Negative result: residual errors recovering from mid-layer concept patching as well as baseline errors refutes the distinct-late-locus claim (b).

Experiment 4 (claim-b - locus separability). Tests that the components fixing paraphrase-baseline errors and those fixing residual errors are distinct. Quantify overlap (Jaccard) over the identified layers/heads/directions whose patching fixes each error type. Model frozen. Decisive metric: Jaccard overlap between the baseline-fixing and residual-fixing component sets. Convincing: Jaccard <= 0.3 (largely disjoint), with the residual-fixing set concentrated in later layers than the baseline-fixing set. Indecision band: Jaccard 0.3-0.5; reported as partial separability. Negative result: Jaccard > 0.5 (the same components fix both) refutes the separability claim.

Experiment 5 (claim-b - prior fixes act on the residual, corroborating the transition locus). Tests whether published cross-lingual-consistency fixes reduce the language-specific residual (as a language-transition intervention should) rather than merely the paraphrase baseline. Apply, faithfully re-implemented, the linear-shortcut (bypassing final layers), the translation-difference vector, and the English-subject-injection (SubInj) fixes; measure each fix's effect separately on the paraphrase baseline and on the residual. Model frozen except as each fix prescribes. Decisive metric: per-fix reduction of the residual vs reduction of the paraphrase baseline (percentage points). Convincing: at least one late-layer-targeted fix reduces the residual by >= 10 pp while leaving the paraphrase baseline largely unchanged (< 5 pp), showing the residual is the genuinely language-transition-addressable component. Indecision band: residual reduction 5-10 pp or comparable reduction of both components; reported as a general-robustness rather than transition-specific effect. Negative result: fixes reducing only the paraphrase baseline and not the residual would indicate they do not address a language-specific transition, qualifying claim (b).

Paraphrase quality and added controls. Beyond back-translation and native-speaker spot checks, a stratified subset receives bilingual human validation and automatic semantic-equivalence scoring, with robustness reported to K and to paraphrase-quality filtering. We include multiple canonical prompts per language (not one), a translationese-vs-native paraphrase comparison, prompt-length and format matching, uncertainty intervals on every rate, and significance tests for all thresholded claims. The additivity of the decomposition is tested explicitly with a hierarchical (fact x language x paraphrase) variance model / ANOVA-style analysis reported alongside the point estimates.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Paraphrase quality across languages is uneven; low-quality paraphrases could inflate the within-language baseline and understate the residual. We validate paraphrases via back-translation and native-speaker checks and report sensitivity to K and to paraphrase-quality filtering. 2. Answer matching across languages/scripts is noisy (aliases, transliterations); we use alias-aware matching and last-token/answer-span normalization and report robustness. 3. It is possible the paraphrase baseline is small and cross-lingual inconsistency IS mostly language-specific; this would refute claim (a) but is itself a valuable, publishable clarification that legitimizes the language-transition narrative on the correct baseline. 4. Logit-lens/patching localization may be diffuse; we report degree of localization honestly and require the recovery-by-error-type contrast (Exp. 4) rather than mere layer identification. 5. The concept-vs-transition split may not be crisp in all models; we validate it per model before the locus test. 6. Prior fixes may interact with our paraphrase set differently than their original setups; we replicate them faithfully and report both baseline and residual effects. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: pragmatic_implicature_gate
Title: Some Means Not All, In Some Languages: A Causal Study of a Language-Set Literal-vs-Implicated Interpretation Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an utterance's LITERAL meaning, but decide how strongly to enrich it with a PRAGMATIC implicature (e.g. 'some' -> 'not all'; an indirect request -> a command) via a language-conditioned 'implicature-strength' control. We deliberately state the mechanistic claim as a FAMILY of hypotheses of decreasing strength -- a single steerable direction, a low-rank subspace, or a distributed but localizable circuit -- so the contribution survives if the strict single-scalar version fails. Consequently the identical utterance is interpreted more literally in one language and more pragmatically in another; this gap scales with the query language's documented cross-linguistic implicature-rate (and typological distance) rather than resource level; and the control is separable from the literal-meaning computation. We soften 'literal meaning computed identically' to an operational criterion: cross-lingual transferability/invariance of a literal-meaning probe within a tolerance.
Related Work: Explicit novelty claims: (N1, problem) the query language covertly sets a literal-vs-pragmatic interpretation strength -- untested cross-lingually; (N2, finding) identical utterances get systematically different enrichment by language, tracking implicature typology not resource; (N3, mechanism) a separable, localizable implicature-strength control (direction/subspace/circuit) distinct from literal meaning; (N4, dataset) PRAG-GATE, a released multilingual literal-vs-implicated benchmark; (N5, safety) an indirect-phrasing compliance gap. Positioning against the closest mechanistic neighbors: multilingual refusal-direction work localizes a refusal gate but not a pragmatic-enrichment control and never addresses implicature; shared-concept-space work (Semantic Hub 2024; From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025) shows late-layer language decoding over shared content but not a language-set interpretation-strength step. What only our gate hypothesis explains: why the SAME literal content yields different enriched readings purely as a function of query language, with a steerable control. Existing multilingual pragmatics resources are behavioral and monolingual-scored (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020; Pragmatic Inference of Scalar Implicature by LLMs 2024; Korean Indirect Speech Acts 2025; Partially Primed 2023; RSA, Goodman & Frank 2013) and lack matched cross-lingual literal-vs-enriched item pairs with the controls needed to answer the causal question -- which is why PRAG-GATE is required. Cross-linguistic pragmatics establishes divergent implicature rates and L1-to-L2 bias inheritance (Scalar Diversity and L2 Processing 2025). A non-obvious ALTERNATIVE theory we explicitly test against the gate account: the differences are language-specific instruction-following priors or translation artifacts, not a genuine interpretation-strength gate.
Abstract: When someone says 'some of the students passed', listeners often infer 'not all' - a scalar implicature. Languages differ measurably in how readily their speakers compute such enrichments, and L2 speakers inherit L1 pragmatic biases. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit language-specific pragmatics, and whether the query language covertly sets how literally versus pragmatically the model interprets an utterance. We hypothesize a shared, language-agnostic literal meaning enriched via a language-conditioned implicature-strength control, and -- to avoid over-committing -- frame the mechanism as a family of hypotheses (single direction, low-rank subspace, or localizable distributed circuit). We build and will RELEASE PRAG-GATE, a controlled set spanning scalar implicatures ('some','most','or','try'), indirect requests, and indirect answers/refusals, each rendered across 12+ languages with documented divergent implicature rates and paired with a question distinguishing the literal from the enriched interpretation, with a rigorous literal-vs-enriched annotation protocol (native-speaker labels, agreement thresholds, exclusion of ambiguous items) and translation controls (independent human translations, back-translation, language-internal paraphrases). Behaviorally we measure per-language implicature rate on identical utterances and test the gate account against two alternatives -- language-specific instruction-following priors and translation artifacts -- using translate-to-English/round-trip and monolingual paraphrase controls. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared literal-meaning representation transferable across languages within a tolerance, (ii) use activation patching, causal mediation, and subspace interventions (with random-direction sham and layerwise-robustness controls) to test that the literal meaning is shared while a separable enrichment control differs, and (iii) steer the control up/down without changing literal content. A safety subset (indirect harmful requests, indirect refusals) is evaluated with a specified refusal taxonomy and coarse scoring, measuring a cross-lingual indirect-phrasing compliance gap without overclaiming broad jailbreak impact. Either outcome is informative for multilingual evaluation, alignment, and deployment. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset PRAG-GATE (constructed, to be released) in three pragmatic categories: (a) SCALAR ('some','most','or','might','try') with a follow-up question / NLI hypothesis distinguishing literal ('some' -> possibly all) from enriched ('some' -> not all); (b) INDIRECT REQUESTS ('Can you pass the salt?', 'It's cold in here'); (c) INDIRECT ANSWERS/REFUSALS ('Are you coming? -- I have to work'). ~150 base items/category with matched clearly-literal and clearly-direct controls; per-item literal-vs-enriched gold labels from native speakers with reported inter-annotator agreement and ambiguous-item exclusion. Rendered in 12+ languages with documented divergent implicature rates, 4+ families/scripts, via independent human translation + back-translation audit + language-internal paraphrases. Expected per-language implicature rates are grounded in cross-linguistic scalar-diversity data; a per-language implicature-typology distance and multiple resource proxies are pre-registered. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, 3 paraphrase seeds. Controls throughout for language-ID effects, decoding/prompt-format, tokenization length, instruction-tuning distribution, and answer-matching artifacts; pooled/clause-final representations, tokenization statistics reported. Power: item counts set so a 20 pp cross-language rate gap and Spearman >=0.5 are detectable at 80% power; all metrics report bootstrap CIs.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- a language-set literal-vs-implicated gate, behavioral, vs alternatives): Decisive metric: per-language IMPLICATURE RATE on identical utterances and cross-language disagreement on the same item; literal/direct controls should agree across languages (gap <=5 pp). Alternative-theory tests: translate-to-English and round-trip conditions and monolingual paraphrase controls distinguish a genuine query-language interpretation gate from language-specific instruction-following priors or translation artifacts (if the effect disappears under round-trip/paraphrase matching, it is an artifact). Convincing result: cross-language implicature-rate gap on identical items >=20 pp while controls agree AND the gap survives the round-trip/paraphrase controls. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = weak; <8 pp, or gap removed by controls = no language-set gate / artifact, refuting H2.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap tracks implicature-typology, not resource): Predictors: pre-registered per-language implicature-typology distance vs multiple resource proxies. Decisive metric: Spearman(per-language implicature-rate deviation, typology) vs Spearman(deviation, resource), bootstrap CIs, mixed-effects across models; key contrast = a lower-resource high-rate language vs a higher-resource low-rate one. Convincing result: |Spearman with typology| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2; if the language count is too small for a robust correlation we report it as correlational and tone down causal language. Indecision band: within 0.05-0.2 = mixed; typology not stronger = refuted.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared literal meaning, causal late gate; multiple mechanistic tests): (a) train probes/logit-lens at each layer to decode the LITERAL truth-conditional content, test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others) -- the operational criterion for 'shared' is transfer within a tolerance (within 10 pp of in-language), NOT identity -- contrasted with a probe decoding the enriched reading; (b) activation-patch the mid-layer literal-meaning representation across runs; (c) causal MEDIATION analysis and SUBSPACE interventions on the late pragmatic-decision components, with layerwise-robustness checks and a random-direction sham control. Decisive metrics: literal-meaning probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy; rate at which patching the literal representation flips interpretation vs rate at which manipulating the late gate flips it, each above the sham. Convincing result: literal-meaning probe transfers within 10 pp of in-language while the enriched-reading probe varies by language; patching the literal representation flips interpretation in <=15% of cases while manipulating the late gate flips it in >=40%, above sham -- localizing the effect to a language-set gate; the mechanism is reported at whichever level of the hypothesis family (direction/subspace/circuit) the interventions support. Indecision band: late-gate flip 20-40% = partial; literal-probe transfer >25 pp below, literal-patch flipping >30%, or sham matching = literal meaning not shared, refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable implicature-strength control, with a scoped safety demonstration): recover an implicature-strength direction/subspace (difference between enriched- and literal-reading runs pooled across languages); steer to (a) INDUCE enrichment in a low-rate language, (b) SUPPRESS it in a high-rate language, (c) dose-response. Systems compared: steering vs explicit prompting ('interpret pragmatically') vs translate-first vs matched-norm random-direction steer (sham). Safety subset: indirect harmful requests and indirect refusals from public red-team resources, scored with a specified refusal taxonomy (refuse / comply / partial) and coarse outputs; no novel operational content released; responsible disclosure. Decisive metrics (in order): induced/suppressed implicature rate; literal-content preservation (specificity, decoded literal meaning unchanged >=95%); fluency (perplexity); and, on the safety subset, the cross-lingual compliance gap on indirect harmful requests and its reduction when the gate is steered up. Convincing result: steering changes implicature rate by >=20 pp in the intended direction with literal content preserved and fluency unharmed, beats the sham, and steering the gate up raises refusal of implied harmful intent in under-enriching languages. Indecision band: 8-20 pp = partial; <8 pp, literal content altered (>5%), or sham matches = not a clean separable control, refuting H3. We frame the safety result as a scoped, coarse demonstration, not broad jailbreak generality.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of 'literal meaning' or 'implicature-strength' may reflect the readout basis; causal patching, mediation, and subspace interventions (Exp. 3) and steering (Exp. 4) with random-direction sham and layerwise-robustness controls, plus the literal-content specificity check, promote correlation to mechanism, and we report the mechanism only at the level (direction/subspace/circuit) the evidence supports. 2. Whether an utterance is 'enriched' is gradient and context-dependent; we restrict to high-agreement items with a rigorous native-speaker annotation protocol and clear literal/direct controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might be genuine pragmatic-norm variation, language-specific instruction-following priors, or translation artifacts rather than a gate; the shared-literal-probe transfer, the literal-same/gate-differs patching, and the round-trip/paraphrase controls (Exp. 1) are designed to separate these. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on language contrasts; we pre-register distance and multiple resource proxies, use mixed-effects modeling, and tone down causal language if the language count is small. 5. Strong models may compute implicatures faithfully per language, shrinking the effect; documenting faithful language-specific pragmatics is still positive, and the induction/suppression steering yields causal evidence. 6. The safety subset touches harmful topics; only borderline public red-team items, coarse refuse/comply scoring with a specified taxonomy, no novel operational content, responsible disclosure, and we avoid overclaiming broad jailbreak relevance from a small demonstration. 7. Tokenization differs across scripts; pooled/clause-final representations and reported tokenization statistics address this. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency/literal preservation; we report all three. 9. 'Computed identically' is operationalized as transferability/invariance within a tolerance, not literal identity. 10. Either outcome is informative for multilingual evaluation, alignment, and deployment; PRAG-GATE and analysis tools will be released. 11. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: language_set_effort_budget
Title: How Hard Is This, in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Effort-Budget That Mis-Allocates Reasoning Length in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: One-sentence novelty: unlike prior work on multilingual overthinking, latent English reasoning pathways, or monolingual stopping, we claim a SEPARABLE mechanism -- a shared, language-agnostic difficulty estimate versus a language-conditioned reasoning EFFORT BUDGET (a stopping/length controller) -- and show the budget is causally steerable. Concretely, multilingual LLMs carry a shared estimate of a problem's intrinsic difficulty but set how many chain-of-thought steps to spend (when to stop) via a language-conditioned scalar only loosely tied to true difficulty, so for a problem of fixed difficulty they systematically UNDERTHINK (truncate early, give up) in low-resource/typologically distant languages and can OVERTHINK in others; this mis-allocation -- distinguishable from a comprehension deficit -- contributes to the multilingual reasoning gap, and extracting an effort-budget direction and steering it re-allocates reasoning length per language and recovers accuracy without retraining.
Related Work: We position against four specific families and state one delta each. (1) Comprehension/pivoting accounts hold that low-resource reasoning fails because the model mis-understands the problem; our identification test (below) separates this from effort mis-allocation. (2) Latent-English-pathway work (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026; Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English 2025) shows reasoning routes through an English-centered but uneven latent pathway -- it does not posit a language-set stopping controller nor steer length. (3) Monolingual stopping/overthinking controllers (When More is Less 2025, the inverted-U CoT-length result) study length as a function of difficulty and capability within one language, never as a language-conditioned budget decoupled from a shared difficulty estimate. (4) Multilingual CoT failure analyses (What Really Counts 2025; Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025; When Less Language is More 2025) analyze which steps/components matter or ablate language-specific components, but do not measure a per-item under/over-thinking gap attributable to language rather than difficulty, and provide no causal effort-budget direction. Our novelty is primarily a new problem framing (language sets an effort budget) plus its causal test/intervention; the mechanistic finding is secondary. Two non-obvious predictions unique to this theory that alternatives do not make: (a) FORCING more steps (or steering the budget up) in an under-thinking language recovers accuracy even though comprehension/pivoting accounts predict no gain from mere length; (b) the SAME model over-thinks (wastes steps, hurting accuracy via the inverted-U) in some languages while under-thinking in others on matched-difficulty items -- a signed, language-indexed mis-allocation a pure competence deficit cannot produce.
Abstract: Multilingual LLMs reason far better in high-resource languages, a gap usually attributed to weaker reasoning ability or to comprehension failure in low-resource languages. We propose a different, testable cause: the query language covertly sets the model's reasoning EFFORT BUDGET -- how many chain-of-thought steps it spends and when it decides it is done -- and this budget is only loosely coupled to the problem's true difficulty. Under this view, for a problem of fixed difficulty the model underthinks (truncates and gives up early) in low-resource, typologically distant languages and can overthink in others, so part of the multilingual gap reflects mis-allocated effort rather than absent competence. We distinguish a shared, language-agnostic difficulty estimate from a language-conditioned effort budget that gates stopping, and give an identification criterion that separates effort mis-allocation from comprehension failure: if injecting the high-resource EFFORT signal (not the reasoning content), or forcing/steering more steps, restores correctness, the deficit is budgeting, not comprehension. Behaviorally we show that, controlling true difficulty via parallel items and multiple difficulty proxies, CoT length and early-give-up vary systematically with query language and predict accuracy loss, estimating the variance in the gap attributable to language versus comprehension. We then probe for a shared difficulty direction and use activation patching and steering -- our primary causal evidence -- to test that low-resource under-reasoning localizes to a language-set stopping controller, and to re-allocate reasoning length per language, comparing against forced-longer-CoT, English-pivot round-trip, and translate-to-English baselines. If the theory is false we still learn whether the gap is comprehension- or competence-bound, informing where to invest. The result matters for benchmark builders, multilingual model developers, inference-time-control researchers, and for accessibility/safety of low-resource deployment. Experiments span MGSM, XCOPA, and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a distilled reasoning model.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Data: multilingual math with matched difficulty -- MGSM (existing; 250 parallel problems) plus 800 GSM-style items (scaled up for per-language/per-model power) annotated with MULTIPLE difficulty proxies (minimum required step count, human difficulty judgments, and English-reference solve rate), XCOPA commonsense (existing), and a translated 2-hop QA subset (400 items). All items are PARALLEL translations across 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels, with human-verified translation quality and native-speaker validation, so true difficulty is held constant across languages. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, frozen; CoT at temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Reasoning length is measured primarily in parsed STEPS (token counts reported separately) via a validated multilingual step-parser whose reliability is reported per language. Confound controls run throughout: comprehension-only baselines (a separate question probing whether the problem was understood), English-pivot round-trip and translate-to-English conditions, same-language paraphrase controls, and ablations for prompting format, answer language, and verbosity priors. Identification criterion (pre-registered): effort mis-allocation is supported iff, at matched difficulty and matched comprehension, (i) length varies by language and predicts errors, and (ii) supplying the effort/stopping signal or forcing more steps recovers accuracy; it is refuted if comprehension baselines fully account for the length/accuracy gap or if adding steps does not help.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- language-attributable effort mis-allocation, with a comprehension control): per item measure reasoning length in steps, EARLY-GIVE-UP rate, and accuracy, plus a comprehension score. Decisive metric: the residual reasoning-length variance attributable to LANGUAGE after regressing length on the multiple difficulty proxies AND the comprehension score (added R^2 from language beyond difficulty and comprehension), plus the correlation between under-length and wrong answers. This directly estimates how much of the gap is effort vs comprehension, so we avoid asserting 'major driver' beyond what the variance decomposition supports. Convincing result: language explains added R^2 >=0.10 beyond difficulty and comprehension, low-resource/distant languages are systematically shorter than their high-resource parallel run, and under-length predicts errors at Spearman >=0.3. Indecision band: 0.03-0.10 = weak; <0.03 = no language-attributable effort effect, refuting H2. Negative result (length explained by difficulty/comprehension) refutes the framing but still tells us the gap is comprehension-bound.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- shared difficulty estimate vs language-set budget): at each layer train (i) a difficulty probe predicting annotated step-count and (ii) a stopping probe predicting imminent final-answer emission; train in one language, test cross-lingually. Probes are treated as correlational evidence only. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the difficulty probe (contrasted with per-language variation in realized length). Convincing result: difficulty-probe cross-lingual transfer within 10 pp of in-language (shared estimate) while realized length for the same items differs by language. Indecision band: 10-25 pp below = partially shared; >25 pp below weakens H1.
