Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows that STATIC representation geometry of multilingual encoders recapitulates the linguistic phylogenetic tree: mBERT distances recover family trees (Probing mBERT for Genetic/Typological Signals 2020), joint matrix factorization of representations yields phylogenetic clustering (Joint Matrix Factorization 2023), and morphosyntactic neuron overlap is higher for same-genus languages (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; What Language Does Aya-23 Think In 2025). Separately, cross-lingual editing/transfer work reports that script similarity dominates knowledge sharing and that edits fail across script families (Beneath the Surface of Consistency 2024; XME 2024). No prior work (i) builds a language tree from CAUSAL, functional interference (how a targeted intervention in language A perturbs behavior in language B) rather than from static similarity, (ii) directly CONTRASTS this functional tree against both the linguistic phylogenetic tree and a script/co-occurrence tree as competing explanations, or (iii) uses the phylogeny-vs-script divergence to predict per-pair transfer/interference. We reframe cross-lingual relatedness as a functional, causal quantity and show the model's operative tree is not the linguists' tree. In one sentence, the primary novelty is a crisp new formal object: the functional interference tree, the neighbor-joining tree over a symmetrized, target-baseline-normalized directed causal-leakage matrix M[s,t], contrasted against the model's own static-representation tree and against script/co-occurrence and genealogy references. Prior cross-lingual edit-transfer papers measure per-pair transfer RATES; they never induce a tree from pairwise causal leakage, never contrast that tree against phylogeny and script as competing explanations, and never show that script dominance in transfer implies a recoverable, predictive interference structure. We contribute the dataset of intervention-by-language-pair leakage measurements, the tree formalism, and the explanatory claim that the operative tree is script/co-occurrence-shaped.
Abstract: A striking result in multilingual interpretability is that the geometry of a model's internal representations recapitulates the linguistic family tree: distances between language representations reconstruct phylogenies close to those drawn by linguists. But representation similarity is correlational. We ask a causal, behavioral question: if we change a model's behavior in one language, which other languages change with it, and does that pattern of functional interference form the same tree? We hypothesize it does not. We define a functional interference tree by measuring, for every ordered language pair, how much a targeted intervention in a source language (a small knowledge edit, a short skill fine-tune, or an in-context skill demonstration) shifts behavior in a target language, then clustering languages by this causal leakage. We predict this tree is dominated by shared script and training-corpus co-occurrence rather than genealogy, so it diverges sharply from the phylogenetic tree recovered from static representations of the SAME model. We test the divergence on diagnostic minimal pairs where genealogy and script disagree (Hindi/Urdu, Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Turkish/Uzbek, Persian/Tajik) across 20+ languages and Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. We further show the phylogeny-minus-script residual predicts, per language pair, where cross-lingual edits and skill transfer unexpectedly succeed or backfire. The result challenges the tidy 'models rediscover the family tree' narrative: the tree the model computes with is a script- and corpus-shaped one, not the linguists' phylogeny, with direct consequences for multilingual editing and transfer. Formally we define the functional interference tree as neighbor-joining over a symmetrized, target-baseline-normalized directed leakage matrix M[s,t]; the causal estimand for M[s,t] is the change in target-language behavior attributable to a source-language intervention on matched probes, normalized by the target's achievable change. Beyond interpretation the tree is directly actionable for multilingual model builders and knowledge-editing practitioners: it prescribes which source language to edit or fine-tune in to reach a target with least collateral damage, flags pairs where an edit will silently corrupt an unrelated language, and yields a transfer-aware evaluation protocol. If the hypothesis holds, best practice for cross-lingual editing shifts from genealogy-based to script/co-occurrence-based source selection; if it fails, the 'edits follow the family tree' heuristic is vindicated.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Languages: 20 languages chosen to span 4+ families (Indo-European, Turkic, Sino-Tibetan, Afro-Asiatic, Dravidian) and 5 scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Perso-Arabic, Devanagari, CJK), and to include the diagnostic minimal pairs where genealogy and script dissociate: Hindi/Urdu (same genealogy, Devanagari vs Perso-Arabic), Serbian written in Cyrillic vs Latin (same language, two scripts), Turkish/Uzbek (Turkic, both Latin), Persian/Tajik (same branch, Perso-Arabic vs Cyrillic). Models (all decoder-only, 7-8B, one A100-80GB each for inference/LoRA; MEMIT edits fit on one GPU): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. Reference resources (all existing, off-the-shelf): Glottolog/URIEL genealogical distances via lang2vec; URIEL typological distance; a binary same-script matrix; two training-corpus co-occurrence proxies (per-language corpus-size similarity from the CC-100 language sizes, and a script-sharing indicator), reported separately because true co-occurrence is unobservable. Three intervention families are used throughout: (a) KNOWLEDGE EDIT via MEMIT applied to 100 source-language facts, all base weights frozen except the MEMIT-targeted MLP down-projection rows at its located layers; (b) SKILL FINE-TUNE via LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, AdamW) on 1,000 source-language items of a from-scratch templated task set (arithmetic + fixed-format extraction, 2,000 items built by template and rendered per language, 1,000 train / 1,000 held-out test), base frozen, adapters trainable; (c) IN-CONTEXT SKILL, base frozen, 8 demonstrations. Facts are 1,000 parallel triples taken from the intersection of mLAMA (multilingual LAMA; ~tens of thousands of templated triples across 53 languages) that exist in all 20 languages, so items are matched across languages. Three seeds vary the edited-fact sample, LoRA init, and demonstration order.

Experiment 1 (H1 - coherent functional interference tree). Tests whether a targeted behavioral change in a source language leaks into other languages in a pattern coherent enough to define a single tree. For every ordered pair (source, target) and each intervention family, apply the intervention in the source and measure the behavior shift in the target on held-out parallel probes (the 1,000 matched facts for edits; the 1,000 held-out task items for fine-tune/in-context), giving a directed interference matrix M[source, target] = mean absolute change in target accuracy (percentage points). Symmetrize and build a tree by neighbor-joining. Data as in the shared setup. Model as above; the interference matrix uses inference only after each intervention. Systems compared: the three intervention families' trees against one another, per model. Decisive metric: mean bootstrap edge support of the functional tree - the fraction of internal edges reproduced across 1,000 item-resampled bootstraps - averaged over the three families; secondary, the normalized quartet distance between the three families' trees (0 = identical, 1 = maximally different). Convincing: mean edge support >= 0.70 AND the three families mutually agree at quartet distance <= 0.25. Indecision band: edge support 0.50-0.70 or quartet distance 0.25-0.40; landing here means we do not assert a single tree and instead carry the interference MATRIX (not a tree) into Experiments 2-5, testing the same structure without the tree claim. Negative result: edge support < 0.50 or families disagreeing at quartet distance > 0.40 refutes H1 - leakage is idiosyncratic, not tree-structured.

Experiment 2 (H2 - functional tree differs from static representation phylogeny). Tests whether the causal functional tree diverges from the model's own static representation tree. Build the representation tree from mean per-language hidden states over 500 held-out parallel sentences drawn from FLORES-200 devtest (1,012 parallel sentences across 200+ languages; 500 used to bound compute), pairwise cosine distance at the best layer, neighbor-joining. Baseline anchor: quartet distance of this representation tree to the Glottolog reference, replicating prior "representations recover phylogeny" claims. Model: same three, inference only, all weights frozen. Systems compared: functional tree (Exp. 1) vs representation tree. Decisive metric: normalized quartet distance between functional and representation trees. Convincing: functional-vs-representation quartet distance >= 0.40 (substantial divergence) WHILE representation-vs-Glottolog quartet distance <= 0.30 (the representation tree genuinely tracks phylogeny, so the divergence is meaningful). Indecision band: functional-vs-representation quartet 0.25-0.40; reported as partial divergence, supporting only the weak "not identical" reading, not "systematically different". Negative result: quartet < 0.25 means the trees coincide, refuting H2. Guard: if representation-vs-Glottolog quartet > 0.30 (representations do not recover phylogeny in these decoder LLMs), the contrast is uninformative for "differs from phylogeny"; we then compare the functional tree to the Glottolog reference directly and report that substitution explicitly.

Experiment 3 (H3 - dominated by script/co-occurrence, not genealogy). Tests what structure the functional tree encodes. Reference matrices from the shared setup: genealogy (Glottolog/URIEL), script identity, and the two co-occurrence proxies. Decisive metric: partial Mantel/Spearman correlation of the functional distance matrix with each reference, each controlling for the others; the contrast is (script + co-occurrence) partial correlation minus genealogy partial correlation. Model/data as Exp. 1-2. Systems compared: functional matrix vs representation matrix against the same references. Convincing: the functional matrix's partial correlation with script/co-occurrence exceeds its partial correlation with genealogy by >= 0.20 in Spearman rho (with the genealogy partial not significantly > 0), AND the representation matrix shows the reverse ordering. Indecision band: difference 0.05-0.20; script/co-occurrence leads but not decisively, reported as suggestive rather than "dominated by". Negative result: genealogy partial rho >= script/co-occurrence partial rho refutes H3.

Experiment 4 (H4 - diagnostic minimal pairs follow script, not genealogy). Tests, on pairs where genealogy and script disagree, whether interference tracks script. Data: the four minimal pairs (Hindi/Urdu, Serbian-Cyrillic/Serbian-Latin, Turkish/Uzbek, Persian/Tajik) plus, as a same-family same-script anchor per region, a control pair (e.g. Hindi/Nepali, both Devanagari). Facts and interventions as shared. Model as above. Decisive metric: within-pair directed interference magnitude (accuracy-point shift on held-out parallel probes), compared against the same-family same-script anchor. Convincing: for the genealogically close but script-different pairs (Hindi/Urdu, Persian/Tajik) interference is < 50% of the same-family same-script anchor's interference, and Serbian-Cyrillic->Serbian-Latin interference (identical language, differing only in script) is likewise suppressed relative to Serbian-Cyrillic->Serbian-Cyrillic self-consistency. Indecision band: cross-script interference 50-75% of the anchor; treated as script partially but not decisively gating, reported per pair. Negative result: cross-script interference within genealogically close pairs at or above the anchor refutes H4 (genealogy, not script, governs leakage).

Experiment 5 (H5 - divergence predicts transfer help/harm). Tests whether the phylogeny-vs-script divergence predicts, per pair, where cross-lingual edits/skill transfer unexpectedly help or backfire. Outcome per ordered pair: sign and magnitude of transfer (edit propagation to matched facts; skill-transfer accuracy change on held-out task items), labeled positive/neutral/backfire relative to no-intervention baseline. Predictors: phylogenetic distance, script identity, co-occurrence proxy, and the phylogeny-minus-script residual. Fit on a random 70% of the ~380 ordered pairs, evaluate on the held-out 30%, 3 seeds. Decisive metric: held-out AUC for classifying backfire vs non-backfire pairs from the residual; secondary, standardized regression coefficients. Convincing: script/co-occurrence terms carry the largest significant standardized coefficients AND the residual predicts backfire pairs at held-out AUC >= 0.70. Indecision band: AUC 0.60-0.70; reported as weak predictive signal, not actionable. Negative result: AUC < 0.60 or genealogy dominating the coefficients refutes H5 - the tree divergence has no predictive payoff for transfer.

Null controls (applied to Experiments 1-3). To show the tree structure is not an artifact of language frequency or measurement noise, we compare the functional tree's edge support and the partial correlations against (i) a label-permutation null that reshuffles the interference matrix across language labels (1,000 permutations) and (ii) a language-frequency-only null that predicts leakage from marginal per-language corpus size alone; the recovered structure must exceed both. We pre-register the KNOWLEDGE-EDIT (MEMIT) family as the PRIMARY intervention for all confirmatory thresholds and treat the skill-fine-tune and in-context families as robustness checks, and we report all tree claims under alternative distance metrics (cosine, correlation) and clustering methods (neighbor-joining, UPGMA, average-linkage) with bootstrap confidence over trees.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The functional tree from edits/fine-tunes could be dominated by which languages the model is simply BETTER at (resource level) rather than pairwise structure; we control by measuring interference relative to each target's baseline competence and by including resource-matched pairs. 2. Different intervention types (edit vs fine-tune vs in-context) may yield different trees, undercutting a single 'functional tree'; this is itself an informative result and we report agreement across the three rather than assuming one. 3. Script and co-occurrence are correlated (same-script languages co-occur more), making them hard to separate; the diagnostic minimal pairs (same genealogy, different script; same script, different family) are designed precisely to dissociate them, and the transliteration ablation further isolates script. 4. Tree-inference is sensitive to distance-metric choice and noise; we report multiple metrics and bootstrap confidence over trees. 5. Knowledge edits can fail entirely in low-resource languages, confounding interference with edit failure; we condition on successful source edits and report edit success separately. 6. The representation-tree replication may be weaker in decoder-only LLMs than in mBERT; even a partial phylogenetic signal suffices to test divergence, and finding NO phylogenetic signal in representations would also be a notable result. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: numeral_inversion_operand_binding
Title: Five-and-Twenty Plus Three: How Number-Word Inversion in the Query Language Reorders Operand Binding in Multilingual LLM Arithmetic
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in whether spoken numerals are inverted (German 'fünfundzwanzig' = five-and-twenty for 25; Arabic) or non-inverted (English, Hebrew). We hypothesize that when a multilingual LLM reads a number written as words, the query language's inversion structure covertly sets the internal ORDER in which digit/operand magnitudes are bound before arithmetic, so that in inverted languages the model tends to bind the units-before-tens order it hears rather than the place-value order it must compute over. This produces systematic, direction-consistent arithmetic errors (e.g. transposition/carry errors) on word-form multi-digit and multi-operand problems that are ABSENT in the same problems posed in digits or in non-inverted languages, and the error rate scales with the language's degree of numeral inversion, not its resource level. The binding order is carried by a locatable, causally-manipulable representation separable from the magnitude content.
Related Work: Bilingualism research establishes that number-word inversion causally shapes arithmetic: inverted-language speakers are faster/more accurate when problems match their language's numeral order, and bilinguals flexibly adapt to L1 vs L2 order (Number word structure in first and second language, 2015; operand-order effects reflecting learning history in Chinese-educated adults, 2025; linguistic-arithmetic interaction in word problems, 2020). On the model side, arithmetic-interpretability work shows LLMs rely on positional information and pattern-matching rather than robust rule induction (Positional Description Matters 2023; Do LLMs Truly Grasp Addition 2025; Unraveling Arithmetic 2024), and that math word problems decompose into an abstract-then-compute mechanism (Can LLMs Reason Abstractly 2025). Cross-lingual reasoning work shows knowledge-free reasoning transfers well across languages (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024). However, ALL LLM arithmetic-interpretability work is monolingual (English digits) and studies digit positional encoding, and ALL number-word-inversion work is human cognitive-linguistics with no model-internal account. My own prior proposal on numeral morphology studied MAGNITUDE distortion from vigesimal words, a different axis. NONE tests whether the QUERY LANGUAGE'S INVERSION STRUCTURE reorders internal OPERAND/DIGIT BINDING during multi-digit/multi-operand arithmetic, nor gives a causal, steerable binding-order mechanism. We uniquely port the number-word-inversion arithmetic effect into multilingual mechanistic interpretability. The novelty is located primarily in the causal, mechanistic account - a steerable binding-order representation set by the query language - plus its behavioral signature; the dataset and setting are supporting. We distinguish this from generic token-order/positional effects by the directional prediction that errors take the specific tens-units TRANSPOSITION form the language's inversion predicts, absent in digit form and in non-inverted word forms - a stronger claim than 'word order affects parsing'. 'Inversion degree' is defined by the numeral GRAMMAR (units-before-tens over the 21-99 range: full / teens-only / none), a property of the spoken-numeral system independent of tokenization or general morphological complexity, which we verify by holding tokenized length fixed and by including within-language order-normalized paraphrases.
Abstract: Human languages disagree on the order of spoken numerals: German and Arabic say the units before the tens ('five-and-twenty' for 25), while English and Hebrew do not. A landmark bilingual finding is that this inversion causally shapes arithmetic performance, with speakers faster and more accurate when a problem's presentation matches their language's numeral order. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit this effect, and whether the query language's inversion structure covertly reorders how the model internally binds operands during arithmetic. We hypothesize that when numbers are given as words, an inverted query language biases the model toward a units-before-tens binding order that conflicts with the place-value order arithmetic requires, producing systematic transposition and carry errors that vanish when the identical problem is posed in digits or in a non-inverted language. We build INVERT-MATH: multi-digit addition and multi-operand word problems whose numbers are spelled out across inverted (German, Dutch, Danish, Arabic) and non-inverted (English, Hebrew, Chinese, Turkish) numeral languages, with matched digit-form controls. Behaviorally we measure a per-language inversion-error rate and its dose-response with numeral-inversion degree. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared magnitude representation and a separable binding-order signal that inherits the query language's inversion; (ii) use activation patching to show magnitude is correctly recovered while a binding-order representation is mis-set, localizing errors to an order-binding step; and (iii) recover a binding-order direction and steer it to repair inversion errors (or induce them in non-inverted languages) without changing the magnitudes. We predict errors track inversion degree, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. Beyond arithmetic microtasks the effect bears on multilingual word problems, finance, and education settings where numbers arrive as words; documenting the OPPOSITE - robust place-value binding regardless of spoken order - would be an equally informative statement that multilingual LLMs internally normalize numeral order.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset INVERT-MATH (built from scratch): 500 multi-digit ADDITION items requiring carries (two- and three-digit operands where tens/units order matters, e.g. "twenty-seven plus forty-eight") and 200 short multi-operand WORD problems, numbers spelled out as WORDS. Each item is rendered in INVERTED numeral languages (German, Dutch, Danish, Arabic - units before tens) and NON-INVERTED ones (English, Hebrew, Chinese, Turkish), each with a matched DIGIT-form control (same numbers in Arabic numerals, same carrier sentence). Number-word rendering is native-speaker-validated; items with ambiguous morpheme segmentation are dropped and reported. Per language: a numeral-inversion-degree index (fully inverted / teens-only partially inverted / non-inverted) and a resource proxy (CC-100 share). Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (operand sampling and template).

Experiment 1 (H2 - inversion-specific arithmetic errors on word forms). Tests whether word-form arithmetic incurs transposition/carry errors in inverted languages that are absent in digit form and in non-inverted languages. Decisive metric: INVERSION-ERROR GAP = accuracy(digit control) - accuracy(word form), per language, and the rate of TRANSPOSITION errors (answer consistent with swapping an operand's tens and units) reported alongside carry errors. Systems compared: inverted vs non-inverted languages, word vs digit, plus a translate-numerals-to-digits prompt and an English word-form baseline. Convincing: the inversion-error gap in inverted languages exceeds that in non-inverted languages by >= 10 percentage points, the transposition-error rate is elevated specifically in inverted word forms, and digit controls are comparable across languages (gap < 3 pp). Indecision band: inverted-vs-non-inverted gap difference 3-10 pp, or transposition errors not preferentially in the inversion-predicted direction; reported as generic word-parsing difficulty, not an inversion effect. Negative result: no excess gap in inverted languages (< 3 pp) refutes H2.

Experiment 2 (H3 - error rate tracks inversion degree, not resource). Tests whether the error gap scales with numeral-inversion degree rather than resource. Regress the inversion-error gap and transposition rate on the inversion-degree index and on the resource proxy. Designed contrasts: a lower-resource inverted language (Danish) vs a higher-resource non-inverted one (Chinese); German (inverted, high-resource) vs Turkish (non-inverted, mid-resource). Decisive metric: Spearman of the error gap with inversion degree vs with the resource proxy (95% CIs) and the partial correlation with inversion controlling for resource. Convincing: the gap correlates with inversion degree (Spearman >= 0.4), surviving resource control, while resource alone does not order it. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or inversion correlation vanishing after resource control; resource-confounded. Negative result: resource dominates and inversion adds nothing refutes H3.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared magnitude vs query-language binding-order signal). Tests whether operand magnitudes are represented consistently across languages while a binding-order signal inherits the query language's inversion. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer at the operand-final token to decode (i) each operand's true magnitude (anchored to digit-form runs) and (ii) the operand's tens-vs-units digit assignment / binding order; evaluate cross-lingual transfer. Probes are the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: magnitude-probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy (should be high and language-consistent) and whether the binding-order probe predicts the MIS-ordered assignment specifically in inverted languages. Convincing: magnitude transfers with <= 10-point drop and is language-consistent, AND the binding-order probe recovers the inverted (units-before-tens) assignment in inverted languages at well above chance while recovering place-value order in non-inverted ones. Indecision band: magnitude transfer drop 10-20 points, or binding-order probe weakly language-dependent; partial support. Negative result: magnitude probe fails to transfer, or binding-order probe shows no language dependence, refutes H1.

Experiment 4 (H4 - errors localized to a binding-order step, magnitude preserved). Tests whether inversion errors are a wrong binding order over correct magnitudes. For an addition item solved correctly in digit/non-inverted form but erred in an inverted word form: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer magnitude representation across runs and confirm magnitudes are correctly present in the erring run (patching changes the answer little); (b) patch/steer the components carrying digit-position binding and test whether the answer corrects. Specificity control = patching a matched non-binding site. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: correction rate from binding-order patching (reported first), with magnitude-patch correction (should be low) and matched-site correction as controls. Convincing: binding-order patching corrects >= 50% of erred items, magnitude patching alone corrects < 15% (magnitudes already present), and the matched site corrects < 15%. Indecision band: binding-patch correction 25-50% or magnitude-patch correction 15-30% (magnitude partly wrong); mixed evidence. Negative result: binding-patch correction < 25% or magnitude patching itself corrects (magnitude was wrong) refutes the binding-order localization.

Experiment 5 (H4 - a steerable binding-order representation separable from magnitude). Tests whether a recovered binding-order direction repairs inversion errors and induces them, without changing magnitudes. Recover a binding-order direction as the mean activation difference between correctly place-value-ordered and inverted-ordered runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) REPAIR inversion errors in inverted-language word problems and (b) INDUCE transposition errors in non-inverted languages, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against an explicit "read the number in place-value order" prompt and translate-to-digits. Decisive metric: arithmetic-accuracy repair in inverted languages (reported first), then induced-transposition rate in non-inverted ones, with magnitude-preservation specificity (operand-value probe unchanged), fluency (perplexity), reported alongside. Convincing: steering raises accuracy by >= 15 pp in inverted-language word problems AND induces >= 15 pp of transposition errors in non-inverted ones, monotone dose-response, magnitudes preserved, < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair/induction or non-monotone dose; weak causal handle. Negative result: < 5 pp effect or only at fluency-breaking doses refutes H4.

Language set, power, and added controls. To give the inversion-degree correlation adequate power we expand to 12+ languages, adding inverted (Norwegian, Icelandic) and non-inverted (Japanese, Korean, Indonesian) numeral systems, and report a power analysis for the inversion-vs-resource regression. Additional controls: (i) order-normalized paraphrases within the SAME language (rendering the numeral in place-value order where the language allows) isolate order from language identity; (ii) synthetic counterbalanced numeral strings dissociate inversion from digit magnitude; (iii) a NON-ARITHMETIC number-word task (read-and-repeat and magnitude comparison) tests whether the binding-order representation is arithmetic-specific or a general parsing artifact; (iv) transliteration/tokenization controls hold token boundaries fixed; (v) intervention specificity is checked with same-layer random-site patches, matched-magnitude patches, and a test that steering the binding-order direction does not perturb unrelated non-numeric word-order tasks. A pre-registered error taxonomy (transposition vs carry vs misparse vs generation noise) is applied by two annotators with reported agreement.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Word-form arithmetic errors could stem from generic difficulty of parsing number words rather than an inversion-specific binding-order effect; the matched DIGIT controls (comparable across languages) and the transposition-error signature (tens/units specifically swapped, in the direction the language's inversion predicts) are the crucial dissociators, and non-inverted word-form languages serve as a further control. 2. Probe decodability of magnitude or binding order may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, plus the specificity check that operand magnitudes are preserved. 3. Tokenization of number words is uneven across languages and scripts and may itself split tens/units unevenly, confounding the effect; we curate items with clean morpheme boundaries, use operand-final/pooled representations, report tokenization statistics, and analyze partially-inverted teens separately. 4. The inversion-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (German vs Chinese, Danish vs Turkish); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the inversion-degree operationalization. 5. Strong models may resolve place value robustly regardless of spoken order, shrinking the effect; even documenting robust place-value binding (a clean shared-magnitude + order-invariant architecture) is an informative positive result, and the induction steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. Some 'errors' may reflect the model answering a different (mis-parsed) problem; we manually classify error types and restrict the causal analysis to clear transposition/carry cases. 7. Steering may trade arithmetic correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across two task families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: cultural_frame_register
Title: Which Answer Is True Here? A Mechanistic Study of How Multilingual LLMs Select Among Culturally-Relative Truths
Short Hypothesis: For claims whose truth value is genuinely relative to a cultural/geographic frame (e.g., 'people drive on the left', 'the head of state is a monarch', 'the school year starts in spring'), multilingual LLMs store multiple mutually-contradictory candidate answers simultaneously and select among them via an internal frame-selective representation ('frame register') set in mid layers. The primary novelty is the problem definition (claims with NO single universal truth, requiring frame-conditioned SELECTION rather than recall) and the selector-vs-content dissociation (a representation that changes which stored answer is emitted while the candidate set stays decodable). We hypothesize (a) the query language acts as an implicit, weak frame selector competing with explicit textual frame cues -- framed as a mechanistic extension of known prompt-language cultural-framing effects, not a new behavioral discovery; (b) selection is mediated by a causally necessary-and-sufficient frame-selective subspace separable from answer-content computation; and (c) selection failures scale with typological/script distance between the query language and the frame's canonical language. We present the mechanism as possibly a distributed frame-selective subspace rather than a discrete register unless the localization evidence is decisive.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work localizes 'culture neurons' separable from language neurons (Isolating Culture Neurons 2025), finds cultural localization in middle layers steerable by cultural vectors (Localized Cultural Knowledge is Conserved 2025), documents a Cultural-Linguistic Synergy (Disentangling Language and Culture 2025), shows cross-lingual alignment causes cultural erasure fixable by Surgical Steering (Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment 2025), and finds internal paths are more language- than content-driven (Language over Content 2025). Factual-storage work (Tracing the Roots of Facts 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025) categorizes facts as shared/independent with a language-agnostic concept space. Contrasts by family: (culture-neuron localization) localizes static cultural CONTENT -- we localize a SELECTOR that arbitrates among simultaneously-stored contradictory answers; (prompt-language cultural framing) shows query language biases outputs behaviorally -- we test it mechanistically as competition against an explicit cue and isolate it from token priors and memorized country-language associations; (factual-storage tracing) assumes a single correct answer per fact -- we study claims with NO single correct answer; (cross-lingual alignment/erasure) steers toward a canonical answer -- we characterize the selection process itself. None studies claims where multiple contradictory answers are simultaneously true under different frames, nor a mechanism that selects among stored competing answers as a function of explicit-vs-implicit (language) cues. Our novelty is primarily the setting/problem and the selector mechanism; the language-competition finding is a mechanistic extension.
Abstract: Many claims about the world have no universal truth value: whether people drive on the left, whether the head of state is a monarch, or when the school year begins depends on the cultural or geographic frame in which the question is asked. Such frame-relative claims are common and consequential -- they span transport, governance, currency, measurement, calendar, education, and etiquette conventions, any of which a multilingual assistant may get wrong for a user's locale. Models must therefore not merely recall facts but SELECT which stored, frame-dependent answer applies. We construct FRAME-REL, a controlled, documented, and to-be-released dataset of culturally-relative claims for which several countries have known, mutually-contradictory ground-truth answers, and probe models under two orthogonal frame cues: an explicit textual cue (naming the country) and an implicit cue (the query language). We first show multiple contradictory candidate answers are simultaneously linearly decodable from mid-layer hidden states before selection collapses to one, evidencing parallel storage. Using activation patching we localize a frame-selective subspace -- components that, when swapped between a same-question run under frame A and under frame B, flip the selected answer while the candidate set stays decodable and answer content is preserved (a quantitatively measured selector-vs-content dissociation, with causal necessity and sufficiency tested). We then quantify how often the query language overrides an explicit country cue and whether this scales with typological/script distance, controlling for token priors, output-language heuristics, memorized country-language associations, country familiarity, and canonical-language exposure. Experiments span 15+ languages and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. So what: if language covertly overrides explicit frame, multilingual assistants, government/service and travel/localization chatbots, and educational tools will silently give locale-wrong answers, and prompt design, alignment, and evaluation must test frame-selection explicitly; we test a training-free frame-register steering fix and compare against explicit-prompting and translate-to-English baselines. The work recasts multilingual cultural knowledge as frame-conditioned selection, bears directly on multilingual fairness and cultural respect, and delivers a releasable benchmark plus a causal, controllable account.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Dataset FRAME-REL (constructed, to be released with documentation and governance): culturally-relative claim templates with verifiable per-country ground truth that differs across countries -- driving side, monarchy vs republic, currency, primary-school start season, calendar/new-year timing, measurement units, plug voltage, and further etiquette/convention types to broaden the taxonomy. Each claim type has >=6 countries with mutually-contradictory answers and their canonical languages; ~40 claim types x countries give ~2,500 base items, each rendered in 15 query languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families, crossed with the explicit country cue present vs absent. Annotation protocol: >=3 native-speaker/expert annotators per country-claim with inter-annotator agreement reported; items that vary over time or admit subnational variation are excluded or flagged with an explicit governance note; a documented datasheet accompanies release. A matched set of ordinary single-answer factual claims serves as a NEGATIVE CONTROL that should show NO parallel storage and NO flippable register; a set where the explicit country cue should dominate serves as a POSITIVE CONTROL to calibrate override rates. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds; short answer tokens, last-token-of-answer representations (tokenisation statistics reported). Heuristic controls applied throughout: same explicit country cue with unrelated query-language changes, transliterated scripts, translated-into-English versions, and synthetic frame tokens decoupled from natural language, to rule out token priors, output-language heuristics, memorized country-language associations, and generic attention to explicit country names.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- parallel storage of contradictory answers and a causally necessary-and-sufficient frame-selective subspace, separable from content): tests that several frame-dependent answers are stored simultaneously and that a frame-selective representation selects among them, separable from answer content. Data/model as Setup. Method: (A) parallel-storage probe -- logit-lens and per-layer linear probes test whether multiple countries' answers are simultaneously decodable in mid layers before output, contrasted with the single-answer negative control; (B) locate the selector -- run the identical question under explicit frame A vs frame B, activation-patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run, and find the minimal set whose patching flips the selected answer to A's while the candidate set stays decodable; test causal NECESSITY (ablating the set disrupts correct selection) and SUFFICIENCY (injecting it imposes the donor frame); (C) selector-vs-content dissociation, quantified -- 'content preserved' is measured as semantic equivalence of the non-frame answer content plus preservation of the decodable candidate set, not asserted qualitatively; a further causal test suppresses ONE candidate's representation and checks selection shifts while the others remain decodable. Localization comparison: contrast patching units -- attention heads, MLP neurons, low-rank subspaces, and distributed directions -- and justify the compactness metric rather than presuming a discrete register; report overlap (Jaccard) with previously reported language- and culture-specific neurons. Decisive metric: the patching flip rate (selection changes to the donor frame with content and candidate set preserved), with the size/location of the patched set, alongside mid-layer co-decodability. Convincing result: >=2 contradictory answers co-decodable in mid layers well above the negative control; patching a set (compact if <5% of the layer's units, else reported as a distributed subspace) flips selection in >=50% of A/B pairs with candidate set preserved; necessity and sufficiency both hold; and the selector overlaps little (<30% Jaccard) with pure language/culture neurons. Indecision band: co-decodability marginally above control, or flip rate 25-50% = a distributed, non-compact selector (reported as such); flip <25% or no parallel co-decodability = no frame-selection mechanism and H1 is refuted. Negative result (single answer stored, patching cannot flip selection) refutes parallel storage and the selector.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the query language competes with the explicit frame cue): tests claim (a) as a mechanistic extension of prompt-language framing. Data: items with the explicit country cue set to country C but posed in language L (the canonical language of a DIFFERENT country D), with the Setup heuristic controls applied. Model as Setup. Decisive metric: language-override rate = fraction of outputs matching D (language wins) rather than C (explicit wins), with a neither bucket, reported net of the heuristic controls. Convincing result: language-override rate >=15% above the control conditions -- the query language measurably shifts selection even against an explicit cue and beyond token priors/memorized associations. Indecision band: 5-15% = weak implicit selection; <5%, or an effect fully explained by the heuristic controls, = the query language does not genuinely compete and (a) is refuted. Negative result (explicit cue always wins) means language is not a frame selector.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- selection failure scales with distance, confounds controlled): tests claim (c). Data: per-language language-override rate (Experiment 2) and frame-selection error rate. Predictors entered together in a multivariate model: lang2vec typological distance and same-script indicator between L and the intended frame's canonical language, plus training-data prevalence, country familiarity, tokenization length, and canonical-language exposure. Decisive metric: partial Spearman / standardized coefficient of distance (and script) with bootstrap CIs, after controlling for the confounds. Convincing result: distance retains an effect corresponding to Spearman >=0.5 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.2, distant/different-script languages showing more wrong-frame selection, not absorbed by prevalence/familiarity/exposure. Indecision band: 0.2-0.5 = weak scaling (suggestive); <0.2, or fully absorbed by confounds, = no genuine distance scaling and (c) is refuted. Negative result (no distance relationship) refutes the dose-response claim. Applied check tied to H1: steering the frame-selective subspace to the intended frame on mismatched items is compared against explicit-country-prompt and translate-to-English baselines, reporting selection-correction rate, fluency (perplexity), and quantitative content/candidate-set preservation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground truth for culturally-relative claims can be ambiguous or change over time; we restrict to unambiguous, stable, verifiable claims, exclude/flag time-varying and subnational cases, and document a governance protocol. 2. Logit-lens/probe decodability of multiple candidates may reflect the readout basis rather than functional parallel storage; we require the causal patching flip, the single-candidate-suppression test, and necessity/sufficiency (Exp. 1). 3. The selector may be distributed rather than a compact register; we compare localization units and report a distributed-subspace account honestly rather than overclaiming a discrete register. 4. Apparent language competition could be token priors, output-language heuristics, or memorized country-language associations; the transliteration, translated-into-English, synthetic-frame-token, and unrelated-language-change controls isolate the genuine effect. 5. Some models may default to a canonical/Western answer regardless of frame; quantifying that near-absence of frame sensitivity and its language dependence is itself a contribution. 6. Tokenization differences complicate cross-language probing; we use clean short answer tokens and last-token representations. 7. Steering may trade content preservation for correct selection; we report both quantitatively. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: aspectual_completion_gate
Title: Did It Finish, or Was It Just Happening? How the Query Language's Aspect System Covertly Sets a Default Completion Interpretation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in how obligatorily they mark whether an event is completed vs ongoing (perfective/imperfective, presence vs absence of a grammaticalized perfect). We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic representation of an event's abstract completion state, but resolve whether an underspecified event counts as COMPLETED (endpoint reached, result achieved) through a scalar 'completion-inference' gate whose default is covertly set by the query language's aspect system. Consequently the identical event description yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing inferences across languages, this gap scales with the query language's aspectual-grammaticalization distance from the dominant language (not resource level), and it is carried by a locatable, steerable representation separable from the propositional content.
Related Work: Probing work shows transformers encode telicity/duration/aspect, mostly in final layers, and are biased by tense/word order (About Time 2022; Probing Verbal Aspect in Russian 2024; Do pretrained transformers infer telicity like humans 2021), that tense/aspect are orthogonal, steerable directions (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025), that tense is easy in morphologically-marked languages but hard in Chinese (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021), and that LLMs fail cross-linguistic perfect-aspect NLI in Chinese/Japanese (LLMs Struggle with NLI for Perfect Aspect 2025). Complement-coercion work studies event recovery (Norwegian 2025). Psycholinguistics shows telicity is encoded differently across languages yet event tracking is similar (Do Cross-Linguistic Differences Influence Event Perception 2024). Crucially, ALL LLM aspect work either (i) probes/steers the surface aspect FEATURE within one language, or (ii) measures behavioral NLI failure, and treats the surface aspect as the target. NONE dissociates a shared abstract COMPLETION-STATE representation from a language-conditioned completion-INFERENCE gate, tests whether the query language causally sets whether an underspecified event is read as finished vs ongoing (biasing downstream semantic/entailment judgments), or provides a causal, steerable completion gate with an aspectual-typology-vs-resource dissociation. My prior tense proposal targeted reference-TIME (past/present/future); this targets a distinct axis: COMPLETION/boundedness. We uniquely port grammatical-aspect typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability, and add a safety-critical task-completion instantiation. In one sentence: we claim a shared, language-agnostic completion-STATE representation resolved by a language-conditioned completion-INFERENCE gate, distinct from prior aspect/telicity work that probes or steers the surface aspect FEATURE within one language. Contrast: Chinese/Japanese perfect-aspect NLI and English ImperfectiveNLI document behavioral failures but do not separate a shared state from a gate; tense/aspect steering manipulates the surface feature, not a cross-lingual default-completion decision. The novelty spans a finding (query-language-set completion gap), a mechanism (state vs gate), and a dataset, with the mechanism primary. We frame the typology-vs-resource contrast as a specific preregistered comparison, not a universal linguistic law.
Abstract: Whether an event is finished ('she was building a house' vs 'she built a house') is marked very differently across languages: Slavic and Romance grammars obligatorily encode perfective vs imperfective, English grammaticalizes the perfect, while Chinese, Indonesian and others leave completion largely to inference. A competent multilingual model must nonetheless recover the same abstract completion state and, when a description is underspecified, decide whether the event counts as completed. We ask whether the language a question is asked in covertly makes that decision. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs compute a shared, language-agnostic completion-state representation but resolve underspecification through a completion-inference gate whose default is set by the query language's aspect system, so the identical event yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing readings across languages. We build ASPECT-GATE, controlled event descriptions whose completion is underspecified, paired with entailment questions that distinguish a completed from an ongoing reading (e.g., 'Is the house finished?'), rendered across 12+ languages spanning perfective/imperfective, perfect-marking, and aspect-lax typologies, with completion-forcing and completion-neutral controls. Behaviorally we measure per-language completion-inference rate on identical events. Mechanistically we (i) probe for a shared completion-state direction that transfers across languages including aspect-lax ones; (ii) use activation patching to show the completion state is computed similarly while a separable gate differs by language; and (iii) recover and steer a completion-inference direction to flip readings without changing the events. We include a safety-relevant subset (inferring whether an instruction/action was actually carried out) where under- or over-inference of completion causes an agent to falsely report task success. We predict the gap tracks aspectual-typology distance, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. We define the completion STATE operationally as the linearly-decodable completed-vs-ongoing variable shared across languages, and the completion GATE as the late, language-conditioned component whose patching flips the interpretation while the state is unchanged. Leading with the concrete hazard - multilingual assistants and workflow agents that falsely report a task as done - the result would tell practitioners to add language-specific calibration or completion checks for completion-sensitive outputs; we qualify the safety claim to the extent the task-completion subset mirrors realistic agent settings. Baselines control for surface morphology, language ID, prompt framing, and answer priors.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Dataset ASPECT-GATE (built from scratch): 300 event descriptions whose COMPLETION is underspecified (no overt endpoint marker), each paired with a yes/no entailment question distinguishing a completed reading (endpoint reached, result state holds) from an ongoing one (event in progress) - accomplishment verbs (build/write/cross/paint) with quantized vs bare objects, plus resultative and durative variants - across a difficulty gradient, with clearly-completed and clearly-ongoing controls that should agree across languages. Rendered in 12+ languages spanning three aspectual types: PERFECTIVE/IMPERFECTIVE-grammaticalized (Russian, Polish, Spanish, French, Greek), PERFECT-marking (English, German), and ASPECT-LAX/inference-based (Chinese, Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese). Native-speaker-validated (two per language), translations checked not to insert completion cues; low-agreement items dropped and reported. Per-language aspectual-grammaticalization index (obligatory perfective/imperfective > perfect auxiliary > lexical/pragmatic only) and a resource proxy (CC-100 share). Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (template and question order).

Experiment 1 (H3 - cross-language completion-inference gap on identical events). Tests whether the identical underspecified event yields opposite completed-vs-ongoing readings across languages. Decisive metric: per-language COMPLETION-INFERENCE RATE (fraction read as completed) on identical items, plus cross-language disagreement; controls (clearly completed/ongoing) must agree across languages. Systems compared: across the three aspectual types; baselines query-in-English and translate-to-English-first. Convincing: completion-inference rate differs across aspectual-type groups by >= 15 percentage points on identical items while controls agree within 5 pp, in all three models. Indecision band: 5-15 pp difference; reported as a weak language effect. Negative result: gap < 5 pp (language-invariant completion inference) refutes H3 - though documenting faithful language-invariant handling is itself informative.

Experiment 2 (H4 - gap tracks aspectual typology, not resource). Tests whether the gap scales with aspectual-grammaticalization distance rather than resource. Regress per-language completion-inference rate (deviation from the English baseline) on the grammaticalization index and on the resource proxy; designed contrast: a lower-resource strongly-aspectual language (Polish) vs a higher-resource aspect-lax one (Chinese). Decisive metric: Spearman with the grammaticalization index vs with resource (95% CIs), partialled for resource. Convincing: the rate correlates with the grammaticalization index (Spearman >= 0.4), surviving resource control. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or vanishing after resource control; suggestive. Negative result: resource dominates and typology adds nothing refutes H4.

Experiment 3 (H1 - shared, language-agnostic completion-state representation). Tests whether the abstract completion state is represented consistently across languages, including aspect-lax ones. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode the completion state (completed vs ongoing) from mid-layer hidden states on held-out items; evaluate cross-lingual transfer. Contrast with a surface-aspect-morphology probe. Probes the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual transfer accuracy of the completion-state probe, including onto aspect-lax languages. Convincing: the probe transfers with <= 10-point drop off in-language accuracy and stays well above chance on aspect-lax languages, dissociating from the surface-aspect probe (which does not carry the state there). Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial support. Negative result: probe near chance across languages (drop > 20 points) refutes the shared-state claim (H1).

Experiment 4 (H2 - a language-set completion gate over a shared state). Tests whether the cross-language difference is a gating step over an equally-present state rather than a different completion computation. For an item read completed in language A but ongoing in language B on the SAME event: (a) activation-patch the mid-layer completion-state representation across runs and confirm it is present in both (patching changes the answer little); (b) patch/steer the late components carrying the completion decision and test whether the interpretation flips. Specificity control = a matched non-gate site. Model frozen; patching at inference. Decisive metric: interpretation-flip rate from late-gate patching (reported first), with state-patch flip (should be low) and matched-site flip as controls. Convincing: late-gate patching flips >= 50% of items, state patching alone flips < 15% (state already present in both), and the matched site flips < 15%. Indecision band: gate-patch flip 25-50% or state-patch flip 15-30% (state partly different); mixed evidence. Negative result: gate-patch flip < 25% or state patching itself flips (a different state computation) refutes the language-set-gate account (H2).

Experiment 5 (H5 - a steerable completion-inference direction separable from content). Tests whether a recovered completion-inference direction induces/suppresses completed readings without changing the event. Recover the direction as the mean activation difference between completed-reading and ongoing-reading runs, pooled across languages; steer to (a) INDUCE a completed reading in an aspect-lax/imperfective-defaulting language and (b) SUPPRESS it (force ongoing) in a perfective-defaulting one, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against explicit "assume the action is finished/still ongoing" prompting and translate-first. Decisive metric: induced/suppressed completion rate (reported first), with propositional-content specificity (the event/entities unchanged), fluency (perplexity), and output-language fidelity alongside. Convincing: steering shifts the completion rate by >= 15 pp in each direction with a monotone dose-response, preserved content, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 5-15 pp shift or non-monotone dose; weak handle. Negative result: < 5 pp shift or only at content/fluency-breaking doses refutes H5.

Experiment 6 (H3 - safety-critical instantiation: multilingual task-completion inference). Tests the same completion-inference gap in an agentic setting where under- or over-inference makes a model falsely report task success. Build a 100-item subset (from scratch, same schema) describing whether an action was carried out ("The system was applying the patch" vs "applied the patch"), rendered across the same 12+ languages. Measure per-language whether the model reports the task DONE vs IN-PROGRESS, and whether steering the gate (Exp. 5) repairs mis-inferences. Model frozen. Decisive metric: cross-lingual FALSE-COMPLETION gap (falsely reporting success) on identical descriptions, and its reduction under gate steering. Convincing: the false-completion gap across aspectual types is >= 15 pp on identical items and gate steering reduces it by >= 10 pp without harming fluency, confirming the gap is a reliability hazard driven by the same gate. Indecision band: 5-15 pp gap or 5-10 pp repair; reported as a minor reliability effect. Negative result: gap < 5 pp (agentic completion reporting is language-invariant) means the phenomenon does not surface in this safety-relevant setting, bounding H3's practical reach.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a 'completion state' or 'completion gate' may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; the causal patching (Exp. 5) and steering induce/suppress (Exp. 6) tests with content-preservation specificity are required to promote correlation to mechanism. 2. Whether an underspecified event is 'completed' can be genuinely ambiguous and gradient; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and include clear completed/ongoing controls. 3. Cross-lingual differences might reflect genuine aspectual-norm variation rather than a gate artifact; the shared-completion-state probe transfer and the state-same/gate-differs patching test are designed to separate a different completion computation from a pure interpretation-strength shift, and translations are validated to avoid inadvertently inserting completion cues. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts (Polish vs Chinese); we report multiple resource proxies and robustness to the grammaticalization-index operationalization. 5. Strong models may infer completion faithfully per language, shrinking the default cross-language effect; even documenting faithful language-specific aspect handling (a clean shared-state + language-set-gate architecture) is a positive result, and the induction/suppression steering still yields causal evidence; multiple models/languages give power. 6. The surface-aspect feature and abstract completion state nearly coincide in strongly-aspectual languages; the aspect-lax languages and the underspecified/neutral conditions are the crucial dissociating cases. 7. Tokenization of aspect morphology varies across scripts; we use verb-final/clause-final or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics; perfective/imperfective vs perfect vs lexical cases analyzed separately. 8. Steering may trade interpretation change for fluency or content preservation; we report both. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: storage_topology_via_edit_propagation
Title: Shared or Duplicated? Using Knowledge Edits to Map the Cross-Lingual Storage Topology of Facts, and Predicting Transfer Before Editing
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs store facts along a spectrum from language-shared (a single set of shared causal components serving all languages) to language-duplicated (redundant per-language components). The primary novel claim is predictive: cross-lingual edit propagation is predictable PER-FACT and PER-LANGUAGE-PAIR from an intrinsic PRE-edit mechanistic signature (overlap of causally-important components across languages) ALONE, without performing the edit, and this predictor beats simple operational heuristics (subject-token similarity, script match, lang2vec distance, resource level, pre-edit behavioral agreement). The taxonomy itself (shared vs duplicated vs hybrid) is a supporting frame, not the contribution. We claim shared *causal components* (activation-level), not literally a single shared parameter, unless parameter-level evidence is obtained.
Related Work: A large body of work shows factual edits fail to propagate across languages, especially across script families (Cross-Lingual Knowledge Editing 2024, Bi-ZsRE; XME 2024; MLaKE 2024), and proposes better editing methods (MEMLA, LU-LAFNs via language-agnostic factual neurons, LangEdit null-space, MEMAT attention editing, ReMaKE retrieval). ECLeKTic (2025) shows SOTA models fail to share knowledge behaviorally; Tracing the Roots of Facts (2024) and One Mind Many Tongues (2024) categorize facts as shared/independent/transferred post hoc. The delta, stated as one-row contrasts: (Cross-lingual editing benchmarks) measure propagation post-hoc after editing -- we predict it before editing; (LU-LAFNs) identify shared neurons and use them only to improve editing -- we use pre-edit overlap as a per-pair transferability predictor and test generalization to held-out pairs; (Tracing the Roots / One Mind Many Tongues) assign facts to shared/independent categories descriptively -- we validate the storage regime causally via edit-locus manipulation and, crucially, show the pre-edit signature forecasts propagation better than resource/behavioral heuristics. None establishes that an intrinsic PRE-edit signature predicts which facts/pairs transfer. Our contribution is diagnostic and predictive; even a negative result is informative because it would challenge the prevailing assumption that localized shared-neuron signatures govern transfer.
Abstract: Editing a fact in one language of a multilingual LLM often fails to update the same fact when queried in another language, particularly across scripts. Prior work treats this as a benchmark failure and proposes better editing algorithms, or categorizes facts as shared/independent after the fact. We instead ask a predictive question: can we tell, BEFORE editing, whether an edit will propagate? We derive, for each fact, an intrinsic pre-edit signature by causal tracing (activation patching + causal mediation) the components most responsible for recalling the fact independently in each language, and computing their cross-language overlap (a sharedness score over shared causal components, not asserted shared parameters). We then perform locate-and-edit updates in one source language and measure recovery in every other language, building a propagation matrix. Our central, falsifiable claim is that the pre-edit sharedness score predicts post-edit propagation per fact and per language-pair, generalizing to held-out facts AND held-out language pairs, and beating operational baselines: subject-token similarity, script/family match, lang2vec distance, resource level, source-edit success, and pre-edit behavioral agreement, in a multivariate analysis that controls for resource level and behavioral similarity. We further show sharedness correlates with typological/script distance (the hybrid pattern), and that editing at the causally-shared components improves propagation. Practical use: a maintainer can pre-screen whether a multilingual edit should be applied globally, localized per language, or retried with a different method, saving the cost of trial-editing every language pair (roughly O(L) pre-edit traces replacing O(L^2) trial edit-and-test cycles). This serves model maintainers, cross-lingual knowledge-editing researchers, benchmark designers, and safety teams auditing fact consistency. We test on mLAMA and Bi-ZsRE across 12+ languages spanning five scripts and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B, with confidence intervals, per-model variance, and pre-registered success criteria.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Data: parallel factual triples from mLAMA (existing; ~44k templated facts over 53 languages) and Bi-ZsRE (existing bilingual edit benchmark), subsampled to 1,500 subject-relation-object facts with clean single-token or short objects. Languages: 12 spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families across resource levels; English is the reference. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen except during edits; greedy, temperature 0. Locate-and-edit uses ROME and MEMIT with the authors' default hyperparameters; causal tracing uses activation patching and causal mediation (ROME-style corrupted-restored runs). Editing 1,500 facts x 12 source languages with per-fact tracing is heavy but each ROME edit and trace is seconds-scale, keeping the whole suite within a single-GPU-week budget per model. Pre-registered criteria and reporting: all headline metrics carry bootstrap 95% CIs and are reported per model; success/failure thresholds below are fixed in advance. Baseline predictors (used throughout Experiment 2): subject-token cosine similarity across languages, binary script/family match, lang2vec typological distance, resource level, source-edit success, and pre-edit behavioral agreement (does the model answer the fact consistently in both languages before any edit); the sharedness signature must beat these individually and add unique variance in a multivariate model.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a measurable, reproducible pre-edit cross-lingual sharedness signature): tests that facts occupy a real, non-degenerate storage spectrum readable before any edit. Data/model as Setup. Method: for each fact, causal-trace independently in each language to find the top-k components (MLP/attention) whose restoration recovers the object token; define per-language-pair sharedness = Jaccard overlap (and rank correlation) of those causally-important components; aggregate to a per-fact sharedness profile. Sensitivity analyses (to show the signature is stable, not an artifact): vary top-k, component type (MLP vs attention), overlap metric (Jaccard vs rank correlation vs cosine of attribution maps), prompt template, and object position, and report signature stability across these. Controls: separate same-script from cross-script pairs; add transliteration controls so shared subword/orthographic overlap is not mistaken for deep sharing; a shallow-embedding control checks whether overlap merely tracks subject-token/embedding similarity rather than deep factual sharing. Decisive metric: the across-fact distribution of sharedness AND its stability across the two tracing methods, measured as Spearman between the two methods' sharedness scores. Convincing result: sharedness spans a wide, non-degenerate range (IQR >0.3 on the 0-1 Jaccard scale), the two tracing methods agree at Spearman >=0.5, and the signature survives the sensitivity analyses and is not explained by subject-token overlap alone. Secondary: sharedness correlates negatively with lang2vec distance and is lower across scripts. Indecision band: method agreement 0.3-0.5 = usable but noisy; <0.3 = tracing artifact, undermining H1; IQR <0.1 = no topology variation, refuting the spectrum. Negative result (no reproducible variation) means there is no measurable storage topology.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- predicting edit propagation from the pre-edit signature, beating heuristics: the core test): tests that cross-lingual propagation is predictable per fact and per language-pair from the pre-edit signature ALONE. Data/model as Setup. Method: apply ROME/MEMIT to change each fact in a single source language and query every target language, recording edit success (source), cross-lingual propagation (target reliability), and locality (unrelated facts unchanged); condition all analyses on successful source-language edits. Train a predictor mapping the Experiment 1 pre-edit sharedness signature to per-pair propagation, on a fact split, and test on held-out facts AND held-out language pairs. Compare against each baseline predictor above, and run a multivariate model that enters sharedness alongside resource level and pre-edit behavioral agreement to test unique contribution. Decisive metric: held-out AUC for transfer vs no-transfer from the pre-edit signature alone (with Spearman(sharedness, propagation) alongside), AND the AUC gain of sharedness over the best single baseline and its unique multivariate contribution. Convincing result: held-out AUC >=0.75 and Spearman >=0.5, generalising to held-out language pairs, AND sharedness beats the best baseline by >=0.05 AUC with a significant unique multivariate contribution after controlling for resource level and behavioral agreement. Indecision band: AUC 0.6-0.75, or a gain over baselines <0.05 = weak/partial predictor; AUC <0.6 (near chance) or no gain over heuristics = the signature does not predict propagation beyond simple cues, refuting H2. Negative result (chance-level or no advantage over heuristics) refutes the pre-edit predictability claim -- itself informative against shared-neuron assumptions.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- edit locus causally governs propagation, validating the topology): tests that the regime is causally real. Data: high-sharedness vs low-sharedness facts from Experiment 1, matched on source-edit success and resource level. Model as Setup. Method: operationalize 'edit at the shared locus' concretely for ROME/MEMIT -- restrict the update to the layers/components in the cross-language shared set (or their union) by projecting the update onto those component subspaces -- and run a small feasibility pilot first to confirm such constrained edits are stable. For each fact edit at (i) a single language's own causal locus, (ii) the union/most-shared locus, and (iii) the default ROME locus; measure cross-lingual propagation and locality. Decisive metric: propagation reliability from editing the shared/union locus versus a single-language locus, contrasted between shared and duplicated facts (the interaction is the evidence). Convincing result: for shared facts, editing the shared components yields >=20 pp higher cross-lingual propagation than a single-language locus, while duplicated facts require multi-locus editing and single-locus edits stay language-locked, with locality preserved (unrelated facts change <5%). Indecision band: shared-locus advantage 8-20 pp = partial causal support; <8 pp = edit locus does not matter and the topology is not the causal propagation mechanism, refuting H3. Negative result (propagation independent of edit locus) refutes the causal reality of the storage topology.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Causal tracing localization is noisy and can be diffuse, weakening the sharedness signal; we mitigate with two tracing methods, report stability, and run the Experiment-1 sensitivity analyses. 2. Tokenization/transliteration differences across scripts complicate identifying comparable components and matching object tokens; we restrict to clean object tokenization, use last-token-of-object representations, add transliteration controls, and analyze same-script vs cross-script pairs separately. 3. Locate-and-edit methods may fail to edit at all in low-resource languages, confounding propagation with edit success; we condition on successful source-language edits. 4. Sharedness and propagation could both track resource level or shallow subject-form/embedding overlap rather than deep storage; we control with resource-matched facts, a shallow-embedding control, the transliteration controls, and a multivariate predictor test, and require generalization to held-out language pairs. 5. The shared/duplicated dichotomy may be a continuum; we present it as a spectrum and report continuous predictive power, not forced discrete classes. 6. We claim shared causal COMPONENTS, not literally shared parameters, unless parameter-level evidence is obtained. 7. 'Editing at the shared locus' may be infeasible for some facts; the Experiment-3 feasibility pilot checks this. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: conceptual_metaphor_override
Title: Anger Is Not Always Fire: How Multilingual LLMs Override Culture-Specific Idiom Meanings with Their Dominant Language's Conceptual Metaphors
Short Hypothesis: When interpreting an idiom in a non-dominant language, multilingual LLMs covertly retrieve the figurative meaning implied by their DOMINANT language's conceptual-metaphor system, and this dominant-language figurative reading is co-activated as a latent competitor. For idioms whose source-language conceptual metaphor differs from the dominant language's (culture-specific idioms), this causes systematic misinterpretation, whereas idioms grounded in a shared/universal conceptual metaphor are interpreted correctly. The override is a locatable figurative-retrieval-and-selection failure whose strength scales with the conceptual-metaphor distance between the query language and the dominant language, not with resource level.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes idiom processing to early-layer 'Idiom Heads' and competing figurative/literal pathways (Anatomy of an Idiom 2025; Tug-of-war between figurative and literal 2025; NMT idiom analysis 2022). Cross-lingual work shows figurative-detection knowledge sits in middle layers and transfers across languages (Metaphors in PLMs 2022), that a reusable cross-lingual figurative-GENERATION steering direction exists (Cross-Lingual Steering for Figurative Language Generation 2026), and that cross-lingual lexical overlap and shared idioms boost PIE disambiguation (MultiCoPIE 2025; Meta4XNLI 2024). All of these treat figurativeness as a single transferable feature and study detection/generation of figurativeness, or literal-vs-figurative disambiguation WITHIN a language. None asks whether the SPECIFIC figurative MEANING retrieved for a foreign idiom is contaminated by the dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping, nor identifies a cross-lingual conceptual-metaphor OVERRIDE as a co-activation/selection failure. We reframe idiom comprehension as a cross-cultural meaning-SELECTION problem grounded in Conceptual Metaphor Theory, provide causal (patching + steering) evidence for a figurative-retrieval locus that inherits the dominant metaphor, and dissociate conceptual-metaphor distance from resource level. Novelty typing: the behavioral weakness on culture-specific figurative language may be partly known from cultural-translation and multicultural-proverb work; our distinct contribution is the MECHANISTIC explanation - a causal selection failure in which the dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping is co-activated and wins - plus an operational conceptual-metaphor DISTANCE metric and a training-free fix. This bears on the cognitive science of analogy/metaphor, language documentation, and multilingual interpretability, and on practical evaluation of multilingual assistants, translation, and cross-cultural QA.
Abstract: Idioms encode culture-specific conceptual metaphors: 'anger is fire' is near-universal, but many idioms map emotions and concepts through images idiosyncratic to one language's cultural history. A multilingual model reading an idiom in a non-dominant language must retrieve the meaning licensed by THAT language's conceptual system, not its own dominant one. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs instead default to their dominant language's conceptual-metaphor mapping, covertly co-activating the dominant-language figurative reading and systematically misinterpreting idioms whose source metaphor diverges from it. We test this with a controlled set of idioms drawn from multilingual idiom corpora (MultiCoPIE, IdiomX, Meta4XNLI), each annotated with its underlying conceptual metaphor and labeled shared (same mapping as the dominant language) or culture-specific (divergent mapping), rendered across 10+ languages spanning several scripts and families. Behaviorally, we measure interpretation accuracy and the rate at which the model's paraphrase/entailment judgment matches the dominant-language metaphor rather than the correct source meaning. Mechanistically, we (i) show via logit-lens and probes that the dominant-language figurative meaning is decodable during foreign-idiom processing (co-activation), (ii) locate a mid/early-layer figurative-retrieval stage via activation patching whose swap flips the selected meaning, and (iii) steer along a recovered conceptual-metaphor direction to causally repair culture-specific misinterpretations and to induce override on shared idioms. We predict override strength scales with conceptual-metaphor distance and not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work gives the first mechanistic account of cross-cultural conceptual-metaphor interference in multilingual LLMs and a training-free fix. We operationalize conceptual-metaphor distance from Conceptual Metaphor Theory source-domain annotations (agreement reported per language pair), so it is not a post hoc label. Falsifiable core: if culture-specific and shared idioms show equal override and accuracy, or if no located component flips the selected meaning, the dominant-language-override account is rejected. The main claim is deliberately narrow - conceptual-metaphor selection in idiom interpretation - and we do not extrapolate to general multicultural reasoning beyond what is tested.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "dominant language" is operationalized per model as English (its highest-resource pretraining language), verified by measuring monolingual idiom-interpretation accuracy per language.
