Decisive metric: truth-value flip rate minus control, with propositional content preserved; secondary: overlap with negation-scope heads (should be partial/low). Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp flip indicates a distributed representation; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp flip means resolution is not causally locatable and that part of the hypothesis fails.

Experiment 5 (H-dose - flip strength tracks negative-concord grammaticalization, not resource): Tests the dissociation between grammaticalization and resource. Data: per-language flip/disagreement rate vs the grammaticalization index and a resource-level proxy; key contrast a lower-resource strong-NC language (e.g. Polish) vs a higher-resource DN language. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of flip/disagreement with grammaticalization controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for grammaticalization. Convincing result: partial correlation with grammaticalization >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: grammaticalization correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: flips track resource (|rho| >=0.4) not grammaticalization, refuting the scaling claim.

Experiment 6 (H-steer - steering repairs safety inversions and induces flips): Tests the training-free causal fix and induction. Data: flipped safety instructions (repair); correctly-resolved items (induction); single-negation and non-negated items (specificity). Polarity-resolution direction = mean activation difference between NC-forced and DN-forced runs, pooled across languages, at the Exp. 4 layer. Systems compared: steering vs explicit disambiguation prompting ("interpret two negatives as cancelling") vs translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: safety-repair rate (fraction of inverted instructions corrected) minus baseline; secondary: induction rate, truth-value/instruction accuracy, specificity (single-negation and non-negated items unchanged), fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: repair rate >=15 pp over baseline with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline; induction confirms functional causality. Indecision band: 5-15 pp repair, or specificity change 5-10 pp, indicates a weak/leaky fix. Negative result: <5 pp repair means the direction is not functionally causal, refuting the steerability claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; adjacent vs long-distance negators; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: truth-value distribution, cross-language disagreement, instruction-inversion rate, polarity probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with grammaticalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of resolved polarity may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance. 2. Even within NC/DN languages, native interpretation of stacked negatives can be prosody/context-dependent and genuinely ambiguous (as the Mandarin-Spanish 2023 study notes); we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and treat mixed languages as a separate class rather than forcing a binary. 3. The flip could be confounded with translation artifacts of negative indefinites across languages; single-negation controls and the cross-language agreement they should show isolate the concord effect from mere translation noise. 4. Strong models may collapse to one default rule (likely DN/English) regardless of query language, weakening cross-language variation; even documenting a near-universal English-DN default that resists explicit NC instructions, and its safety consequences, is a valuable finding, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of negators/negative indefinites varies across scripts; we use pooled-span or clause-final token representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The grammaticalization-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to index operationalization and alternative language choices. 7. Steering may trade polarity correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: language_as_temporal_anchor
Title: What Year Is It in Your Language? Query Language as a Covert Temporal Anchor for Time-Sensitive Facts in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: For facts whose correct answer changes over time (e.g., current heads of state, champions, populations), the language a question is asked in covertly sets the model's default temporal anchor: the model tends to answer with the fact-state that was dominant in that language's training data era, so different languages return answers 'frozen' at different points in time. We hypothesize (a) a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation exists that determines which fact-version is retrieved; (b) the query language causally sets this anchor, producing systematic per-language recency offsets on time-sensitive facts; and (c) the size of the offset scales with the resource/coverage recency of the language rather than with typological distance, and can be causally corrected by steering the shared temporal-anchor direction without retraining.
Related Work: Parametric Temporal Conflict (Hossain et al. 2026) shows LLMs store both outdated and updated facts and default to the outdated one via a localized upper-layer representational preference, but the study is monolingual (English) and never treats language as a variable. Time Travel Engine (2026) shows a continuous, cross-lingually isomorphic temporal manifold and steers 'zeitgeist', but studies stylistic/era navigation, not factual-recency errors and not the query language's causal role in choosing which factual version is recalled. TiEBe (2025) and LiveCLKTBench (2025) document geographic and language-dependent recall gaps for time-sensitive events, but interpret them as resource/transfer gaps and provide no mechanistic account. EverGreenQA (2025) classifies question mutability but does not study per-language temporal drift. Multilingual knowledge-editing work (MLaKE, XME, LangEdit, LU-LAFNs) treats facts as static and studies edit propagation. None frames the query language as an implicit temporal anchor that selects among stored fact-versions, nor gives causal (patching + steering) evidence for a language-set temporal-anchor variable that produces predictable per-language recency offsets. We contribute this reframing, a quantitative per-language 'temporal offset' metric, and a training-free anchor-steering fix. Novelty typing: prior work separately shows temporal manifolds (Time Travel Engine), timeliness gaps (TiEBe, LiveCLKTBench), and temporal-drift directions, but none shows the QUERY LANGUAGE causally selecting among co-present fact-versions; that causal claim, plus the per-language Temporal Offset metric and the anchor-steering fix, is the new part. Beneficiaries include multilingual QA/RAG builders, benchmark designers, and knowledge-editing researchers. Falsifiable core in one sentence: language-identity signals set the retrieval anchor for time-sensitive facts - refuted if per-language offsets vanish, if date-prefixing cannot recover the current value (i.e. the offset is ignorance, not anchoring), or if patching the language signal does not shift the fact-version.
Abstract: Many facts have no timeless answer: the head of state, the reigning champion, or a country's population all change over time, and a language model must decide which era's answer to give. We ask whether the language in which a question is posed covertly determines this decision. We hypothesize that the query language acts as an implicit temporal anchor, biasing a multilingual LLM toward the fact-state dominant in that language's training data, so the same question answered in different languages returns answers effectively frozen at different times. We build TIME-DRIFT, a set of time-sensitive facts with dated ground-truth transitions (from Wikidata position-holder changes and dated records), rendered in 12+ languages spanning several scripts and families, and measure a per-language Temporal Offset: how far behind the true current state each language's default answer sits. Mechanistically, we test for a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation using linear probes and vocabulary projection, then use activation patching to test whether swapping late-layer language-identity signals shifts the retrieved fact-version, and whether steering a recovered temporal-anchor direction moves answers forward or backward in time. We predict systematic per-language offsets that scale with a language's data-recency/coverage rather than typological distance, that the offset is causally set by a language-conditioned anchor separable from fact content, and that anchor-steering recovers the current answer in low-recency languages without harming fluency, outperforming date-prefix prompting and translate-to-English baselines. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. The work reframes cross-lingual factual disparities as a controllable temporal-anchoring phenomenon. The user-facing failure mode is concrete: the same current-fact question returns inconsistent, differently-outdated answers across languages. Practically, we chart when to translate-to-English, when not to, and when anchor-steering helps, and we include evergreen and matched-paraphrase controls so the effect is shown to be time-specific rather than generic drift.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic/linear regressors on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by fact, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); default answers are elicited by greedy decoding with no date cue. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points. Dataset (TIME-DRIFT), constructed from Wikidata: facts with dated transitions - position-holders (heads of state, club managers, CEO tenures) and dated records (sports champions, tallest building, world-population brackets) - each with a full timeline of (value, valid-from, valid-to). Wikidata exposes hundreds of thousands of such position statements; we select facts with >=2 transitions inside the models' plausible pretraining window and clean, matchable answer tokens, targeting ~400 facts x 12+ languages (Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari, 4+ families) with matched entity names, plus an evergreen/timeless-fact control set (~100 facts). Fewer than all Wikidata positions because each fact needs a verified transition timeline and cross-language name matching. Per language we compute data-recency/coverage proxies (topic Wikipedia edit recency, article length, pretraining-share estimate) and lang2vec typological/script distance to the dominant language.

Experiment 1 (H-behavior - query language produces per-language recency offsets): Tests whether the same time-sensitive question, asked in different languages, returns answers frozen at different times. Data: the ~400 TIME-DRIFT facts in each language; each default answer is mapped to its validity interval via the timeline. Decisive metric: per-language Temporal Offset = (true current date) minus (midpoint of the answered value's validity interval), in years; secondary: fraction returning the outdated vs current value, and cross-language answer-disagreement rate on identical facts. Systems compared: each language vs the dominant-language offset; evergreen control set (should show near-zero offset). Convincing result: at least half the non-dominant languages show a mean offset differing from the dominant language by >=1.0 year with 95% CI excluding 0, and cross-language disagreement on time-sensitive facts exceeds disagreement on evergreen facts by >=15 pp. Indecision band: per-language offset differences of 0.3-1.0 year, or CIs touching 0, are reported as suggestive only. Negative result: offsets within 0.3 year of the dominant language across languages means the query language does not set a temporal anchor and the behavioral claim fails.

Experiment 2 (H-a - a shared, language-agnostic temporal-anchor representation): Tests whether a single representation encodes the retrieved fact's era across languages. Data: TIME-DRIFT hidden states at answer positions, mid/late layers. A probe decodes the era/date of the retrieved fact; a probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: within-language probe, cross-language transfer probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language transfer accuracy of the era probe minus shuffled control; secondary: agreement between decoded era and the answered value's actual date. Convincing result: transfer accuracy >=15 pp above control and decoded era matches the answered value's date on held-out languages (evidence of one shared anchor). Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control indicates a partially shared representation; reported as such. Negative result: transfer within 5 pp of control means anchors are language-specific, not shared, weakening claim (a). Decodability is not use; Exp. 3 is required.

Experiment 3 (H-b - the query language causally sets the anchor): Tests whether swapping the language-identity signal shifts which fact-version is retrieved. Data: facts where a low-recency language returns the outdated value and the dominant language returns the current value. Activation patching transfers the late-layer language-identity signal from the dominant run into the low-recency run. Systems compared: patch at the language-identity component vs random-component control; also compare against date-prefix prompting ("As of 2024, ...") to confirm the newer value is present but not defaulted-to (distinguishing anchoring from ignorance). Decisive metric: fact-version shift rate (fraction of low-recency runs that flip toward the current value) minus control, with fact identity preserved. Convincing result: shift rate >=15 pp above control AND date-prefix prompting also recovers the current value on the same items (co-present versions, not missing knowledge). Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is inconclusive - reported as partial causal role. Negative result: <=5 pp above control, or date-prefix failing to recover the current value, means the offset reflects missing knowledge rather than a language-set anchor, and claim (b) fails.

Experiment 4 (H-c - offset scales with data-recency, not typological distance): Tests the dissociation between recency/coverage and typology. Data: per-language Temporal Offset vs (i) recency/coverage proxies and (ii) lang2vec typological/script distance; the key contrast is a typologically distant but well-covered language vs a close but sparsely-covered one. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of offset with recency controlling for typology, and with typology controlling for recency. Convincing result: partial correlation with recency >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while partial correlation with typology is indistinguishable from 0 (CI includes 0). Indecision band: recency correlation 0.2-0.4, or both partials overlapping in CI, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: offset tracks typology (|rho| >=0.4) and not recency, refuting claim (c)'s scaling half.

Experiment 5 (H-c - training-free correction by steering the shared anchor): Tests whether steering the temporal-anchor direction moves answers in time without retraining. Data: low-recency-language queries returning outdated values; the evergreen control set for specificity. A temporal-anchor direction = mean activation difference between "as of [recent year]" and "as of [older year]" framings, pooled across languages. Systems compared: anchor steering vs date-prefix prompting vs translate-to-English-first; a reverse-steer control (steer backward) to confirm the direction is temporal, not a generic correctness push. Decisive metric: recency-correction rate (fraction flipped to the current value) minus the outdated-answer baseline; secondary: specificity on evergreen facts (should stay unchanged), output-language fidelity, fluency (perplexity), and a monotone dose-response for reverse steering (older values recalled at larger backward magnitude). Convincing result: forward steering corrects >=15 pp more items than the baseline while changing <=5 pp of evergreen facts, and reverse steering yields a monotone shift to older values. Indecision band: 5-15 pp correction, or evergreen change of 5-10 pp, is reported as a weak/selective effect. Negative result: <5 pp correction or evergreen change exceeding forward correction means the direction is not functionally temporal, refuting the steerability claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; fact-type breakdown (positions vs records); model scale. Reported metrics throughout: Temporal Offset, outdated-answer rate, cross-language disagreement, probe/transfer accuracy, patching shift rate, steering correction/induction rate, specificity, fluency, Spearman with recency vs typology.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground-truth 'current' value and exact transition dates can be ambiguous or lag reality; we restrict to Wikidata-verified transitions with clear valid-from/valid-to intervals and exclude contested cases. 2. The observed offset could reflect missing recent knowledge rather than a language-set anchor over co-present versions; the patching (Exp. 3) and the demonstration that date-prefix prompting recovers the current value (as in PTC) test whether newer knowledge is present but not defaulted-to, distinguishing anchoring from ignorance. 3. Probe decodability of era may reflect the readout basis, not a used representation; we require the causal patching and steering results to establish functional relevance. 4. Per-language recency proxies are noisy; we use multiple proxies and report robustness, and the typology-vs-recency dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts. 5. Steering may over-shift and harm evergreen facts; the evergreen control set and specificity/fluency metrics test selectivity. 6. Tokenization/entity-name differences across scripts complicate answer matching; we restrict to entities with clean, matchable answer tokens and use last-token-of-answer representations. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: reasoning_language_mismatch
Title: Thinking in One Language, Writing in Another: Measuring the Cost of Surface-Latent Reasoning-Language Mismatch in Multilingual CoT
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs have a per-item 'latent reasoning language' (the language whose token representations dominate hidden states during the reasoning steps), which is often but not always English. The primary novel contribution is (i) a rigorous per-item measurement of this latent language and (ii) a causal estimate of a 'mismatch cost': reasoning accuracy is governed less by the surface language of the prompt than by the *mismatch* between the surface CoT language the model is forced to write in and its latent reasoning language, and this cost is confirmed by a steering control that alters the internal language while holding surface tokens fixed. We predict the mismatch cost grows with representational and typological surface-latent distance, and that per-item alignment of the surface CoT language to the latent language improves multilingual reasoning more than uniformly forcing English or the prompt language. The intervention is a secondary demonstration, not the core claim.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-centric latent space (Do Llamas Work in English? 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English? 2025; Transfer Neurons Hypothesis 2025), that latent multilingual reasoning is English-aligned but uneven (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026), that language mixing in traces reflects internal preferences and that constrained/switch-aware decoding helps (Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025; EMNLP 2025 switch-utility probe work), and that ablating language-specific components boosts reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025). We explicitly acknowledge that language mixing and helpful step-level switching are already known; we do NOT claim them. The contrast, by row: unit of prediction -- prior work is global (a fixed English pivot) or step-level (which token to switch on); ours is the WHOLE-ITEM latent language and its variation across items. Causal test -- prior work correlates mixing with outcomes or ablates language; ours isolates internal-vs-surface language via a steering control that changes only the internal language. Intervention type -- prior work does step-level switch-aware decoding; ours does per-item surface-language selection matched to the measured latent language. Benchmark setting -- we add a setting (single-language-enforced monolingual CoT, where step-level switching is disallowed) in which switch-level methods are not directly applicable, isolating whole-item alignment. We claim only the whole-item latent-language framing and the causal internal-vs-surface isolation as new.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are widely believed to 'think in English' internally while writing chain-of-thought (CoT) in the prompt's language. We challenge the assumption that this latent reasoning language is a fixed, global, English-centric pivot. Instead we hypothesize that each reasoning problem induces a per-item *latent reasoning language*—the language whose token representations dominate hidden states during the reasoning steps—that varies across items, and that accuracy is driven by the *mismatch* between the surface language the model is forced to verbalize CoT in and this latent language. Our contribution is a measurement plus a causal estimate, not merely an intervention. We introduce (1) a per-item Latent Language Profile, computed by applying logit-lens/probing to hidden states at reasoning-step token positions, aggregating over a specified layer band and step-token set with an explicit per-item uncertainty/confidence estimate; and (2) a Mismatch Cost, the accuracy change when the model reasons in a surface language that agrees vs disagrees with its latent profile, whose causal status we confirm with a steering control that changes only the internal language while holding surface tokens fixed and controlling for output-language fidelity and token entropy. We predict Mismatch Cost grows with representational and typological surface-latent distance. We validate on multilingual math (MGSM), commonsense (XCOPA), and multi-hop QA across 15+ languages and Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and a reasoning-distilled model, using human-verified parallel data on a subset to rule out MT artifacts. Practice: either outcome is decision-relevant -- confirmation supports alignment-aware decoding defaults and deployment-time per-item language selection (e.g. low-resource educational QA and customer support where a single monolingual trace is required), while refutation supports language-mixing as the better paradigm. We compare per-item alignment against uniform-English, prompt-language, forced-Latin/Han, a published switch-level baseline, no-CoT, and free-mixing, and quantify low-resource accuracy gains at fixed compute.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Tasks: MGSM multilingual grade-school math (existing; 250 parallel problems), XCOPA commonsense (existing; ~500 items/language), and a translated 2-hop QA subset (300 items). Languages: 15 spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families; items are parallel translations so true difficulty is fixed across languages, with human-verified parallel data on a 10% subset (and native-speaker spot-checks) so item-level latent-language variation cannot be an MT artifact. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (documented language mixing). All weights frozen; CoT at temperature 0, 3 prompt seeds. Language-ID probes are L2 logistic regressions trained on a held-out, item-disjoint split, validated by cross-language transfer accuracy before use. Latent-language operationalization (fixed in advance): at reasoning-step token positions, per layer in a specified mid-to-late band, take the probe's language posterior; aggregate across the band and step tokens by mean posterior; the per-item latent language is the argmax, and we record a confidence = margin between top two languages, carrying items below a confidence floor as 'undetermined' rather than forcing a label. All analyses are script/tokenization-normalized (probes restricted to clean answer/step tokens; per-language token-budget effects reported). Decision thresholds below are set from a pilot power analysis (effect sizes from prior multilingual-CoT gaps), not chosen arbitrarily.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a per-item latent reasoning language that varies across items): tests that the latent language is item-dependent, not a single fixed pivot. Data/model as Setup. Method: compute the per-item latent language and confidence as in Setup. Decisive metric: fraction of (confident) items whose latent language differs from the model's MODAL latent language, tested against a globally-fixed null. Convincing result: >=20% of confident items have a non-modal latent language and the variation is systematic (shifts with task or target language), rejecting the globally-fixed null. Indecision band: 8-20% = weak variability, mostly a global pivot (the non-English fraction and its predictive value still a contribution); <8% = effectively globally fixed and the per-item claim collapses to the known global-pivot picture. Negative result (latent language essentially always English) refutes per-item variation; the reasoning-distilled model is the decisive test case.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- Mismatch Cost, causal and distance-scaled): tests that accuracy is driven by surface-latent mismatch, grows with distance, and is internal rather than a surface artifact. Data/model as Setup. Method: for each item elicit CoT under surface languages that (a) match the measured latent language, (b) equal the prompt language, (c) equal English, (d) are maximally distant, enforcing the reasoning-step language via constrained decoding; Mismatch Cost = accuracy(matched) - accuracy(mismatched). Causal control (steering, specified in detail): construct a language direction as the mean activation difference between latent-language and target-language reasoning-step states at the identified band; sweep steering strength; steer to align/misalign the INTERNAL language while holding the surface language fixed; apply semantic-preservation checks and NEGATIVE CONTROLS (norm-matched random directions, non-language directions) that must produce no accuracy change; analyses control for output-language fidelity and token entropy. Decisive metric: Mismatch Cost in exact-match accuracy points, Spearman(Mismatch Cost, distance) with distance both representational (cosine of mean reasoning-step activations) and lang2vec typological, and the steering-induced accuracy change under the causal control. Convincing result: matched exceeds mismatched by >=3 accuracy points on average, Spearman >=0.4 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.15, AND the steering control reproduces the accuracy change when only internal language is altered while random/non-language controls do not. Indecision band: matched advantage 1-3 points = weak (suggestive); <1 point = no mismatch cost, refuting H2; a null steering control (or an effect matched by random-direction controls) means decodability is epiphenomenal and the causal claim is refuted even if the behavioral gap holds. Negative result (no accuracy difference by match) refutes the mismatch account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- per-item alignment beats uniform choices and step-level baselines): tests that selecting the surface CoT language per item to match the measured latent language improves reasoning more than any single global choice, and situates it against step-level and free-mixing paradigms. Data/model as Setup, including a monolingual-enforced setting where mid-trace switching is disallowed (isolating whole-item alignment from step-level switching). Method: at inference measure the latent language from a short forced CoT prefix, then generate the full CoT in that language. Systems compared: per-item alignment vs uniform-English, prompt-language, forced-Latin/Han, a published switch-level language-mixing decoding baseline, no-CoT, free-mixing (unconstrained), and an oracle (best language per item, upper bound). Decisive metric: exact-match accuracy averaged over the 15 languages (extra compute and output-language fidelity reported), plus low-resource-subset accuracy at fixed compute. Convincing result: per-item alignment beats the best fixed baseline by >=2 accuracy points and closes >=50% of the oracle gap at <2x inference compute; the no-CoT and free-mixing conditions establish whether forcing any monolingual surface CoT is itself the degradation source. Indecision band: 0.5-2 point gain = marginal (full comparison and oracle gap reported); <0.5 point = no benefit over a fixed choice, refuting H3; if free-mixing beats all aligned monolingual conditions, we report that language-mixing is the better paradigm (a decision-relevant refutation). Negative result (a fixed choice or free-mixing matches/beats per-item alignment) refutes the actionable per-item-alignment claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Logit-lens/probe decodability at reasoning-step positions may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally-used latent language; we require the causal steering control with random/non-language negative controls (Exp. 2) and control for output-language fidelity and token entropy. 2. The per-item latent language may in practice be almost always English for some models, collapsing the hypothesis to a global-pivot story; even so, quantifying the small non-English fraction and its predictive value is a contribution, and the reasoning-distilled model provides larger latent variability. 3. Constrained decoding can degrade fluency and confound accuracy with generation difficulty; we report output-language fidelity, use steering as a fluency-preserving alternative, and include no-CoT/free-mixing conditions. 4. Item-level latent variation could be an MT artifact; human-verified parallel data on a subset guards against this. 5. Tokenization/script differences complicate cross-language logit-lens comparison; probes are restricted to clean answer/step tokens, analyses are script/tokenization-normalized, and per-language token budgets are reported. 6. The per-item intervention adds a short extra forward pass; we report compute overhead and compare to the oracle to bound achievable gains. 7. Decision thresholds are set from a pilot power analysis, not chosen arbitrarily. 8. Findings may be model-specific; four models across families and one reasoning model address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: digraphia_script_language_dissociation
Title: Same Language, Two Scripts: Using Digraphia to Causally Dissociate Script Identity from Language Identity in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: What prior work calls a model's 'language-identity' representation is substantially a *script-identity* representation. Using digraphic languages (one spoken language written in two scripts, e.g. Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Uzbek Latin/Cyrillic, Punjabi Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi, Hindi/Urdu), we hypothesize that (a) script and language are separable, causally-manipulable directions; (b) factual/semantic knowledge stored while reading one script of a digraphic language fails to transfer to the SAME language in its other script far more than the near-identical spoken content warrants, and this failure is a script-binding artifact, not genuine language separation; and (c) a training-free 'latent transliteration' steering (swapping only the script direction) recovers cross-script knowledge without translation.
Related Work: Prior work shows script is linearly encoded and that writing-system identity is what token-embedding geometry captures (Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023), that LLMs latently romanize non-Roman scripts as an intermediate bridge (RomanLens 2025), that script vectors linearly steer output script in speech models (Linear Script Representations 2026), that script similarity dominates cross-lingual knowledge sharing and cross-lingual editing fails across script families (Beneath the Surface 2024; XME 2024), and that transliteration to a common script improves multilingual modeling (Does Transliteration Help 2023; Aksharantar 2022). All of these treat script and language as entangled, or study script effects across *different* languages, where script and language covary. None uses digraphia—the unique natural experiment where language is held constant and only script varies (and where the same script can be shared across different languages)—to causally *dissociate* a script-identity representation from a language-identity representation, nor tests whether cross-script knowledge-transfer failure within one language is a re-bindable script artifact. We contribute this dissociation, a causal script-vs-language localization, and a training-free latent-transliteration fix. Novelty typing (narrow): we do not claim to newly discover that script matters or 'dominates' language; the specific new contribution is the CAUSAL DISSOCIATION - independent intervention on a script direction versus a language direction with an off-target-change control, which prior digraphia and script-dominance work does not test - with cross-script knowledge transfer and latent transliteration as applications. Real-world relevance spans the many digraphic and transliterated communities (Serbian, Uzbek, Kazakh, Punjabi, Hindi/Urdu, Sindhi, and romanized input generally), and the diagnostic informs benchmarking, cross-lingual editing, and transliteration pipelines.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are said to compute in a shared concept space and carry a 'language-identity' variable that governs decoding. But in almost all prior studies, language and script covary, so it is unknown how much of that 'language' variable is really *script*. Digraphic languages—a single spoken language written in two scripts (Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin, Uzbek in Latin and Cyrillic, Punjabi in Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi, Hindi/Urdu)—provide a clean natural experiment: they hold language constant while varying script, and (via shared scripts across languages) hold script constant while varying language. We use them to dissociate a script-identity representation from a language-identity representation. First, we train linear probes and use activation patching to test whether script and language are separable, causally-manipulable directions, and whether the classic 'language vector' is dominated by its script component. Second, we measure within-language cross-script knowledge transfer: a fact taught or queried in one script of a digraphic language should be recoverable in the other script if knowledge is language-shared, but we predict a large script-bound gap, especially where the two scripts are orthographically dissimilar. Third, we localize where script gates retrieval and test a training-free 'latent transliteration'—steering only the script direction—to recover cross-script knowledge, compared against surface transliteration and translation baselines. Experiments span Serbian, Uzbek, Kazakh, Punjabi, Hindi/Urdu, and Sindhi using Dakshina/Aksharantar transliteration resources and mLAMA facts, on Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. The work turns digraphia into a precise instrument for separating what multilingual models know about *languages* from what they know about *scripts*. The primary contribution is the causal script-vs-language dissociation; the knowledge-transfer and latent-transliteration results follow from it. Falsifiable core: if a mean-difference 'language vector' places most of its norm off the script direction and script and language cannot be flipped independently with low off-target change, the reframing is rejected.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by utterance, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); factual queries scored under greedy decoding. Steering, activation patching, and locate-and-edit (ROME/MEMIT) modify activations/weights only as each experiment specifies; base weights are otherwise frozen. "pp" = percentage points; "digraphic" = one spoken language written in two scripts. Data: identical utterances/facts rendered in both scripts of each digraphic language - Serbian (Cyrillic/Latin), Uzbek (Latin/Cyrillic), Kazakh (Cyrillic/Latin), Punjabi (Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi), Hindi/Urdu (Devanagari/Perso-Arabic), Sindhi (Perso-Arabic/Devanagari) - using Dakshina (~10k romanization/native pairs per language) and Aksharantar (~26M transliteration pairs across 21 Indic languages) as verified transliteration sources; facts from mLAMA/BMLAMA (tens of thousands of templated facts across 50+ languages). We use ~2,000 parallel utterances and ~1,500 facts per digraphic language (both scripts), fewer than the pools because each item must be verified in both scripts and clean-tokenizing. Cross-language same-script controls (Serbian-Cyrillic vs Russian-Cyrillic; Uzbek-Latin vs Turkish-Latin) hold script constant while varying language. Per script pair we compute an orthographic-dissimilarity index (character-overlap and romanization edit distance).

Experiment 1 (H-a - script and language are separable, and the classic "language vector" is mostly script): Tests whether script identity and language identity are distinct decodable directions, and whether the standard mean-difference language vector projects onto the script direction. Data: hidden states from digraphic parallel items (decorrelating script from language) plus same-script cross-language controls. Per-layer probes decode (i) script identity and (ii) language identity. Systems compared: script probe, language probe, label-shuffled controls; the mean-difference "language vector" projected onto recovered script vs language directions. Decisive metric: cosine angle between the recovered script and language directions at the peak layer, and the fraction of the language-vector norm lying along the script direction; secondary: per-layer probe accuracies above shuffled control. Convincing result: script and language are both decodable >=15 pp above control AND the language vector places >50% of its norm on the script direction (supporting "language-identity is substantially script-identity"). Indecision band: language-vector script-projection of 35-50%, or direction angle near 45 degrees, is reported as partial entanglement. Negative result: language-vector script-projection <35% and a large script/language angle means the two are already well separated, refuting the reframing. Decodability is not use; Exp. 2 supplies causal separability.

Experiment 2 (H-a - script and language are independently, causally controllable): Tests whether each attribute can be flipped by patching without disturbing the other. Data: (i) same Serbian sentence run in Cyrillic vs Latin (swap script signal, language constant); (ii) same-script different-language runs Serbian-Cyrillic vs Russian-Cyrillic (swap language signal, script constant). Activation patching transfers the targeted signal between runs. Systems compared: patch at the targeted (script or language) component vs random-component control. Decisive metric: independent controllability = flip rate for the targeted attribute minus preservation-error of the other attribute; reported as a pair (targeted-flip rate, off-target-change rate). Convincing result: targeted-flip rate >=15 pp above control with off-target change <=5 pp, for both the script swap and the language swap. Indecision band: targeted flip 5-15 pp above control, or off-target change 5-10 pp, indicates entangled control; reported as such. Negative result: targeted flip <=5 pp above control, or off-target change exceeding the flip, means the attributes are not independently manipulable and claim (a) fails.

Experiment 3 (H-b - within-language cross-script knowledge fails beyond what surface differences warrant, and the gap tracks orthographic distance): Tests whether knowledge in one script of a digraphic language transfers to the other script, and whether the gap scales with orthographic dissimilarity rather than typology (language is held constant). Data: for each digraphic language, (a) query-side - the same fact asked in each script; (b) edit-side - a ROME/MEMIT update applied while reading one script, then queried in the other. Systems compared: same-script paraphrase control (upper bound), different-language control (lower bound), and the cross-script condition; gap correlated with the orthographic-dissimilarity index. Decisive metric: cross-script accuracy gap = same-script-paraphrase accuracy minus other-script accuracy (query-side), and edit-propagation rate across scripts (edit-side); dose-response Spearman of the gap with orthographic dissimilarity. Convincing result: cross-script gap exceeds the same-script-paraphrase gap by >=15 pp (a script-bound loss beyond surface variation) AND Spearman of gap with orthographic dissimilarity >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0). Indecision band: a 5-15 pp gap, or Spearman 0.2-0.4, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: cross-script gap within 5 pp of the same-script-paraphrase gap means knowledge transfers across scripts and the script-binding-artifact claim fails. Coverage proxies and same-content controls rule out ignorance as the cause.

Experiment 4 (H-c - training-free latent transliteration recovers cross-script knowledge): Tests whether steering only the script direction (language fixed) recovers knowledge without translation. Data: the low-performing script of each digraphic language; a script direction extracted from digraphic pairs. Systems compared: latent-transliteration steering (script direction toward the model's stronger script) vs surface transliteration-then-query vs translate-to-English vs RomanLens-style romanization; a shared-script cross-language control to check steering script alone never changes language. Decisive metric: cross-script knowledge-recovery rate = accuracy gain over the untouched low-performing script; secondary: output-script fidelity, language-preservation (should not flip language), and fluency (perplexity). Convincing result: latent-transliteration recovers >=15 pp accuracy with output-script fidelity >90%, language unchanged (<5 pp language flips), and fluency within 10% of baseline, matching or beating surface transliteration without a separate translation step. Indecision band: 5-15 pp recovery, or language flips of 5-10 pp, indicates a weak/leaky fix; reported as such. Negative result: <5 pp recovery, or steering that flips language, means the script direction does not carry recoverable knowledge and claim (c) fails. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep for where script is malleable; probe transfer across models; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: probe accuracy, script/language direction angle and language-vector projection, causal flip/preservation rates, cross-script accuracy gap, edit-propagation across scripts, Spearman with orthographic distance, steering recovery rate, output-script fidelity, language-preservation, fluency.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of script vs language may reflect the readout basis; the causal patching (Exp. 2) and steering recovery (Exp. 4) are required to establish functional relevance. 2. For some digraphic pairs the two scripts share many characters (Serbian) while others do not (Hindi/Urdu), so effect sizes vary; this is exactly the orthographic-distance dose-response (Exp. 3) rather than a confound. 3. Low-resource scripts (Shahmukhi, Sindhi-Devanagari) may have thin pretraining coverage, confounding script-binding with ignorance; we control with same-language same-content items and report coverage proxies. 4. Transliteration ground truth can be noisy for context-dependent scripts (Perso-Arabic vowel omission); we use validated Dakshina/Aksharantar pairs and native-speaker spot-checks. 5. Tokenization differs sharply across scripts, complicating representation alignment; we use last-token / pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. Steering may trade knowledge recovery for fluency or accidentally change language; the shared-script control (Exp. 4) and fidelity/fluency metrics test selectivity. 7. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: transfer_predictive_gradient_signature
Title: Which Examples Teach the World, Not Just the Language? Predicting Cross-Lingual Transfer of Fine-Tuning Examples from Their Gradient Signature
Short Hypothesis: During source-language fine-tuning, individual training examples vary continuously in how much the skill they teach will transfer to other languages, and this per-example transferability is structured by WHERE the example's learning signal lands: examples whose gradient update falls predominantly on empirically language-shared middle-layer components transfer broadly, whereas those recruiting language-specific top/bottom-layer components stay language-locked. The prediction target is the per-example target-language accuracy delta (averaged over held-out target languages), and the predictor -- a layer-aware Shared-Recruitment Signature computed in a single source-language pass BEFORE any target-language evaluation -- ranks examples by this delta better than magnitude-only or influence-only predictors. Consequently, curating a source-language training set toward high-signature examples yields larger cross-lingual gains than random, size-matched, or unweighted-influence selection, at no extra data cost.
Related Work: The contribution is two-fold and should be read as separable: (i) a new layer-aware, pre-transfer predictor of per-example cross-lingual transferability, and (ii) a curation method built on it. Prior work shows reasoning/skill transfers cross-lingually far better than knowledge (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024), that skill vs. language capabilities occupy separable, largely non-overlapping parameters (Layer Swapping 2024; Unreasonable Effectiveness of Model Merging 2025), that middle-layer representation alignment aids transfer (Middle-Layer Alignment 2025), that language distance predicts transfer gaps (Language Distance & Transfer 2023), and that circuit-targeted fine-tuning of task heads improves low-resource adaptation (CT-SFT 2026). Blevins et al. 2023 analyze which pretraining/data factors predict cross-lingual transfer and use representation/retrieval analyses, but operate at the corpus/language-pair granularity and post hoc: their retrieval and layerwise probes describe aggregate transfer, they do not attribute transfer to individual source-language training examples, and they compute nothing before target evaluation that could RANK examples. Standard data-attribution (TracIn, influence functions) attributes example importance but is agnostic to WHERE in the network the update lands and is not layer-aware. Our new information is precisely the discovery that example-level transferability is organized by shared-vs-specific layer recruitment, expressed as a cheap intrinsic signature computable from the fine-tuning gradient itself, plus its use for curation. We do not claim a general theory of transfer; we claim evidence that some examples are more transferable than others and that a layer-aware score predicts and selects them. To make this measurable we also define a per-example cross-lingual transfer-prediction protocol (validated influence ground truth + held-out target languages) that prior per-example influence work in multilingual fine-tuning does not provide. The mechanism is domain-general: the same shared-vs-task-specific-feature logic should apply to any transfer setting (cross-domain, cross-task) where representations split into shared and specific components.
Abstract: It is well established that skills fine-tuned in one language often transfer to others while knowledge does not, and that skill and language capabilities live in separable parts of a language model. But transfer is measured coarsely, at the level of whole tasks or language pairs. We ask a finer, actionable question: within a single fine-tuning task, do individual training examples differ in how much they transfer cross-lingually, and can we predict which ones will before running any transfer? The exact prediction target is the per-example target-language accuracy delta averaged over held-out target languages. We hypothesize this delta is governed by where the example's gradient update lands: examples whose learning signal is carried predominantly by empirically-identified language-shared middle layers transfer broadly, whereas examples recruiting language-specific top/bottom layers stay language-locked. We define a per-example Shared-Recruitment Signature, the fraction of the example's fine-tuning gradient (update) magnitude falling on language-agnostic middle layers versus language-anchored peripheral layers, plus a sharedness-weighted variant, computable in a single source-language pass. We validate on multilingual reasoning (MGSM-style math, XCOPA, logical/arithmetic templates) by fine-tuning Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B on a source language and measuring per-example contribution to target-language gains via validated influence with a retraining check. Crucially we separate the signature from generic usefulness by controlling in-language gain, example difficulty, gradient norm, and lexical overlap, and we benchmark it against simpler predictors (loss, gradient norm, length, memorization, unweighted influence). We report ranking and calibration metrics, not only correlation. We predict the signature (1) predicts cross-lingual transfer per example, (2) predicts it more strongly than generic usefulness and than magnitude-only baselines, (3) strengthens for typologically distant targets, and (4) enables curation that beats random and size-matched baselines. In a realistic low-resource scenario this yields target-language accuracy at reduced source-annotation cost, turning cross-lingual transfer into a predictable, curatable property of training data.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across experiments). Tasks: multilingual math word problems (MGSM, existing; 250 parallel problems each in the target languages) with an English GSM8K training pool (existing; 8.5k) subsampled to 2,000 for tractable per-example influence estimation; plus XCOPA and logical/arithmetic templates as additional task families. Targets: 10 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B; fine-tuned on English (source) with LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32, LR 2e-4, 3 epochs) plus a full-fine-tuning replicate (LR 1e-5); 3 seeds (0,1,2), temperature 0 at eval. Prediction target (fixed): per-example target-language accuracy delta averaged over the 10 held-out target languages.

Experiment 0 (layer-sharedness estimation and its stability): identify each model's language-shared vs language-specific layers via (a) layer-wise cross-lingual representation-retrieval alignment and (b) language-ID linear probes, assigning each layer a sharedness weight. Ablation: report the stability of this layer-sharedness profile across the three models and across task families (rank correlation of per-layer sharedness), since a brittle profile would make the signature brittle. Convincing result: middle layers consistently rank as most shared with cross-model/task rank correlation >=0.6.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- examples vary in cross-lingual transferability; ground-truth protocol): tests whether per-example transferability is a real, continuous, non-degenerate quantity. Method: estimate each training example's contribution to the target-language delta via TracIn-style gradient influence; validate on a 150-example subset by leave-one-group-out RETRAINING (groups of 10, 3 seeds each, reporting between-seed variance of the estimated delta so the reliability of the ground truth is quantified). A brief power note: 150 verified examples give a Spearman-CI half-width <=0.15 at rho=0.5. Decisive metric: verified-vs-TracIn Spearman, plus top- vs bottom-quartile realized transfer ratio. Convincing result: Spearman >=0.5 AND top-quartile examples carry >=2x the mean per-example transfer of the bottom quartile. Indecision band: 0.3-0.5 = usable but noisy (downstream claims caveated); <0.3 = ground truth unreliable. Negative result (flat influence) refutes the premise.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the Shared-Recruitment Signature predicts transfer, beyond baselines): the core predictive test. Compute, for each English example, the signature = (gradient/update magnitude on shared middle layers)/(total gradient magnitude), and the sharedness-weighted variant, from a single fine-tuning pass. Controls/baselines it must beat: loss, gradient norm (magnitude-only), token length, a memorization score, in-language (English) gain, example difficulty, and source-target lexical overlap, plus UNWEIGHTED layerwise influence (influence without the sharedness weighting). Decisive metrics: Spearman(signature, cross-lingual delta); ranking/calibration metrics (NDCG@k and precision@k for top-transfer examples, since curation depends on top-k quality); and partial correlation controlling the above confounds. Convincing result: Spearman >=0.4 for cross-lingual delta, at least 0.15 higher than Spearman(signature, in-language gain), retains significance after partialling out difficulty/gradient-norm/lexical-overlap, and beats every simpler baseline on NDCG@k. Indecision band: 0.2-0.4 = weak (partial); <0.2, or no gap over in-language gain (<0.15), or no gain over gradient-norm baseline = the signature is a generic-usefulness/magnitude proxy, refuting H2. 

Experiment 3 (H2 -- causal dependence on the shared components): tests that high-signature examples transfer BECAUSE of their shared middle-layer update. Data: high- vs low-signature examples MATCHED on in-language gain, difficulty, and gradient norm. Method: ablate (zero/freeze) the middle-layer portion of each example's update and re-measure its cross-lingual transfer. Decisive metric: transfer drop under middle-layer ablation, contrasted across matched groups. Convincing result: high-signature examples lose >=50% of cross-lingual transfer under ablation while matched low-signature examples lose <=20% (the interaction is the evidence). Indecision band: high-signature drop 25-50% = partial; <25% demotes the signature to a correlate. Negative result refutes the mechanistic reading while leaving Exp. 2 intact.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- curation beats baselines at fixed data cost; deployment magnitude): rank the 2,000-example pool by signature; fine-tune (same config, 3 seeds) on top-k, random size-matched, bottom-k, full pool, and an unweighted-influence-selected size-matched set. Decisive metric: target-language accuracy averaged over 10 languages (source retention reported), as a full k-vs-accuracy curve; also report the annotation-cost framing -- the fraction of source examples needed to reach full-pool target accuracy (the practical payoff for low-resource adaptation under a fixed labeling/compute budget). Convincing result: top-k beats random size-matched by >=2 points and bottom-k by >=4 points at equal k, beats unweighted-influence selection, with source accuracy dropping <=1 point, and reaches full-pool target accuracy using a clearly smaller labeled subset. Indecision band: 0.5-2 point gain over random = marginal; <0.5 = no practical benefit, refuting H3. Negative result (random >= top-k) refutes the actionable claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Ground-truth per-example transferability is expensive and noisy; we rely on validated gradient-influence (TracIn) confirmed on a retraining-verified subset and report the between-seed variance of the retraining estimates so the reliability of the ground truth is explicit. 2. Gradient magnitude on a layer may not equal functional contribution; the causal middle-layer ablation (Exp. 3) is required to promote correlation to a functional claim. 3. The shared/specific layer split may be model- or task-dependent; Experiment 0 validates and reports its cross-model/task stability, and a brittle profile is an informative negative. 4. The signature may merely track difficulty, gradient norm, or generic usefulness; controlling against in-language gain, difficulty, gradient norm, and lexical overlap (Exp. 2) and matched-group ablation (Exp. 3) isolate the cross-lingual component, and simpler predictors are explicit baselines. 5. Effects may be small for very close languages where almost everything transfers; typologically distant targets provide power. 6. Curation gains could be modest if high-signature examples are rare; we report the full ranking curve and calibration metrics, not a single operating point. 7. We do not claim a general theory of transfer; the mechanism is hypothesized to extend to other shared-vs-specific-feature transfer settings but that generalization is left as future work. 8. Findings may be model- or task-specific; three model families and multiple task types address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: classifier_carved_categories
Title: One Long Thin Thing: How Numeral-Classifier Systems Covertly Carve the Concept Space of Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Numeral-classifier languages (Chinese, Japanese, Thai, Vietnamese) group nouns into shape/animacy/function-based categories (a 'long-thin' classifier for pens, roads, rivers). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM builds a shared, language-agnostic conceptual-category representation shaped by its dominant classifier language, and that (a) when asked to supply a classifier in a target classifier-language, it lazily inherits the dominant language's classifier boundaries, mis-classifying nouns whose category differs across classifier languages; and, more strikingly, (b) this classifier-induced category structure covertly biases genuinely semantic judgments (noun similarity, object grouping) even when the query and output are in classifier-FREE languages like English, and (c) both effects scale with cross-linguistic classifier-boundary divergence, not with resource level, and are carried by a locatable, causally-steerable 'classifier-category' representation.
Related Work: Cognitive-linguistics and typology establish numeral classifiers as noun-categorization devices carving the lexicon by shape/animacy/function (Aikhenvald 2000; the World Atlas of Classifier Languages 2022; gender-vs-classifier trade-offs 2019), and model classifier categories as radial/exemplar-based, extending by semantic chaining (Habibi, Kemp & Xu, Cognition 2020). Interpretability work shows multilingual models share cross-lingual circuits for grammatical processes (subject-verb agreement, grammatical number) via language-independent directions (Same But Different 2024; Similarity of Circuits 2024; Probing for Usage of Grammatical Number 2022) and share/split morphosyntactic neurons across languages (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; Causal Analysis of Agreement Neurons 2022). However, ALL prior mechanistic work targets agreement features (number, gender, person) whose values are grammatically forced and semantically thin; NONE studies numeral classifiers, which are unique in that their assignment reflects a language-specific CONCEPTUAL categorization of the noun's referent (shape/animacy/function). No work asks whether classifier systems leak across languages, whether the model's classifier assignment carves a shared concept space, or whether this carving covertly biases downstream SEMANTIC judgments in classifier-free languages (a Whorfian effect). We uniquely port classifier typology into multilingual mechanistic interpretability and give a causal, steerable account plus a training-free fix. Novelty typing: the primary claim is the Whorfian LEAKAGE of classifier-category structure into classifier-free English semantic judgments and its single causal representation; the cross-lingual inheritance and divergence-vs-resource results are supporting. We soften the literature position to 'we are not aware of mechanistic work on numeral classifiers' and add a generic cross-lingual transfer/interference baseline so the inheritance effect is shown to exceed ordinary multilingual confusion. CLASSIFIER-CARVE is offered as a curated evaluation set built from existing resources (the World Atlas of Classifier Languages plus native-validated dictionaries), not a wholly new corpus.
Abstract: In hundreds of languages, counting a noun requires a numeral classifier that reflects a culturally-shaped categorization of the noun's referent: Mandarin uses tiao for long, thin, flexible things (roads, rivers, fish, pants), and languages disagree on where these category boundaries fall. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs internalize classifier systems as a genuine conceptual carving of their noun space, and whether that carving leaks across languages and contaminates non-classifier semantic reasoning. We hypothesize that a model builds a shared classifier-category representation dominated by its highest-resource classifier language, causing two effects: (1) when generating a classifier in a target classifier-language, the model lazily inherits the dominant language's category boundaries, mis-assigning classifiers for nouns whose category differs cross-linguistically; and (2) more strikingly, the same category structure covertly biases genuinely semantic judgments (noun similarity ratings, 'which two objects go together') even when queried entirely in classifier-free English, so English-language judgments of unrelated objects are pulled together merely because they share a classifier in the model's dominant classifier language. We build CLASSIFIER-CARVE from the World Atlas of Classifier Languages and native-validated classifier assignments across Mandarin, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese, plus classifier-neutral controls. Behaviorally we measure classifier accuracy, cross-lingual inheritance rate, and the classifier bias on English similarity judgments. Mechanistically we probe for a shared classifier-category direction, use activation patching to localize a compact category representation whose swap flips both the classifier and the similarity judgment, and steer it to repair mis-assignments and remove the English-language bias without harming fluency. We predict effects scale with classifier-boundary divergence, not resource level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. Why it matters operationally: a classifier-driven distortion of English similarity would bias retrieval, clustering, and evaluation that assume a language-neutral concept space, so we report effect sizes (Cohen's d) large enough to change practitioner behavior, not only significance. If true, multilingual concept representations are not language-neutral and need de-biasing (the steering fix is a candidate mitigation); if false, the shared concept space is cleaner than feared - either outcome informs model design and evaluation. We also test a less-multilingual, low-classifier-exposure comparator to check the effect is specifically classifier-driven.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout; the "dominant classifier language" is operationalized per model as its highest-resource classifier language (verified by monolingual classifier accuracy), typically Mandarin. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by noun, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); classifiers and judgments elicited under greedy decoding. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points. Dataset (CLASSIFIER-CARVE, constructed from existing resources): from the World Atlas of Classifier Languages and native-speaker-validated dictionaries, ~400 concrete nouns with canonical numeral classifiers in Mandarin, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese, each annotated for classifier semantic basis (shape long-thin/flat/round; animacy; function). We mark DIVERGENT nouns (different classifier category across these languages) vs CONVERGENT nouns (same category everywhere) and compute cross-language classifier-boundary divergence scores; classifier-free control languages are English and German. Fewer than every noun in the atlas because each needs validated classifiers in all four languages; items kept above 0.7 inter-annotator agreement.

Experiment 1 (H-a - lazy inheritance of the dominant language's classifier boundaries): Tests whether generating a classifier in a target classifier-language mis-assigns divergent nouns toward the dominant language's category. Data: prompt "two ___ [noun]" per noun in each of the four classifier languages. Systems compared: monolingual-native accuracy per language (upper bound), convergent-noun control (should be high everywhere), the divergent-noun condition, and a generic cross-lingual interference baseline (inheritance expected from ordinary multilingual confusion on non-classifier lexical choices) as a floor. Decisive metric: INHERITANCE RATE = fraction of divergent-noun errors where the produced classifier matches the dominant language's category rather than the target language's; secondary: classifier accuracy per language. Convincing result: inheritance rate on divergent-noun errors exceeds the chance rate (uniform over plausible classifiers) by >=15 pp AND classifier accuracy is >=15 pp lower on divergent than convergent nouns, averaged over models. Indecision band: a 5-15 pp excess is reported per language rather than as a global inheritance claim. Negative result: inheritance within 5 pp of chance means errors are not dominant-language-directed and claim (a) fails.

Experiment 2 (H-b - a Whorfian classifier bias on classifier-free English semantic judgments): Tests whether nouns sharing a classifier in the dominant language are judged more similar in English, beyond baseline semantic similarity. Data: entirely in English, (a) pairwise noun-similarity ratings and (b) odd-one-out over triples, over matched pairs that do vs do not share a dominant-language classifier, holding embedding and corpus co-occurrence similarity fixed; divergent nouns provide cases where classifier grouping conflicts with semantic similarity. Systems compared: classifier-congruent vs classifier-incongruent matched pairs; convergent-noun control; native-English-speaker norms (as the no-bias reference). Decisive metric: classifier-congruent bias = difference in judged similarity between congruent and incongruent matched pairs, as an effect size (Cohen's d) beyond baseline semantic similarity. Convincing result: bias d >= 0.3 with 95% CI excluding 0, present even for divergent nouns where classifier grouping opposes semantic similarity. Indecision band: d 0.1-0.3, or CI touching 0, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: d < 0.1 means classifier structure does not leak into English judgments and the striking claim (b) fails.

Experiment 3 (H-shared - a shared classifier-category representation present even without classifiers): Tests whether a noun's classifier category is decodable from mid-layer states, including from English prompts, and transfers cross-lingually. Data: hidden states on held-out nouns from prompts in classifier languages and in English. A probe decodes the classifier category; an English-prompt probe tests recovery of the dominant-language category; cross-language transfer tested. Systems compared: within-language probe, English-prompt probe, cross-language transfer probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: English-prompt classifier-category probe accuracy minus shuffled control; secondary: cross-language transfer accuracy. Convincing result: category decodable from English prompts >=15 pp above control (carving present without classifiers) and transfers across classifier languages. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: within 5 pp of control means no shared carving, weakening the hypothesis. Decodability is not use; Exp. 4 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 4 (H-c - one causally-manipulable representation drives both the classifier and the English judgment): Tests whether the same component flips the produced classifier and the English similarity judgment. Data: for a divergent noun, runs under contexts forcing category A vs B (different classifiers). Activation patching transfers mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run; the SAME patched components are then tested on the English similarity judgment. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control. Decisive metric: classifier-flip rate AND English-similarity-judgment-flip rate under the same patch, each minus control, with noun identity preserved. Convincing result: both flip rates >=15 pp above control under the same components (linking the two effects to one representation), with identity preserved and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp on either flip, or a large gap between the two flip rates, indicates partially distinct mechanisms; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp on either flip, or no shared component driving both, means the two effects are not one causal representation and claim (c)'s mechanism half fails.

Experiment 5 (H-c - effects scale with classifier-boundary divergence, not resource): Tests the dissociation. Data: inheritance rate, English-bias magnitude, and probe cross-lingual disagreement vs the divergence score and a resource-level proxy; key contrast a lower-resource classifier language with divergent boundaries vs a higher-resource one. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of each effect with divergence controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for divergence. Convincing result: partial correlation with divergence >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0. Indecision band: divergence correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: effects track resource (|rho| >=0.4) not divergence, refuting claim (c)'s scaling half.

Experiment 6 (H-c - steering repairs mis-assignment and removes the English bias): Tests the training-free causal fix. Data: mis-assigned classifiers in target languages (repair); English similarity judgments carrying the bias (removal); a classifier-free language for induction; non-noun items (specificity). Classifier-category direction = mean activation difference between category A and B, pooled across languages. Systems compared: steering vs explicit-instruction prompting vs translate-to-English. Decisive metric: classifier repair rate minus baseline, and bias-removal = return of English similarity toward native-English norms (reduction in Cohen's d); secondary: induction rate (spurious grouping induced in a classifier-free language), fluency (perplexity), specificity. Convincing result: repair >=15 pp over baseline and bias-d reduced by >=50% toward the native norm, with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline; induction confirms functional causality. Indecision band: repair 5-15 pp, or bias reduction 20-50%, indicates a weak/partial fix. Negative result: repair <5 pp and bias reduction <20% mean the direction is not functionally causal, refuting the steerability claim. Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; separability of the classifier-category direction from grammatical-number and gender directions; shape vs animacy vs function subcategory separability; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: classifier accuracy, inheritance rate, English classifier-congruent bias (Cohen's d), probe accuracy and transfer, causal classifier/similarity flip rates, identity preservation, Spearman with divergence vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of classifier category may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 4) and the steering repair/removal/induction (Exp. 6) to establish functional relevance, and crucially require the SAME components to drive both the classifier and the English similarity judgment. 2. Classifier assignment is sometimes optional, register-dependent, or has multiple acceptable choices; we restrict to native-speaker-validated high-agreement items and treat multi-classifier nouns separately. 3. The English semantic-bias effect could be confounded with genuine semantic/co-occurrence similarity (classifiers often track real semantic classes); we explicitly control for embedding and corpus co-occurrence similarity, use divergent nouns where the classifier grouping conflicts with dominant semantic similarity, and compare against convergent controls and native-English norms. 4. Strong models may fully abstract classifiers away, making the English bias negligible; even documenting near-absence (a genuinely clean concept space) is an informative result, and multiple models/languages give statistical power. 5. Tokenization of nouns/classifiers varies across scripts; we use last-token-of-noun or pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The divergence-vs-resource dissociation hinges on carefully chosen language contrasts; we report robustness to divergence-score operationalization. 7. Steering may trade classifier correctness or bias removal for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: color_category_boundary_shift
Title: Russian Blues in a Text Model: How the Query Language's Color Lexicon Covertly Carves a Shared Continuous Color Space
Short Hypothesis: Exact novelty: the first text-only causal dissociation of continuous color geometry from a language-conditioned categorical readout in multilingual LLMs. We hypothesize (not assume) that, given colors specified purely as text coordinates (hex/RGB), multilingual LLMs build a shared, largely language-agnostic continuous color representation, but the CATEGORICAL boundaries imposed on it are set by the query language's basic-color-term inventory. So the identical pair of colors is judged 'same/more similar' vs 'different/less similar' depending on the query language (two blues straddling the goluboy/siniy line separated in Russian but merged in English). We frame color as one clean instance of a general template -- category formation over a shared continuous representation -- and predict the effect scales with color-lexicon distance rather than resource level, and (as a testable claim contingent on strong causal evidence) is carried by a locatable, steerable boundary signal separable from the continuous representation.
Related Work: Berlin & Kay and the World Color Survey (Lexical Color Categories 2021) established that color lexicons vary yet show universal tendencies; the classic Russian-blues result shows lexical distinctions cause categorical-perception effects. Modeling shows color categories emerge from vision/communication (Emergent Color Categorization 2021; Categorical Nature of Colour Perception 2024, which finds category perception largely language-INDEPENDENT in vision nets but shaped by linguistic terms). The closest prior LLM work -- the 2024 multilingual color-perception study (Studying the Effect of Globalization 2024) -- MEASURED that LLMs have language-specific color naming/representations and that color-term counts correlate with humans, but it is purely behavioral/descriptive over NAMED colors: it does not use text coordinates to remove naming/vision, does not test a shared CONTINUOUS geometry, and performs no intervention. Our unique contribution over it is causal and text-only: we (i) use hex/RGB coordinates so the same physical color is presented identically across language conditions, isolating the lexicon from naming and vision; (ii) test, as a hypothesis, a shared continuous representation dissociable from a language-SET categorical boundary; and (iii) causally move/add/remove a boundary via steering. The novelty is thus jointly a new mechanistic finding and a new text-only mechanistic testbed for category formation over continuous representations, of which color is the cleanest case.
Abstract: A landmark result in language and thought is that speakers of a language obligatorily distinguishing two shades (Russian's light blue goluboy vs dark blue siniy) discriminate colors straddling that boundary faster and treat them as more different. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit such language-specific color categories, and crucially whether this happens even when colors are given purely as text coordinates (hex/RGB), removing vision and color naming entirely. Our claim is a text-only causal dissociation: models compute a shared, largely language-agnostic continuous color representation but impose categorical boundaries drawn from the query language's basic-color-term inventory, so the identical pair of coordinates is judged same-vs-different category depending on the query language. We treat the shared-continuous claim as a hypothesis to be tested, not assumed. We build COLOR-CARVE, text-specified colors densely sampling regions where languages disagree on basic-term boundaries (blue goluboy/siniy, green/blue 'grue', red/orange, purple/pink), each posed as similarity-rating, same/different-category, and odd-one-out tasks across 12+ languages spanning divergent color-lexicon typologies, with World-Color-Survey-grounded, native-speaker-validated boundaries and a pre-registered lexicon-distance metric and language contrast set. Each hypothesis has one primary falsifiable metric. Behaviorally we measure per-language categorical-perception discontinuities on identical coordinates, controlling lightness/saturation, tokenization, prompt wording, and order effects. Mechanistically we separate representational evidence (probes decode continuous CIELAB and transfer across languages) from causal evidence (activation patching and steering, with random-boundary-direction, non-color-task, and English-to-English null baselines) that a separable categorical boundary differs by language and can be induced, removed, or shifted without changing the continuous representation. We predict the effect scales with color-lexicon distance not resource level. The result gives multilingual prompting, culturally-faithful generation, and lexical-bias auditing a concrete handle, and a general template beyond color.
