Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset COLOR-CARVE (constructed): colors specified as text hex/RGB (CIELAB retained for analysis) densely sampling axes where languages disagree on basic-color-term boundaries -- the goluboy/siniy blue axis, green-blue 'grue', red/orange, purple/pink. Per-language boundaries from the World Color Survey (existing) plus native-speaker validation (protocol and inter-annotator agreement reported). ~500 color pairs matched in CIELAB distance, plus triples for odd-one-out; pairs are balanced so lightness and saturation are matched across the boundary (controlling the known human confounds). Three task formats: similarity rating (0-10), same-vs-different basic-category judgment, odd-one-out. Rendered in 12+ languages spanning divergent color-lexicon typologies (Russian, Greek, English, Chinese, Turkish, Korean, Vietnamese, Hindi, plus grue-type/low-term languages). Lexicon distance is defined PRE-REGISTERED as the difference in number/placement of basic-term boundaries along the sampled axes, and the language ordering/contrast set is fixed in advance; a resource-level proxy is recorded separately. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, 3 paraphrase seeds. Controls/ablations: because coordinates are identical across language conditions only the prompt language varies; we also run RGB and named-swatch formats, prompt-wording and answer-order ablations, an English-to-English language-swap null, and report tokenization statistics.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- text-only categorical perception set by the query language; primary metric = CP index): tests that identical text-specified colors are judged more/less similar depending on the query language's lexical boundary. Decisive (single primary) metric: categorical-perception (CP) index = the discontinuity (drop in judged similarity / rise in 'different' rate) at a language's lexical boundary, over and above a smooth function of CIELAB distance (with lightness/saturation matched). Convincing result: languages with an obligatory split show a CP discontinuity at their boundary absent in languages without it (blue-axis discontinuity in Russian but not English; no green/blue discontinuity in grue languages), with a boundary-straddling CP index >=1.5 similarity points (or >=15 pp in 'different' rate) beyond the CIELAB-distance baseline, and no discontinuity in the English-to-English null. Indecision band: 0.5-1.5 points (5-15 pp) = weak; below = no language-set categorical perception, refuting H2.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- CP tracks color-lexicon distance, not resource; primary metric = correlation contrast): Predictors: pre-registered per-language lexicon distance vs resource proxy. Decisive metric: Spearman(CP index, lexicon distance) vs Spearman(CP index, resource), bootstrap CIs, mixed-effects across models; key contrast = a lower-resource fine-distinguishing language vs a higher-resource coarse one. Convincing result: |Spearman with lexicon distance| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, key-contrast pair ordered by lexicon. Indecision band: within 0.05-0.2 = mixed; lexicon not stronger = refuted.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared continuous representation, causal late boundary; representational vs causal separated): representational evidence -- train linear probes/logit-lens at each layer to decode continuous CIELAB from hidden states, test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others), contrasted with a categorical-label probe. Causal evidence (kept distinct from the probe claim): activation-patch the mid-layer continuous-color representation across language runs, and separately patch/steer the late categorical-decision components, with null baselines -- random-direction patch, a non-color control task, and English-to-English swaps. Decisive metrics: continuous-color probe cross-lingual transfer error (CIELAB Delta-E); rate at which patching the continuous representation changes the category judgment vs rate at which patching the late boundary flips it, each above null baselines. Convincing result: continuous-color probe transfers across languages (Delta-E within measurement noise) while the categorical-label probe varies by language; patching the continuous representation flips the category judgment in <=15% of cases while manipulating the late boundary flips it in >=40%, above null baselines. Indecision band: late-boundary flip 20-40% = partial; continuous-probe transfer degraded, continuous-patch flipping >30%, or nulls matching = the continuous representation is not shared, refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable boundary signal; primary metric = CP-index change with specificity): recover a category-boundary signal as the mean activation difference between within- and cross-category runs pooled across languages; steer to (a) INDUCE a goluboy/siniy split when querying in English, (b) REMOVE it when querying in Russian, (c) shift the boundary. Systems compared: steering vs explicit prompting ('treat light and dark blue as different colors') vs translate-to-English vs matched-norm random-direction steer (sham). Decisive metrics (in order): induced/removed CP-effect magnitude; continuous-representation preservation (specificity -- decoded CIELAB unchanged, Delta-E within noise); fluency; dose-response monotonicity. Convincing result: steering changes the CP index by >=1.5 points (>=15 pp) in the intended direction while decoded CIELAB is unchanged, fluency unharmed, dose-monotone, and beats the sham. Indecision band: 0.5-1.5 points = partial; below, continuous representation shifted, or sham matches = not a clean separable boundary control, and we then report only the weaker readout-localization result from Exp. 3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a continuous color representation or boundary signal may reflect the readout basis; the causal patching (Exp. 3) and steering induce/remove (Exp. 4), with random-direction/non-color/English-to-English null baselines and the CIELAB-preservation specificity check, are required to promote correlation to mechanism, and we keep representational and causal claims explicitly separate and temper 'shared continuous representation'/'boundary signal' language accordingly. 2. Color-lexicon boundaries are graded and individual/dialect variable; we ground them in the World Color Survey with native-speaker validation and restrict to high-agreement regions. 3. Effects could be confounded with hex/RGB tokenization; since coordinates are identical across language conditions, color tokenization is constant while only prompt language varies, and we additionally test RGB and named-swatch formats and report tokenization statistics. 4. Lightness/saturation, prompt wording, and answer order are known human confounds; pairs are matched on lightness/saturation and we ablate wording and order. 5. A model might lack any color geometry from text coordinates, so the continuous probe fails -- an informative outcome the transfer contrast is designed to decide. 6. The lexicon-distance-vs-resource dissociation hinges on language contrasts; the distance metric and contrast set are pre-registered, with multiple resource proxies and robustness checks. 7. Strong models may carve categories faithfully per language, shrinking the default cross-language effect; documenting faithful carving is still a positive result and the induction/removal steering yields causal evidence. 8. Downstream: if confirmed, multilingual prompting and culturally-faithful generation should account for language-set category boundaries and audits can flag lexical bias; if absent, cross-lingual semantic judgments over continuous attributes can be trusted more. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: implicit_comparative_method
Title: Does the Model Know the Comparative Method? Causally Isolating an Implicit Sound-Correspondence Engine in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs can predict cognate forms across related languages by internally applying REGULAR sound-correspondence rules (an implicit 'comparative method') rather than only memorizing attested cognate pairs, and this rule-application is driven by an identifiable, causally-manipulable internal mechanism that generalizes to held-out language pairs and even nonce (invented) words.
Related Work: Historical-linguistics NLP shows specialized character-based models learn sound correspondences and latent diachronic information (Probing Multilingual Cognate Prediction, Fournier 2022; List 2018 automatic correspondence inference), and that mBERT/NMT representations cluster by phylogenetic/typological relatedness (Probing mBERT for Genetic/Typological Signals 2020; Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations 2023; Investigating Multilingual NMT Representations 2019). Transfer work exploits cognates and phonetic alignment for low-resource languages (PhoneXL 2023; Transliteration for Morphological Inflection 2020; Hamshentsnag 2025). ALL of this either (i) uses task-specialized character-level cognate/NMT models, or (ii) probes STATIC encoder representations for typology, treating relatedness as a similarity signal. None asks whether a modern GENERATIVE multilingual LLM, prompted in-context, applies REGULAR sound-correspondence rules productively (to nonce/unseen forms), nor gives CAUSAL mechanistic evidence that a specific internal component implements this rule-application distinct from lexical memorization. We reframe cognate prediction as a test of an implicit, causally-real comparative-method engine and provide the first location+intervention account. To be explicit about novelty: the phenomenon (in-context cross-language cognate generation) is partly established, but our contributions are a new TEST SETTING that isolates productive REGULAR rule application from analogical/frequency-based retrieval using nonce forms and frequency-controlled splits, and a new CAUSAL MECHANISM claim - locating and manipulating the internal correspondence representation - which prior cognate-prediction, automatic-correspondence-inference (Cognate Transformer, List 2018), and nonce-morphology work does not provide. We define a 'correspondence rule' as a deterministic mapping from a source phonological segment in a defined environment to a target segment; evidence for an internal comparative-method engine is productive application of such a mapping to unseen/nonce forms plus a locatable, intervention-sensitive representation that switches the applied mapping. This connects to the cognitive science of analogy and rule-learning, to language documentation (assisted reconstruction), and to multilingual interpretability.
Abstract: Historical linguistics reconstructs language history via the comparative method: identifying REGULAR sound correspondences (e.g., Latin 'p' -> English 'f' in pater/father, pisces/fish) and applying them productively. We ask whether multilingual LLMs have implicitly acquired such an engine. The sharp question is whether a model predicts cognates by APPLYING a regular rule that generalizes to words it has never seen paired (including invented nonce forms), or merely RETRIEVES memorized cognate pairs. We first establish the behavior: given a few in-context correspondence exemplars from a language pair, can the model transform a held-out real word, and crucially a NONCE word (which cannot be memorized), into its cognate form obeying the correspondence? We test across language families (Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Indo-Aryan, Turkic) using established cognate resources (NorthEuraLex, CogNet, IELex) and nonce stimuli constructed to obey known correspondences. We predict above-chance productive rule application that degrades gracefully with the number/regularity of correspondences and with typological distance. We then locate the mechanism: probing and vocabulary-projection to find where correspondence rules are represented, and activation patching / steering to test causality. Consistent with a locatable mechanism (stated conservatively as evidence for, not proof of, a dedicated component), we predict that a small set of mid-layer features/heads carries the active correspondence rule: patching it from a Latin->English run into a Latin->German run should switch the applied correspondence, and steering along a recovered 'correspondence direction' should induce or repair rule application on nonce words. Experiments use Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. This bridges the comparative method with mechanistic interpretability and dissociates rule-based generalization from lexical memorization in multilingual LLMs. Why it matters: productive rule application would mean multilingual LLMs abstract sound-correspondence structure usable for better cognate reconstruction, low-resource transfer, and diagnostics of hidden phonological competence; a negative result is informative, bounding current models to memorization-like cognate behavior. Falsifiable core: if nonce-word correspondence-obedience does not exceed retrieval and analogy baselines and no intervention switches the applied correspondence, the implicit-comparative-method claim is rejected.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters); base weights are frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers trained on cached hidden states with a 60/20/20 train/validation/test split by item and 3 seeds {0,1,2} for probe initialization and split; behavioral generation is greedy decoding with 3 prompt-sampling seeds (exemplar choice and order); activation patching and steering add or replace activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "correspondence-obedience rate" = fraction of rule-relevant segments transformed exactly as the annotated sound-correspondence rule dictates.

Experiment 1 (H1 - productive rule application vs lexical memorization): Tests whether the model applies a regular sound-correspondence rule to forms it cannot have memorized, rather than only retrieving attested cognate pairs. Data: real cognate pairs used as-is from NorthEuraLex (~1,016 concepts x 100+ languages), CogNet (~8M pairs, 338 languages), and IELex (~200 Indo-European concepts); we sample 120 pairs per family for Romance, Germanic, Slavic, Indo-Aryan, and Turkic (600 real items), keeping only pairs with clean single-word tokenization and an annotated regular correspondence. We also construct 60 nonce source words per family (300 total) that obey source-language phonotactics and to which an annotated correspondence set applies deterministically, so the correct target cannot have been seen. Fewer than the full resource because each item requires per-segment correspondence annotation and clean tokenization. In-context prompt gives k=5 correspondence exemplars, then asks for the cognate of a held-out real word and of a nonce word. Systems compared: model output vs (i) copy-source baseline, (ii) random-correspondence baseline, (iii) memorization ceiling (obedience on already-seen real pairs), (iv) a nearest-neighbor retrieval baseline returning the target of the most orthographically similar training cognate, (v) an analogy-based string-transform baseline applying the edit operations of the nearest exemplar pair, (vi) a supervised character-level seq2seq transducer trained on the correspondence exemplars, and (vii) a transliteration-only baseline. To guard against leakage/memorization we use frequency-controlled splits (source-word frequency matched across seen and held-out items) and verify that no nonce target string appears in an available corpus proxy. Decisive metric: nonce-word correspondence-obedience rate (exact-match and normalized edit distance secondary). Convincing result: nonce obedience exceeds both the copy-source and random-correspondence baselines by >=15 pp averaged over the three models AND is within 20 pp of real-word obedience. Indecision band: a nonce-vs-baseline gap of 5-15 pp is inconclusive (weak/partial rule use); we then report per-family results and withhold the global productive-rule claim. Negative result: nonce obedience within 5 pp of baseline means the model does not apply the rule productively, and the central claim of the hypothesis fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 - a locatable internal representation of the active correspondence): Tests whether a compact set of mid-layer components carries the identity of the correspondence being applied and is decodable before output. Data: the Exp. 1 items; hidden states cached at every layer at the source word's last token and at exemplar-pair positions. A per-layer linear probe decodes (i) the target segment corresponding to the source segment and (ii) the active correspondence-set identity (e.g. Latin->English vs Latin->German); logit-lens vocabulary projection and attention attribution rank the heads that read exemplar pairs. Systems compared: trained probe vs label-shuffled-control probe vs random-direction baseline. Decisive metric: peak-layer probe accuracy for correspondence-set identity minus shuffled-control accuracy; secondary: number of heads accounting for 80% of attribution mass. Convincing result: identity decodable at a mid-layer >=15 pp above the shuffled control with <=10 heads carrying most attribution, yielding ranked candidate components for Exp. 3. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control means a weak/diffuse signal; we still pass candidates to the causal test but flag low localization. Negative result: <=5 pp above control means no decodable correspondence representation, and we rely solely on the causal search in Exp. 3. Decodability alone is not evidence of use; Exp. 3 is required.

Experiment 3 (H2/H3 - the representation is causally manipulable): Tests whether intervening on the located component switches the applied correspondence and induces or repairs rule application, dissociating rule from retrieval. Data: the five families plus a held-out language pair per family not used in Exp. 2 probe training, and the nonce items. (a) Activation patching: run one source word under correspondence set A (Latin->English) vs B (Latin->German), patch the candidate mid-layer component from the A-run into the B-run. (b) Steering: a "correspondence direction" = mean activation difference between correct-rule and wrong-rule runs, computed on training items and applied to held-out/nonce items. Systems compared: patch/steer at the candidate component vs random-component and random-direction controls; effect on nonce items (pure rule) vs high-frequency memorized cognates (retrieval control). Decisive metric: correspondence-switch rate (fraction where the applied correspondence flips A->B under patching), and steering repair/induction rate, each minus its control; lexical-identity preservation (edit distance to intended stem unchanged within noise) reported alongside. Convincing result: switch and repair/induction rates >=15 pp above control with specificity (unrelated segments unchanged) AND larger on nonce than on memorized cognates. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is inconclusive - consistent with a distributed rather than localized mechanism; we then report degree of localization and fall back to a direction-based account. Negative result: <=5 pp above control means the correspondence signal is epiphenomenal and the causal-mechanism claim fails.

Experiment 4 (H1/H3 - generalization scope, dose-response): Tests the hypothesis's scope claim that productive rule application generalizes across held-out pairs and degrades predictably. Data: Exp. 1 items, varying exemplar count k in {1,3,5,10}, regular vs irregular/exceptional items, and lang2vec typological distance between source and target. Decisive metric: Spearman correlation between nonce correspondence-obedience and each of (typological distance, correspondence regularity). Convincing result: |rho| >= 0.4 with a 95% CI excluding 0 in the predicted direction (obedience falls with distance and with irregularity). Indecision band: |rho| 0.2-0.4, or CI touching 0, is reported as suggestive only, not confirmatory. Negative result: rho approximately 0 means no systematic generalization structure, bounding the hypothesis to memorized-like behavior. Ablations (secondary, not hypothesis tests): layer sweep for where the rule is malleable; exemplar order/count; probe transfer across the three models; proto-form reconstruction as an exploratory productive task. Reported metrics throughout: correspondence-obedience, exact-match, edit distance, switch/repair/induction rates, Spearman with distance and regularity, specificity, and generation fluency (perplexity).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Nonce words may still partially overlap memorized substrings, blurring the rule-vs-memorization line; we control by using segments/positions where the correspondence is the only cue and by comparing against a copy baseline. 2. Probe/logit-lens decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; the causal patching-switch and steering induction (Exp. 3) are required to establish functional relevance. 3. The correspondence mechanism may be diffuse rather than localized; we report degree of localization and fall back to a direction-based account. 4. Some models may simply copy or transliterate rather than apply correspondences, collapsing the effect; even documenting the near-absence of productive rule use, and its dependence on family/distance, is an informative finding, and three models give statistical power. 5. Tokenization fragments words unevenly across scripts, complicating segment-level attribution; we restrict to clean-tokenizing pairs, work at last-token-of-word where needed, and report tokenization statistics. 6. Ground-truth 'correct' cognate forms for real words can involve irregular changes; we separate regular vs irregular items and rely on nonce items for the cleanest rule test. 7. Steering may trade rule application for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: false_friend_meaning_leak
Title: Gift Means Poison: Causally Tracing How Interlingual Homographs Leak the Wrong-Language Meaning Into Multilingual LLM Computation
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM processes an interlingual homograph (a false friend, e.g. German 'Gift' = poison vs English 'gift' = present), the wrong-language meaning is automatically co-activated as a latent competitor in mid layers, and semantic errors occur when the model fails to disambiguate using context. The single primary novelty is the first causal localization of a mid-layer meaning-selection step for cross-lingual homographs in large decoder LLMs; parallel co-activation (a phenomenon), the driver analysis, and the steering intervention are supporting claims. A non-obvious prediction that distinguishes this mechanism from a token-frequency bias or shallow language-ID gating: patching the localized selection components flips the meaning while the surface language of the context and the token-frequency profile are held fixed, and does so even on frequency-balanced items where a frequency-bias or language-ID account predicts no flip. We hypothesize (a) both meanings are simultaneously linearly decodable before disambiguation collapses to one, (b) a causally-identifiable mid-layer meaning-selection step resolves the competition, (c) selection failure scales with meaning-frequency balance and with query-context-vs-dominant-language mismatch, and (d) steering a recovered meaning direction causally repairs or induces the wrong reading. This is a minimal test case for a broader question of multilingual semantic binding.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs perform below random on interlingual-homograph disambiguation and rely on orthography over semantics (Multilingual LLMs Struggle to Link Orthography and Semantics 2025). Small bilingual-model studies show shared embeddings produce facilitation for both friends and false friends, driven by frequency (Skrjanec et al. 2026; Cumulative Frequency 2021). Tokenizer-level work maps false friends to shared subwords and proposes language cues at tokenization (Tokenizing Crosslingual Homographs 2026; False Friends Are Not Foes 2025). Embedding-geometry work characterizes shared vs language-partitioned spaces (Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023; BERT is Not an Interlingua 2019). Separately, monolingual mechanistic-interpretability work studies polysemy and word-sense disambiguation circuits within a single language (sense neurons, attention-mediated context integration). Delta: the multilingual literature is behavioral, embedding-level, or in tiny bilingual models and gives no generation-time causal circuit; the monolingual polysemy work localizes WITHIN-language sense selection but never tests whether a CROSS-lingual competitor (a different language's meaning) is co-activated and selected against, nor what language-specific factors (dominance, frequency balance) drive failure. We include monolingual polysemy controls precisely to show the mechanism is specifically cross-lingual rather than generic lexical competition. Our contribution is the first causal, generation-time localization of a cross-lingual meaning-selection step in a large decoder LLM, plus a released dataset/tooling resource, a driver analysis, and a causal steering fix.
Abstract: Interlingual homographs, or false friends, are words with identical surface form but different meanings across languages: German 'Gift' means poison, but English 'gift' means present. They are a natural stress test for the shared subword vocabularies of multilingual LLMs. Behavioral studies show models resolve them poorly, but how the wrong meaning enters computation, where it is (or is not) suppressed, and what governs failure remain unknown mechanistically. Our central, deliberately narrow claim is the first causal localization of a mid-layer meaning-selection step for cross-lingual homographs in large decoder LLMs. Using a curated, publicly-released cross-lingual false-friend set with matched cognate, monosemous, and MONOLINGUAL-POLYSEMY controls, we first show via logit-lens and linear probes that in mid layers both meanings of a false friend are simultaneously decodable before selection collapses to one, unlike controls. Using activation patching with strong controls (random patching, neighboring-layer patching, unrelated-token patching, and lexical-identity/syntax preservation checks), we localize the meaning-selection step: swapping its activation between a context that forces meaning A and one that forces meaning B flips the model's downstream semantic judgment while preserving that the word is a false friend, and does so even on frequency-balanced items where a frequency-bias account predicts no flip. We then model, with hierarchical mixed-effects regression over item, language pair, and model family, what drives selection failure: meaning-frequency balance, query-context-vs-dominant-language mismatch, and context strength. Finally we steer a recovered meaning direction to repair mis-selections and induce wrong readings, compared against logit-biasing, non-selected-layer steering, and language-ID prompting baselines, and validated on an END TASK (cross-lingual sense-disambiguated translation/QA). We quantify false-friend collision prevalence in deployed multilingual usage and common benchmarks. So what: if selection is causally localizable, translation, retrieval, customer support, code-switching assistants, and safety-critical multilingual settings gain a targeted diagnostic and fix; if not, the failure is diffuse and must be addressed at data/tokenization level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across five language pairs, with power-justified item counts.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed from validated databases, released as a dataset/tooling resource): a cross-lingual false-friend set from the Dutch-English homograph database (existing) plus curated English-German/Spanish/French/Russian pairs; item count is set by a pilot power analysis targeting the Experiment-2 flip-rate effect across five language pairs, models, and contexts (expanded well beyond an initial ~200 if power requires, and reported explicitly), with a MONOLINGUAL-POLYSEMY control set (single-language ambiguous words) sized to match. Each false friend has its two meanings and canonical languages, matched COGNATE controls (same form, same meaning), MONOSEMOUS single-language controls, and the monolingual-polysemy controls. For each false friend: paired disambiguating contexts (one forcing meaning A, one forcing meaning B) and a weak/neutral context, each rendered with the surrounding context in language A vs language B; per-meaning corpus frequency gives a frequency-balance score; intended meaning is native-speaker validated. 'Meaning' is operationalized carefully: where answer tokens are multi-token, paraphrastic, or asymmetric across languages, meaning is scored by a fixed set of probe answer tokens plus an entailment check, defined per item in advance. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; primarily greedy, temperature 0, but the selection signal is also tested across prompts, templates, paraphrases, and sampling decoding to show generality; homograph-token representations; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out items); tokenisation reported and shared-token vs split-token cases both tracked AND analyzed as explicit matched subsets. Prevalence estimate: we measure how often false-friend-like collisions occur in a sample of deployed-style multilingual prompts and common benchmarks. All numerical thresholds below are justified by the pilot power analysis or reported as effect sizes.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- parallel activation of both meanings, specifically cross-lingual): tests claim (a). Data/model as Setup. Method: at the homograph token position apply logit-lens and per-layer probes to test whether BOTH meaning answer tokens (e.g. 'poison' and 'present') are decodable in mid layers before one dominates, contrasted with monosemous controls AND the monolingual-polysemy controls (to show the effect is cross-lingual, not generic within-language ambiguity). Decisive metric: mid-layer co-decodability of the two meanings for false friends versus the secondary-meaning decodability of monosemous controls, and versus the two-sense co-decodability of monolingual-polysemy controls. Convincing result: both meanings decodable above chance in mid layers for false friends, secondary-meaning decodability >=15 pp above the monosemous baseline, and a cross-lingual signature distinguishable from monolingual polysemy. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control = weak co-activation; <5 pp = no parallel activation and (a) is refuted. Negative result (only the context-appropriate meaning decodable) refutes co-activation.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a causally-identifiable mid-layer meaning-selection step: the primary claim): tests claim (b). Data: identical false friends under context A vs context B yielding different answers, including a frequency-balanced subset. Model: frozen, activation patching. Method: patch mid-layer components from the A-run into the B-run and find the minimal set whose patching flips the semantic judgment to A's meaning while lexical identity (that it is this word) and local syntax are preserved. Strong causal controls: random-component patching, neighboring-layer patching, and unrelated-token patching, all of which must produce far smaller flips; the frequency-balanced subset tests the non-obvious prediction that the flip occurs even where a frequency-bias or language-ID account predicts none. Decisive metric: flip rate vs number/location of patched components, with identity/syntax-preservation checks and the control flip rates. Convincing result: a compact mid-layer set flips the semantic judgment in >=50% of pairs while preserving lexical identity (>=95%) and syntax, exceeding all controls, and flips frequency-balanced items above the frequency-bias prediction. Indecision band: flip rate 25-50% = a diffuse selection step (direction-based account); <25%, or flips matched by controls, = no localisable cross-lingual meaning-selection step and (b) is refuted. Negative result (patching cannot flip the judgment) refutes the selection-step claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- what drives selection failure): tests claim (c) with proper hierarchical modeling. Data/model as Setup. Method: model selection-failure rate with a mixed-effects/hierarchical regression with random effects for item, language pair, and model family, and fixed effects for (i) frequency-balance score, (ii) context-language vs dominant-language mismatch (lang2vec typological distance), and (iii) context strength. Decisive metric: standardised fixed-effect coefficients with CIs for each driver. Convincing result: failure rises with balanced/dominant-favouring frequency and with language mismatch, each with a coefficient whose 95% CI excludes 0 and an effect size corresponding to |Spearman| >=0.3. Indecision band: effect corresponding to |Spearman| 0.15-0.3 = weak; <0.15 or CI including 0 = that driver does not modulate failure and the corresponding part of (c) is refuted. Negative result (failure unrelated to frequency balance or mismatch) refutes the driver claim.

Experiment 4 (H4 -- causal steering repairs and induces the reading, and improves an end task): tests claim (d) and its practical value. Data: disambiguating-context items where the model errs (repair), weak-context items (induction), and a downstream cross-lingual sense-disambiguated translation/QA task. Model: extract a meaning direction (mean activation difference between meaning-A and meaning-B runs) at the selection layer; (a) steer toward the correct meaning in disambiguating context (repair); (b) steer to induce the wrong reading in weak context. Systems compared: steering vs logit-biasing, vs steering at non-selected layers, vs a language-ID / tokenizer-language-cue prompt, vs translate-to-context-language. Decisive metric: repair rate, induction rate, AND downstream end-task accuracy gain, with fluency (perplexity) and specificity (unrelated items unchanged). Convincing result: steering repairs >=40% of mis-selections, induces the wrong reading in >=40% of weak-context items, and improves the end task over baselines, with fluency unharmed and specificity preserved. Indecision band: repair/induction 20-40%, or end-task gain within noise = partial; <20%, or effects only by harming fluency, or no end-task gain = the direction is not usefully causal and (d) is refuted. Negative result (steering neither repairs nor induces, nor helps the end task) refutes the steering claim. Ablations: layer sweep, shared-token vs split-token matched subsets, whether the competitor is the dominant-language or higher-frequency meaning, and probe transfer across models.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe co-decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than functional co-activation; we require the Exp.-2 causal patching flip (above random/neighboring-layer/unrelated-token controls) and Exp.-4 steering repair/induction and end-task gain for functional relevance. 2. False-friend meanings often differ in frequency, confounding co-activation with frequency; we model frequency balance (Exp. 3), include frequency-matched subsets, and use them for the non-obvious prediction in Exp. 2. 3. Tokenization varies: some homographs split differently across contexts; we analyze shared-token-only and split-token subsets as explicit matched analyses. 4. Strong models may resolve context so well that interference is rare; the weak-context and induction experiments still yield causal results, and prevalence is quantified. 5. Ground-truth intended meaning in weak contexts can be ambiguous; we use native-speaker-validated high-agreement items. 6. 'Meaning' with multi-token/paraphrastic answers is defined per item via fixed probe tokens plus an entailment check. 7. The mechanism could be generic lexical competition, not cross-lingual; the monolingual-polysemy controls test this. 8. Item counts and thresholds are justified by a pilot power analysis. 9. Steering may trade correctness for fluency; we report both. 10. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: numeral_morphology_magnitude_leak
Title: Four-Twenty-Ten Is Not Ninety: How Numeral-System Morphology Distorts the Shared Magnitude Representation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a number is written as words, multilingual LLMs are supposed to recover a language-agnostic magnitude, but the surface *morphology* of a language's numeral system leaks into the internal representation. For languages with opaque/non-decimal numeral construction (French vigesimal 'quatre-vingt-dix' = 90, Danish 'halvfems', Georgian, Basque), the internal magnitude estimate is systematically pulled toward the values of the literal component morphemes, and this compositional-leakage grows with the typological distance of the numeral system from a transparent base-10 system. The novelty lives in three places, stated explicitly: (i) a mechanistic FINDING (morpheme-value contamination of the internal magnitude), (ii) a typology-grounded METRIC (a numeral-system Opacity Index and a compositional-leakage score), and (iii) a causal INTERVENTION (training-free magnitude steering), NOT in the probing tools, which are established. Predictions: (a) measurable, direction-consistent magnitude distortion; (b) distortion tracks numeral-system opacity rather than resource level, tokenization fragmentation, or frequency; (c) a training-free steering correction along the recovered clean magnitude direction repairs the leak.
Related Work: A rich interpretability literature shows LLMs encode numbers as digit-wise base-10 (Zhu et al. 2024), sinusoidally (2025), as log-magnitude linear directions (LLMs Know More About Numbers 2026), and in low-dimensional monotonic subspaces (Heinzerling & Inui 2024). Multilingual numeracy work shows accuracy drops across scripts/formats (The Effect of Scripts and Formats on LLM Numeracy 2026), that models fail cross-linguistic numeral puzzles for lack of compositional numeral structure (Investigating linguistic-mathematical reasoning 2025), and that embeddings support grammaticality but not value comparison across languages (Probing for Multilingual Numerical Understanding 2020). Actual delta: LLMs Know More About Numbers (2026) establishes a log-magnitude direction but only for digits in one language and never tests morphology; The Effect of Scripts and Formats (2026) measures behavioral accuracy across notations but not whether morpheme values contaminate the internal magnitude; Investigating linguistic-mathematical reasoning (2025) shows behavioral failure on numeral puzzles but offers no representational or causal account. None asks whether, when a value is expressed as number WORDS, the recovered internal magnitude is language-agnostic and whether morphological transparency causally distorts it. We uniquely use cross-linguistic numeral morphology as a controlled probe, contribute the Opacity Index and compositional-leakage metric, and provide a causal steering fix. More broadly this is a case study of when multilingual semantic abstraction fails specifically under compositional morphology.
Abstract: Multilingual language models must map number words in any language onto a shared notion of magnitude: French 'quatre-vingt-dix', literally 'four-twenty-ten', and English 'ninety' should both point to 90. Numeral systems differ dramatically in morphological transparency -- some cleanly decimal (Chinese, English), others vigesimal or idiosyncratic (French, Danish, Georgian, Basque). We ask whether the model recovers a language-agnostic magnitude regardless of surface morphology, or whether the literal values of a numeral's component morphemes leak in. Using established magnitude-probing tools (linear log-magnitude probes, monotonic subspaces) -- our novelty is the finding, the metric, and the intervention, not the tools -- we decode internal magnitude for numbers spelled as words across 12+ languages spanning transparent-decimal, additive, vigesimal, and irregular numeral systems, using MULTIPLE anchors (within-language digits, cross-language digits, and transparent-language word forms) rather than a single English-digit anchor, and span-pooled/layerwise representations chosen empirically. We define a numeral-system Opacity Index (a released, annotator-validated artifact) and a compositional-leakage score. We predict (1) leakage is measurable and direction-consistent; (2) it correlates with opacity and is dissociable from resource level, tokenization fragmentation, and frequency; and (3) training-free steering along the recovered clean magnitude direction repairs downstream comparison and arithmetic errors on opaque numerals without retraining. So what: word-form numerals are ubiquitous and consequential in finance (spelled amounts on checks/contracts), medicine (dosage/frequency in non-English clinical text), education, and voice/text interfaces in non-English languages; if leakage exists, these pipelines need magnitude correction or digit normalization, and if it does not, the shared magnitude representation is genuinely robust and the concern is narrowed. We quantify how often opaque forms appear and how much task error they induce. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B with layerwise and model-scale analyses. The study turns numeral-system typology into a precise instrument for measuring where the multilingual magnitude representation is shared versus contaminated by surface form.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed): parallel numbers 0-1000, oversampling ranges where morphology diverges (70-99, teens, round hundreds), spelled as words in 12 languages spanning numeral-system typology -- transparent-decimal (English, Chinese, Turkish, Japanese), additive/subtractive (Welsh, a Latin-style set), vigesimal (French, Danish, Basque, Georgian), irregular teens/inversion (German, Dutch). Each numeral is annotated with a PRECISE morpheme parse and the literal value composed from its morphemes; the parsing rules, including irregulars and ambiguous analyses, are documented per language and validated by multiple annotators, and each language gets a numeral-system Opacity Index (mean absolute difference between morpheme-implied composition and true decimal value, plus a non-decimal-base indicator). The Opacity Index and morpheme-annotated stimuli are a released dataset artifact with a datasheet. Anchors: instead of a single English-digit anchor we use within-language digits, cross-language digits where available, and transparent-language word forms. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; representations are span-pooled over the numeral plus layerwise, with the representation choice justified empirically (compared to last-token); probes are ridge/linear log-magnitude regressions, 3 seeds, validated on held-out numbers. Tokenisation statistics are reported and stimuli curated for clean morpheme boundaries. To avoid circularity, diagnosis stimuli (used to fit probes and measure leakage) and repair stimuli (used to evaluate steering) are DISJOINT sets.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- measurable, direction-consistent compositional leakage, causally due to morphology): tests claim (a) and the causal core. Data/model as Setup. Method: train log-magnitude probes / identify monotonic subspaces on digit anchors, then apply the SAME probe to hidden states of word-form numerals in every language; define the compositional-leakage score by regressing decoded-magnitude error on (true value) and (morpheme-implied value), the coefficient on morpheme-implied value being the leakage. Baseline alternative explanations tested jointly: a lexical-frequency regression, a token-count/tokenization-fragmentation regression, and a language-ID indicator are entered alongside morpheme-implied value, so leakage must survive controlling for frequency, fragmentation, and language identity; a direct-translation-to-digits baseline and matched synthetic numeral forms/paraphrases further isolate morphology. Causal test: patch/ablate the component-morpheme token representations across MATCHED numeral pairs (e.g. an opaque numeral vs its transparent counterpart) and test that decoded magnitude shifts toward vs away from morpheme-implied values, and that shifts are SPECIFIC to value-relevant morphemes rather than arbitrary subwords. Decisive metric: the leakage coefficient (fraction of morpheme-implied deviation reflected in decoded magnitude) for opaque numerals after the controls, plus the causal shift under value-relevant-morpheme patching relative to arbitrary-subword patching. Convincing result: probe transfer is valid (held-out digit numbers decoded within 5% relative error), the leakage coefficient is significantly positive and direction-consistent at >=0.15 after controlling for frequency/fragmentation/language-ID, AND value-relevant-morpheme patching causally moves decoded magnitude toward the morpheme-implied value more than arbitrary-subword patching. Indecision band: leakage 0.05-0.15, or partly absorbed by the controls = weak leakage; <0.05, CI including 0, or a null/non-specific morpheme patch = no morphology-driven leakage. Negative result (no leakage, or probe fails to transfer) means the magnitude representation is genuinely shared -- an informative refutation.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- leakage tracks numeral-system opacity, not resource level or fragmentation): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup. Predictors entered together: per-language leakage coefficient (Experiment 1) against the Opacity Index, a resource-level proxy (pretraining token share / mLAMA accuracy), a tokenization-fragmentation measure, and a frequency proxy. Decisive metric: partial Spearman / standardized coefficient of Opacity Index vs the other predictors, with bootstrap CIs, and the crucial contrast of a transparent LOW-resource language (Turkish or Swahili) vs an opaque HIGH-resource one (French). Convincing result: |Opacity Index effect| corresponds to Spearman >=0.5 and exceeds the resource, fragmentation, and frequency effects by >=0.2, with the contrast pair ordered by opacity (French leaks more than Turkish) not resource. Indecision band: Opacity Index within 0.05-0.2 of the strongest competing predictor = mixed account; not stronger, or gap <0.05 = the opacity claim is refuted. Negative result (leakage tracks resource or fragmentation) reassigns the effect.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- training-free steering repairs the leak): tests claim (c) on the disjoint repair set. Data: magnitude-comparison ('which is larger, [word-form A] or [word-form B]?') and simple word-form arithmetic over opaque numerals, plus non-numeric prompts for a fluency control. Model: extract the clean magnitude direction from digit/transparent anchors; at inference, project out the morpheme-leakage component (or steer toward the correct-magnitude location) for opaque numerals. Systems compared: steering vs a translate-numeral-to-digits prompting baseline vs no intervention. Decisive metric: reduction in decoded-magnitude relative error on opaque numerals, then comparison/arithmetic accuracy gain, with a specificity check that non-numeric fluency (perplexity) is unharmed; the pre-intervention link that high-leakage items have higher error is reported first, and a realistic-pipeline estimate of how often opaque forms appear and their induced error accompanies it. Convincing result: steering cuts decoded-magnitude error by >=50% and raises comparison/arithmetic accuracy by >=4 points on opaque numerals while fluency is unharmed and matches or beats the translate-to-digits baseline. Indecision band: 20-50% error reduction or a 1.5-4 point gain = partial repair; <20% reduction or <1.5 point gain = steering does not repair the leak and H3 is refuted. Negative result (no repair, or repair only by harming fluency) refutes the steering claim. Additional analyses: layerwise leakage profile (where it appears) and a model-scale comparison (whether it decreases in stronger/larger models).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used magnitude; we require the causal value-relevant-morpheme patching (Exp. 1) and the steering-repair behavioral effect (Exp. 3) for functional relevance. 2. Tokenization of number words differs across languages and may split morphemes unevenly; we curate clean morpheme boundaries, use span-pooled/layerwise representations, report tokenization statistics, and enter a fragmentation control. 3. Leakage might be confounded with frequency or translationese; we include frequency, token-count, and language-ID controls, matched synthetic forms/paraphrases, and the resource-level dissociation. 4. The Opacity Index and morpheme parses are hand-constructed; we document the annotation protocol, validate with multiple annotators, release the artifact, and report robustness to alternative operationalizations. 5. Diagnosis-repair circularity is avoided by using disjoint stimulus sets. 6. Some models may resolve morphology so well that leakage is negligible -- still a positive finding (magnitude is genuinely shared); multiple models/languages give power to detect small effects, and layerwise/model-scale analyses characterize it. 7. Steering may trade repair for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: kinship_granularity_collapse
Title: Uncle or Mother's-Younger-Brother? How the Query Language's Kinship System Sets the Granularity of Relational Reasoning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a largely language-agnostic genealogical-tree representation of a family, but the SPECIFIC kin category they output is resolved through a granularity setting covertly fixed by the query language's kinship system. For a fixed genealogical fact, the model tends to collapse to the (usually coarser, dominant-language) kin distinctions, systematically failing to produce the finer distinctions (maternal vs paternal side, relative age, gender) that a target language grammaticalizes -- a category-resolution failure downstream of a correctly-computed tree. Kinship is chosen as a clean, richly-typologized probe of a more general phenomenon: language-conditioned semantic underspecification, i.e. the query language setting the granularity at which a shared continuous/structured representation is read out. We hypothesize this collapse scales with kinship-typology distance rather than resource level, and (as a testable, not assumed, claim) is carried by a locatable, steerable granularity signal separable from the tree representation.
Related Work: Explicit novelty claims: (N1, problem definition) we introduce language-conditioned readout GRANULARITY as a distinct failure mode, with kinship as the cleanest instance; (N2, finding) we show granularity collapse to dominant-language kin categories on a correctly-computed tree; (N3, mechanism) we test a separable late category-resolution step and a steerable granularity signal; (N4, dataset) KIN-RESOLVE, a controlled genealogy-to-kinterm benchmark keyed to kinship-system typology. Closest prior, one-sentence delta each: anthropology (Kinbank 2023; kinship-system typologies; efficient-communication accounts 2025) catalogues kinterms but has NO in-LLM mechanism; cross-linguistic semantic-alignment (Thompson et al. 2018) finds kinship aligned yet structurally divergent but is behavioral/embedding-only; relational-subspace interpretability (Investigating Representation Universality 2024; Hernandez et al. 2023; LRC 2023; Locating Relational Concepts 2024) shows tree-like causal relational subspaces but is MONOLINGUAL and treats kin categories as fixed; multilingual concept-space work (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Semantic Hub 2024) shows shared directions but not a language-set granularity readout. Rather than claim 'none asks', we position kinship as a case study of the broader underspecification problem and note an extension to a second domain (below) to show it is not niche.
Abstract: Languages carve the family tree very differently: English lumps father's and mother's brother into one 'uncle', while Chinese, Turkish, Hindi and many others obligatorily distinguish the paternal from the maternal side, elder from younger sibling, or the gender of the linking relative. A competent multilingual model must recover the same underlying genealogy but then name relatives at whatever granularity the target language demands. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs instead default to the coarser kin categories of their dominant language. We frame this as a case of language-conditioned semantic underspecification -- the query language setting the granularity at which a shared structured representation is read out -- with kinship as a clean, richly-typologized probe. We hypothesize that models compute a largely language-agnostic genealogical-tree representation but resolve it into kin terms through a granularity setting covertly fixed by the query language, causing systematic 'granularity collapse': for a fixed genealogical fact, the model omits the finer side/age/gender distinctions a target language grammaticalizes. We build KIN-RESOLVE, controlled genealogy-description-plus-question items whose correct kin term differs across kinship systems, rendered across 12+ languages spanning Eskimo, Sudanese, bifurcate-merging and other typologies, using Kinbank ground-truth terms, with native-speaker annotation for morphologically-marked/multiword terms. Behaviorally we measure per-language granularity-collapse rate and dissociate it from resource level via kinship-typology distance in a mixed-effects analysis. Mechanistically we probe for a shared tree subspace that transfers across languages, use activation patching with strong controls to show the tree is correctly computed even when the term is wrong, and test whether a recovered granularity signal steers repair or induced collapse without altering the genealogy. We also verify the model actually knows the target kin vocabulary, and pilot the same readout-granularity effect in a second obligatory-distinction domain to show generality. User-facing stakes include translation, genealogy, education, and culturally-specific assistants that silently drop kin distinctions for speakers of fine-distinguishing languages. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Dataset KIN-RESOLVE (constructed from Kinbank, existing): 400 short genealogy descriptions (e.g. 'A is B's father; C is A's younger brother; ...') each paired with a question whose CORRECT kin term differs across kinship systems. What makes it new beyond Kinbank/synthetic family-tree benchmarks: items are keyed to kinship-SYSTEM typology so the correct answer's required FEATURES (side, generation, relative age, gender) vary by language, with per-item gold terms and feature annotations validated by native speakers (including morphologically-marked/multiword terms, with agreement thresholds and exclusion of ambiguous items). Rendered in 12+ languages spanning Eskimo (English, Spanish), descriptive/Sudanese (Chinese, Turkish, Hindi, Arabic), bifurcate-merging/classificatory (a Bantu and a Dravidian language), relative-age (Japanese, Korean); the language set is expanded as far as native-speaker validation allows for power. A per-language kinship-typology distance (difference in encoded-feature set) and MULTIPLE pre-registered resource proxies are built. Translation-artifact controls: native-written prompts where possible, back-translation audits, and balanced paraphrases per language. The 'dominant language' per model is IDENTIFIED empirically (default-term behavior on unmarked queries; pretraining-share evidence) rather than assumed English. Vocabulary-competence pre-check: a separate test that the model can produce/recognize each target-language kin term in isolation; the main collapse analysis is restricted to items whose required terms the model demonstrably knows, separating resolution failure from a lexical gap. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen, greedy, 3 paraphrase seeds. Sample sizes and uncertainty: all decisive metrics report bootstrap CIs; per-language item counts set so a 15 pp collapse-rate difference is detectable at 80% power. Error analysis separates feature-omission (right relation, missing side/age/gender) from wholly-wrong relations, with per-feature breakdowns.

Experiment 1 (H2 -- behavioral granularity collapse): score genealogical correctness (relation right, ignoring granularity) and term correctness (term carries all required features) separately. Decisive metric: GRANULARITY-COLLAPSE RATE = fraction of genealogically-correct answers whose term is under-specified relative to the target-language requirement (collapsing toward the dominant-language category), among vocabulary-known items. Systems compared: query in target language vs in the model's dominant language (coarse upper bound) vs translate-to-dominant-first. Convincing result: for fine-distinguishing languages, collapse rate >=25% among genealogically-correct, vocabulary-known answers, markedly higher than for Eskimo-type languages not requiring the distinction. Indecision band: 10-25% = weak/partial; <10% = faithful resolution, refuting H2.

Experiment 2 (H3 -- collapse tracks kinship typology, not resource; mixed-effects): Predictors: per-language kinship-typology distance vs multiple resource proxies. Decisive metric: in a mixed-effects model (random effects for item and model) the standardized effect of typology distance vs resource on collapse rate, plus Spearman contrasts with bootstrap CIs; key contrast = a lower-resource fine-distinguishing language (Dravidian) vs a higher-resource coarse one. Convincing result: typology effect significant with |Spearman| >=0.5 and exceeding the resource effect by >=0.2, key-contrast pair ordered by typology not resource. Indecision band: within 0.05-0.2 = mixed; typology not stronger = refuted. Negative result assigns collapse to resource.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- shared tree, causal late-resolution failure; controlled): Target latent defined operationally -- the tree probe predicts standardized pairwise relation features (side, generation, relative-age, gender, ancestor/descendant direction) over the described individuals, a fixed label space across items. Method: (a) train probes to decode these features from mid-layer states, test cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others), contrasted with a surface-term probe; (b) activation-patch the mid-layer tree representation across a fine-correct vs collapsing run, with CONTROLS: random-direction patch, same-language patch, wrong-tree (mismatched-genealogy) patch, layer sweep, and token-position control; (c) patch/steer late-layer term-resolution components. Decisive metrics: tree-probe cross-lingual transfer accuracy; rate at which patching the tree changes the answer vs rate at which manipulating late resolution recovers the finer term, each above its control. Convincing result: tree probe transfers within 10 pp of in-language while surface-term probe does not; patching the tree changes answers in <=15% (tree already correct, above random/wrong-tree controls) while late-resolution manipulation recovers the finer term in >=40%. Indecision band: tree-transfer 10-25 pp below, or late-recovery 20-40% = partial; tree-transfer >25 pp below, or tree-patch >30%, or controls match = refutes H1.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- a locatable, steerable granularity signal, stated as a testable hypothesis): recover a granularity direction (mean activation difference between fine-resolved and coarse-resolved runs pooled across languages); steer to (a) REPAIR collapsed terms and (b) INDUCE collapse where correct. Systems compared: steering vs explicit feature-prompting ('specify maternal vs paternal') vs translate-first vs matched-norm random-direction steer (sham). Decisive metrics (in order): repair rate and induction rate on term correctness; genealogical-correctness preservation (specificity, within 2 pp); fluency (perplexity); all with bootstrap CIs. Convincing result: steering repairs >=40% of collapsed terms and induces collapse in >=40% of correct ones, beats the sham, preserves genealogical correctness (>=95%) and fluency. Indecision band: 20-40% = partial; <20%, genealogy degraded (>5%), or sham matches = the granularity signal is not a clean separable control (we then report only the weaker readout-localization claim from Exp. 3). Extension pilot: replicate the collapse + readout-localization on a SECOND obligatory-distinction domain (e.g. motion-path/manner verbs or evidentiality) on a small item set to show the underspecification effect is not kinship-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of a tree or granularity signal may reflect the readout basis; the causal patching with random/same-language/wrong-tree/layer/position controls (Exp. 3) and steering repair/induction with a sham control (Exp. 4), plus the genealogy-preservation specificity check, are required to promote correlation to mechanism, and we present the separable-granularity-signal claim as a testable hypothesis that the weaker readout-localization result does not depend on. 2. Kin terms can be genuinely ambiguous, optional, or dialect-dependent; we restrict to Kinbank-attested high-agreement terms with native-speaker annotation and treat multi-term relations separately. 3. Collapse could reflect a lexical gap (not knowing the target kin vocabulary); the vocabulary-competence pre-check and the demonstration that the tree is correctly computed distinguish resolution failure from missing knowledge. 4. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on language contrasts; we expand the language set, pre-register multiple resource proxies, and use mixed-effects modeling rather than simple correlations. 5. Strong models may resolve fine terms well, shrinking the effect; documenting faithful resolution is itself informative, the induction experiment still yields causal evidence, and multiple models/languages give power. 6. Tokenization of multi-morpheme kin terms varies; we use last-token/pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. Translation artifacts could confound; native-written prompts, back-translation audits, and balanced paraphrases address this. 8. 'Dominant language' is identified empirically per model, not assumed. 9. Practitioners: if positive, multilingual evaluation should score feature-level term correctness (not just relation), and decoding/steering can enforce target-language granularity; if negative, current lump-then-translate pipelines are safer than feared. 10. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: abstract_vs_surface_priming_channels
Title: Priming Across the Word-Order Divide: Two Competing Structural Channels Behind Cross-Lingual Structural Priming in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual structural priming in multilingual LLMs is carried by TWO coexisting, dissociable channels: an abstract, word-order-invariant structure representation and a surface token/order-copying channel. For typologically aligned language pairs both channels agree, but for word-order-divergent pairs (e.g. verb-final vs. verb-medial) they conflict, and the model's realized priming reflects whichever channel dominates. We predict (a) genuine abstract, order-inverting priming (a structure primed in one language raises the analogous structure in another even when the surface word orders differ), (b) that a locatable abstract-structure representation is causally responsible for this order-invariant transfer while a separate surface-copy channel drives order-matched priming, and (c) that the abstract channel's dominance scales with typological/word-order distance being bridged, and can be causally amplified to repair failed cross-lingual priming across divergent word orders.
Related Work: A rich line shows LLMs exhibit structural priming that behaviorally indexes abstract grammar (Sinclair et al. 2022; Prasad et al. 2019; Finding Structure in Language Models 2024) and cross-lingual priming that causally influences generation across languages (Structural Priming Demonstrates Abstract Grammatical Representations in Multilingual LMs 2023; Michaelov et al. 2023; RNN/Transformer Chinese-English priming 2024; acquisition dynamics 2023/2025). Human/connectionist work debates whether identical word order is required for cross-language priming (error-driven learning account, Kaan et al. 2021) and finds it is not. Mechanistic multilingual work shows shared syntactic subspaces (Universal Grammatical Relations in mBERT 2020), shared circuits for shared processes (The Same But Different 2024), and shared agreement neurons (Causal Analysis of Agreement Neurons 2022). ALL existing LLM priming work is BEHAVIORAL and treats priming as a single effect indexing 'abstract structure'; none dissociates an abstract order-invariant channel from a surface order-copying channel, none uses word-order-divergent pairs as a controlled instrument to separate them, and none provides a causal (patching + steering) account of which internal representation carries order-inverting cross-lingual priming. We uniquely turn cross-lingual priming into a two-channel diagnostic with a causal, steerable abstract-structure locus. Prior LLM priming work already establishes, behaviorally, that cross-lingual priming exists and indexes some abstract structure; our delta is the DISSOCIATION of two channels (abstract order-invariant vs surface order-copying) with causal localization and steering repair, which is our single strongest and primary claim - the typological-distance scaling and the repair steering are secondary extensions. We do not claim broad societal impact; the impact is scientific understanding and multilingual evaluation methodology.
Abstract: Structural priming—where encountering a syntactic structure makes its reuse more likely—has become a key behavioral probe showing that multilingual LLMs share abstract grammatical representations across languages. But behavior alone cannot tell whether cross-lingual priming rides on a genuinely abstract, order-invariant representation of structure or on a shallower channel that copies surface token order. We propose that both channels coexist and can be dissociated by pitting them against each other: in language pairs with divergent word order (e.g. a verb-final prime language and a verb-medial target), abstract structural priming predicts the analogous construction should be primed despite different surface orders, whereas a surface-copy channel predicts priming only when orders match. We build a controlled cross-lingual priming suite over alternating constructions (dative, active/passive, genitive) across language pairs spanning aligned and divergent word orders, and measure order-invariant versus order-matched priming. Mechanistically, we (i) probe for an abstract construction representation that is shared and decodable across languages independent of surface order, (ii) use activation patching to test whether this abstract representation is causally sufficient to prime the analogous target structure across a word-order divide, while a separate surface-form representation drives order-matched priming, and (iii) recover an abstract-structure direction and steer it to repair cross-lingual priming that fails across divergent orders. We predict the abstract channel's contribution scales with the word-order distance being bridged and that steering it induces order-invariant priming without harming fluency. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B. We estimate the abstract- and surface-channel contributions as coefficients in a mixed-effects decomposition of log-odds priming over templates and languages, and test them against one-channel (surface-only and abstract-only) accounts by nested model comparison rather than a single threshold. If confirmed, multilingual transfer diagnostics and failure repair gain a principled handle for word-order-divergent, low-resource settings; if falsified and a single channel suffices, cross-lingual priming is simpler than the two-channel view implies. To keep the design clean we foreground the dative and voice alternations and a small set of well-matched aligned/divergent pairs, expanding only if the signal is robust, and treat probes and the logit lens as supportive diagnostics rather than core evidence of mechanism. The primary audience is the multilingual evaluation, interpretability, and psycholinguistic-modeling communities.
Experiments:
Shared setup. Priming suite (adapted from the Prime-LM cross-lingual priming framework plus new templates): parallel prime-target items over three alternating constructions with clear structural variants - dative (double-object vs prepositional-object), voice (active vs passive), genitive (of- vs 's-type or cross-linguistic analogues) - 200 item templates per construction (600 total), each with a congruent, an incongruent, and a neutral prime. A prime is presented in a SOURCE language and a target continuation describing a NEW event is elicited in a TARGET language, forcing a construction choice. Language directions cover WORD-ORDER-ALIGNED pairs (English<->Spanish, both SVO) and WORD-ORDER-DIVERGENT pairs (Japanese/Korean/Hindi/Turkish verb-final <-> English/Spanish verb-medial), plus within-language priming as an upper-bound calibration. Lexical overlap and semantic similarity are controlled following Prime-LM factors, with no-overlap conditions. Templates native-speaker-validated for grammaticality; low-agreement items dropped and reported. Per-pair word-order/typological distance from lang2vec; resource proxy from CC-100. Models (7-8B, single A100-80GB, inference + steering, frozen weights): Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B. 3 seeds (item sampling and prime order).

Experiment 1 (H1/prediction-a - order-invariant vs order-matched priming coexist). Tests whether cross-lingual priming shows an abstract order-invariant component (present across divergent word orders) and a surface order-matched component (present only when orders match). Decisive metric: priming strength = log-odds increase of the target construction after a congruent prime vs an incongruent/neutral prime, decomposed into an ORDER-INVARIANT component (priming that persists across word-order-divergent pairs) and an ORDER-MATCHED component (priming that appears only for aligned pairs), per construction. Systems compared: divergent vs aligned pairs; within-language priming as the upper bound. Convincing: a significant positive order-invariant component across divergent pairs (log-odds shift with 95% CI excluding 0) AND a distinct order-matched component larger for aligned than divergent pairs, in all three models. Indecision band: order-invariant component present but small (log-odds shift 0-0.1) or CI touching 0; reported as weak abstract priming, not a clean two-channel picture. Negative result: no order-invariant component across divergent pairs (shift indistinguishable from 0) refutes the abstract channel; no order-matched excess for aligned pairs refutes the surface channel.

Experiment 2 (prediction-c - abstract-channel share scales with word-order distance). Tests whether the abstract channel's relative contribution rises (or surface-copy fails) as the word-order gap grows. Correlate the order-invariant priming magnitude and the abstract:surface ratio with lang2vec word-order distance between prime and target. Dissociate from resource via matched contrasts (a divergent low-resource pair vs an aligned high-resource pair). Decisive metric: Spearman of abstract-channel share with word-order distance (95% CIs), partialled for resource. Convincing: abstract-channel share rises with word-order distance (Spearman >= 0.4) and survives resource control. Indecision band: Spearman 0.2-0.4 or vanishing after resource control; reported as suggestive. Negative result: no relationship (< 0.2) refutes prediction (c)'s scaling claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 - a shared, order-invariant abstract construction representation). Tests whether an abstract construction identity is decodable across languages independent of surface order. Train linear probes and read the logit lens at each layer to decode abstract construction identity (e.g. dative-DO vs dative-PO) from post-prime hidden states; evaluate cross-lingual transfer (train one language's primes, decode another's) and invariance to surface order. Contrast with a surface-order probe (which token order appeared). Probes are the only trainable parameters; base frozen; 3 probe-split seeds. Decisive metric: cross-lingual, order-invariant transfer accuracy of the abstract-construction probe. Convincing: the abstract probe transfers across languages and across word orders with <= 10-point drop off in-language accuracy and well above chance, while the surface-order probe does not carry construction identity across divergent orders. Indecision band: transfer drop 10-20 points; partial sharing. Negative result: abstract probe near chance across orders (drop > 20 points) refutes a shared order-invariant representation.

Experiment 4 (prediction-b - causal channel dissociation). Tests whether the abstract representation is causally sufficient to prime across a word-order divide while the surface representation drives only order-matched priming. (a) Abstract-channel sufficiency: extract the mid-layer abstract construction representation from a divergent-order source prime and patch it into a neutral target-language run; test whether it primes the analogous target construction WITHOUT forcing the source's surface order. (b) Surface-channel test: patch the surface-order representation and test whether it drives order-matched priming but misfires across divergent orders. Model frozen; patching at inference; specificity = matched non-construction site. Decisive metric: construction-choice shift induced by the abstract patch across the divide (log-odds), reported first, with output order-fidelity and the matched-site shift as controls. Convincing: the abstract patch induces the analogous construction across divergent orders (log-odds shift with CI excluding 0) without copying source order, the surface patch induces order-matched priming that fails across divergence, and the matched site does neither. Indecision band: abstract-patch shift positive but small (0-0.1 log-odds) or CI touching 0; weak causal support. Negative result: abstract patch produces no cross-divide priming refutes prediction (b).

Experiment 5 (prediction-c - steering the abstract channel repairs failed cross-lingual priming). Tests whether amplifying a recovered abstract-structure direction repairs priming that fails across divergent orders (and can induce a construction unprompted). Recover an abstract construction direction as the mean activation difference between the two construction variants, pooled across languages and orders; steer during target generation, over a dose-response. Model frozen; only the vector varies; compare against explicit-instruction prompting and within-language priming. Decisive metric: increase in order-invariant priming (log-odds) for previously-failing divergent pairs (reported first), then unprompted induction rate, with grammaticality/fluency (perplexity) and specificity (non-target constructions unchanged) alongside. Convincing: steering raises order-invariant priming by >= 0.2 log-odds on failing divergent pairs with a monotone dose-response, preserves grammaticality, and < 5% perplexity increase. Indecision band: 0.05-0.2 log-odds gain or non-monotone dose; weak handle. Negative result: < 0.05 log-odds gain or repair only at grammaticality-breaking doses refutes the abstract-channel steering claim.

Statistical rigor. We run 5 seeds, fit mixed-effects models over templates and languages, report a power analysis, and apply a pre-specified multiple-comparisons plan; steering is checked against a global-bias control confirming it induces the target construction rather than uniformly shifting outputs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Cross-lingual priming may be dominated by lexical/semantic overlap rather than structure; we control lexical overlap and semantic similarity (Prime-LM style) and include no-overlap conditions to isolate abstract structure. 2. Probe decodability of an 'abstract construction' representation may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used channel; the activation-patching sufficiency test (Exp. 5) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 6) are required to promote correlation to mechanism, with order-fidelity and specificity checks. 3. The two-channel dissociation may be fuzzy—real behavior could be a graded mixture rather than clean channels; we present the abstract vs. surface contribution as a continuous decomposition and report effect sizes rather than forcing a binary. 4. Eliciting a clean construction choice in the target language across divergent-order languages is nontrivial; we use native-speaker-validated templates, constrained elicitation, and grammaticality checks, and analyze order-aligned vs. divergent pairs separately. 5. Strong models may show robust order-invariant priming everywhere (only an abstract channel), which would simplify the picture—still an informative positive result establishing genuine abstract structural sharing, and the steering/patching still localizes it. 6. Priming magnitudes can be small and noisy; we aggregate over many items/constructions and report confidence intervals, and use within-language priming as a calibration upper bound. 7. Tokenization and length differ across scripts/orders, confounding probability comparisons; we use log-odds between minimally-different construction variants (length-matched where possible) and report tokenization statistics. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families across multiple constructions and language pairs address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: grammatical_gender_concept_leak
Title: The Gender You Didn't Ask For: Causal Leakage of Query-Language Grammatical Gender into the Shared Concept Space and Cross-Lingual Semantic Judgments
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM represents an inanimate concept, the grammatical gender that concept happens to carry in the query language covertly enters the model's language-agnostic concept representation and causally biases downstream *semantic* judgments (attribute association, pronoun choice, adjective selection), even when the answer is produced in a gender-neutral output language (English or Chinese). The narrowest genuinely new setting is exactly this: neutral-output semantic judgment after gendered-language prompting.
