We hypothesize (a) a covert 'concept-gender' direction -- decodable from the concept's mid-layer representation, inheriting the query language's grammatical assignment, and distinct BOTH from surface agreement features (which morphological form is emitted) AND from a generic already-known latent grammatical-gender direction, because it rides on the CONCEPT representation used in reasoning rather than on the wordform; (b) that this leakage is causally responsible for cross-lingual semantic-gender inconsistencies; and (c) that leakage strength scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes gender and can be selectively removed by a training-free projection. This is a case study of morphosyntax leaking into semantics, not only a gender-specific artifact.
Related Work: Prior work shows grammatical gender contaminates static/contextual word embeddings of inanimate nouns (Gonen et al. 2019; embedding-disentangling 2020-2022), that gender subspaces are partly shared across languages so classification transfers but removal does not (Analyzing Gender Representation 2022), that grammatical concepts including gender share cross-lingual feature directions (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), and that grammatical gender biases text-to-image outputs (Beyond Content 2025). Distributional accounts test whether opposite-gender noun pairs shift embedding semantics (Testing a Distributional Account 2024). Novelty boundary, stated explicitly: prior cross-lingual bias-transfer work establishes that 'bias transfers across languages' in embeddings or generations -- a re-implementation of that in an LLM would NOT be novel; Latent Grammatical Concepts (2025) already exhibits a shared latent grammatical-gender direction at the mechanism level. What is new here is (i) that the query language's grammatical gender enters the CONCEPT representation used during reasoning (not the surface wordform) and (ii) that it causally alters GENUINELY SEMANTIC judgments produced in a gender-NEUTRAL output language, tested by activation patching. Activation patching is required for the novelty, not merely as evidence: only a causal swap of the isolated concept-gender direction between a masculine-language and a feminine-language run -- flipping the semantic judgment while preserving concept identity -- can distinguish covert concept-level leakage from a correlated surface-agreement or lexical feature that mere probing would confound.
Abstract: Many languages grammatically gender inanimate nouns, and these assignments are largely arbitrary and disagree across languages: a bridge is feminine in German but masculine in Spanish. We investigate whether multilingual LLMs, widely believed to compute in a shared language-agnostic concept space, keep that space free of the query language's grammatical gender, or whether it covertly leaks in and biases genuinely semantic judgments. We restrict to the narrowest new setting: semantic-gender judgments produced in a gender-NEUTRAL output language (English or Chinese) after the concept is introduced in a gendered query language. Using cross-lingual noun pairs with OPPOSITE grammatical genders as a natural experiment, we ask the model which attribute/adjective/pronoun best fits a concept while varying the gendered introduction language. We test three separable contributions. Finding: a covert 'concept-gender' direction is linearly decodable from mid-layer concept representations and inherits the query language's grammatical gender, distinct from surface agreement and from a generic latent-gender direction. Mechanism: activation patching swapping this isolated direction between a masculine-language run and a feminine-language run flips the semantic judgment while preserving concept identity -- causal evidence, not correlation, that grammatical-gender leakage drives cross-lingual semantic inconsistency. Debiasing: a training-free projection along a shared concept-gender direction reduces leakage while preserving legitimately gendered concepts and unrelated-task utility. We predict leakage scales with how strongly the query language grammaticalizes gender (Slavic/Germanic/Romance vs English/Chinese controls), not with resource level. So what: if leakage exists, multilingual evaluation authors, bias auditors, translation-pipeline builders, and prompt designers must treat the 'shared concept space' as contaminated by query-language morphosyntax and test cross-lingual semantic consistency directly; if it does not, prior embedding-level concerns are narrowed at the generation level. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 8+ languages, with pre-registered tests and multiple-comparison correction. The work is a case study of morphosyntax leaking into semantics.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed from existing lexica): ~300 inanimate concrete nouns with attested grammatical gender across 6 gendered languages spanning gender-marking strength -- Romance (Spanish, French, Italian), Germanic (German, 3-gender), Slavic (Russian, Polish) -- plus 2 gender-neutral output controls (English, Chinese). A key subset has OPPOSITE grammatical gender across >=2 languages (key, bridge, sun, moon), giving matched minimal pairs that dissociate grammatical from semantic gender. Each opposite-gender pair is annotated with human-rated semantic similarity and stereotype associations, so semantic confounds and stereotype matching can be controlled. Per-language grammatical gender is annotated. A separate semantically-gendered control set (man/woman/king/queen) is included, which SHOULD retain gender. Language of introduction, output language, and prompt template are fully counterbalanced. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0, multiple paraphrases; the patched/decoded representation is the last-token-of-concept (or neutral-prompt final-token) hidden state at the mid-layers where the concept is assembled -- we justify this as the 'concept representation' by verifying it predicts the concept identity and is downstream of surface wordform tokens; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out nouns); tokenisation reported. Statistics: all hypotheses, effect-size thresholds, and the multiple-comparison correction across models/languages/layers are pre-registered; we avoid strong verbs ('establish'/'reveal') unless the causal and selectivity controls are decisive.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a covert concept-gender direction, distinct from surface agreement and from a generic latent-gender direction): tests the FINDING. Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) concept-gender probe -- per-layer linear probes decode the grammatical gender of the concept from mid-layer hidden states on held-out nouns; test that decoded concept-gender inherits the QUERY language's assignment, that a probe on the gender-neutral languages is near chance, that it is distinct from surface agreement features, and that it is not merely the generic latent-gender direction (by testing whether it is concept-position-bound rather than wordform-bound); (b) behavioural leakage -- semantic-gender judgments with the answer forced into a gender-NEUTRAL output language: masculine- vs feminine-associated adjective choice, personification pronoun, adjective-fit ranking, controlling for the human-rated semantic similarity and stereotype scores. Decisive metric: cross-lingual inconsistency = fraction of opposite-gender pairs whose neutral-language judgment flips with the query language, plus concept-gender probe accuracy above the neutral-language baseline, after covarying out semantic-similarity/stereotype confounds. Convincing result: the probe decodes concept-gender well above baseline and inherits the query-language assignment, AND the behavioural flip rate on opposite-gender pairs is >=15 percentage points (pp) above the neutral-query baseline net of confounds. Indecision band: 5-15 pp = weak leakage; <5 pp, or a probe at chance, = no covert concept-gender and the finding is refuted. Negative result (no decodable concept-gender, judgments invariant to query language) refutes leakage.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- grammatical gender causally drives the semantic judgment): tests the MECHANISM. Data: opposite-gender pair concepts, matched on semantic similarity and stereotype scores. Model: frozen, activation patching. Method: run two forward passes introducing the concept in a masculine- vs feminine-marking language, both answering in English; activation-patch the isolated concept-gender direction (and, for comparison, the whole mid-layer concept representation) from the masculine run into the feminine run and measure whether the English semantic judgment flips to match the donor's grammatical gender while concept identity (topic/answer content) is preserved. Specificity control: patch an UNRELATED matched direction of equal norm, which must not flip the judgment. Decisive metric: causal flip rate vs number/location of patched components, with an identity-preservation check and the unrelated-direction control. Convincing result: patching flips the semantic judgment in >=50% of pairs with identity preserved (>=95%), the isolated concept-gender direction alone suffices, and the unrelated-direction control flips <10%. Indecision band: flip rate 25-50% = partial causal role; <25%, or a flip rate matched by the unrelated-direction control, = grammatical gender is not causally responsible and the mechanism claim is refuted. Negative result (patching does not flip judgments, or only by destroying identity) refutes causality.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- leakage scales with grammaticalisation and is selectively removable without collateral damage): tests scaling and the DEBIASING result. Data/model as Setup, including the semantically-gendered control set and a battery of unrelated neutral tasks for utility preservation. Method: (a) dose-response -- correlate per-language leakage (behavioural flip rate + probe decodability) with a gender-marking-strength index vs a resource-level proxy, entered together; (b) training-free debiasing -- extract a shared concept-gender direction (mean activation difference masculine vs feminine, pooled across gendered languages) and project it out of the concept representation at inference; (c) selectivity and utility -- verify the semantically-gendered control set retains gender AND that unrelated-task accuracy/entropy is unchanged, so the projection is not merely reducing accuracy or flattening the output distribution. Systems compared: projection vs embedding-debiasing-style baselines vs translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: reduction in cross-lingual inconsistency after projection, Spearman(leakage, grammaticalisation) vs Spearman(leakage, resource) as partial correlations, plus selectivity and unrelated-task utility deltas. Convincing result: |partial Spearman with grammaticalisation| >=0.5 exceeding resource by >=0.2 with English/Chinese controls near zero, AND projection cuts cross-lingual inconsistency by >=50% while semantically-gendered controls retain gender (<10% change) and unrelated-task utility and fluency are unharmed. Indecision band: correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed account; inconsistency reduction 20-50% = partial debiasing; reduction <20%, controls stripped of gender, or unrelated-task utility harmed = the debiasing fails or is non-selective and H3 is refuted. Negative result (leakage tracks resource, or projection cannot remove it selectively) refutes the scaling and debiasing claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability of concept-gender may reflect the readout basis rather than a functionally used representation; we require the Exp.-2 causal patching flip (with the unrelated-direction specificity control) and Exp.-3 behavioural debiasing for functional relevance. 2. Some 'semantic gender' judgments may reflect genuine cultural stereotypes rather than grammatical leakage; opposite-gender minimal pairs, gender-neutral output languages, and covarying out human-rated semantic-similarity and stereotype scores isolate the grammatical contribution. 3. Leakage may be small in strong models that fully abstract away grammar -- still an informative result (concept space is genuinely clean); multiple languages/models give power. 4. Tokenization differences complicate concept-token localization; we use last-token-of-concept / neutral-prompt final-token representations, justify them as the concept representation, and report tokenization statistics. 5. Debiasing may over-remove; the semantically-gendered control set and unrelated-task utility battery test selectivity. 6. Behavioral tasks may be prompt-sensitive; we counterbalance and average over paraphrases and pre-register tests with multiple-comparison correction. 7. We use cautious wording and avoid claiming to 'establish' effects unless the causal and selectivity controls are decisive. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: spatial_frame_of_reference_default
Title: Left of the Tree or North of the Tree? How the Query Language Sets a Default Spatial Frame of Reference in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Human languages default to different spatial frames of reference (FoR) - egocentric-relative (English, Dutch), object-intrinsic, or geocentric-absolute/cardinal (Guugu Yimithirr, Tzeltal, some Tamil/Balinese conventions). We hypothesize that (a) a multilingual LLM builds an abstract, language-agnostic spatial-relation representation, but (b) the query language covertly sets a DEFAULT frame of reference that is applied when a spatial description is ambiguous, so the SAME ambiguous scene ('the ball is left/front of the tree', 'X is beyond Y') is resolved differently depending on the query language; (c) this frame default is carried by a small, causally-manipulable 'frame-register' representation separable from the underspecified spatial content; and (d) the strength with which a language imposes its default (overriding explicit frame cues) scales with how strongly that language grammaticalizes/conventionalizes a single FoR, not with resource level, and can be repaired by steering the recovered frame direction.
Related Work: The Levinson/Pederson semantic-typology program (Semantic Typology and Spatial Conceptualization 1998; 527 cites) established that languages systematically differ in default frame of reference (relative/intrinsic/absolute), and that a community's non-linguistic cognitive frame correlates with its linguistic one - a foundational linguistic-relativity result. A computational Sapir-Whorf study (2016) modeled spatial-relation naming across five languages. On the model side, COMFORT (2024) shows VLMs are behaviorally inconsistent about frames of reference and default to English conventions, but it is a purely behavioral VLM benchmark with no mechanistic account. Interpretability work shows LLMs encode linear spatial world models and space/time directions (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Linear Spatial World Models 2025; More than Correlation 2023), and that multilingual models have orthogonal language-sensitive vs language-neutral axes (Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022). None of these (i) studies frame of reference (the interpretive coordinate system), as opposed to absolute geolocation or object position; (ii) tests whether the QUERY LANGUAGE sets a default FoR that biases resolution of ambiguous spatial descriptions in a text LLM; or (iii) provides a causal, steerable 'frame-register' representation. We uniquely port the classic FoR typology into multilingual text LLMs and give a causal, controllable mechanistic account. Novelty typing (narrow): behavioral language-conditioned frame effects are expected from COMFORT-style VLM results; the central new contribution is the causal/mechanistic frame-register account in TEXT LLMs - patching that flips the frame while preserving non-frame spatial semantics and generalizes across languages and models. Constructed very-low-resource absolute-language items are used as STRESS TESTS, not as evidence about those natural languages. Downstream stakes are concrete: navigation instructions, map and scene QA, and robotics commands where a frame mismatch changes the executed action.
Abstract: When someone says 'the cat is to the left of the tree', the meaning depends on an unstated coordinate system: is 'left' from the speaker's viewpoint (relative), the tree's intrinsic sides (intrinsic), or a cardinal direction (absolute)? A classic result in cognitive linguistics is that languages default to different frames of reference, and this default shapes how speakers interpret and remember space. We ask whether multilingual LLMs inherit these language-specific spatial defaults. We hypothesize that a model computes an abstract, underspecified spatial relation but resolves its ambiguity using a frame of reference that is covertly set by the query language, so the identical ambiguous scene is interpreted differently across languages. We construct FRAME-SPACE, a controlled set of spatial-description items with (i) frame-ambiguous versions whose truth value flips depending on the assumed frame, and (ii) frame-forcing versions with explicit relative/intrinsic/absolute cues, rendered across 12+ languages spanning relative-default, intrinsic-favoring, and absolute/cardinal-favoring conventions. Behaviorally, we measure per-language frame-choice distributions and how often the query language overrides an explicit frame cue. Mechanistically, we probe for an abstract spatial-relation direction shared across languages, then use activation patching to localize a compact frame-register whose swap flips the interpretation without changing the spatial content, and steer a recovered frame direction to repair or induce frame choices. We predict frame-override strength tracks a language's frame-conventionalization index rather than resource level. Experiments span Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2. The work ports spatial frame-of-reference typology into mechanistic interpretability and yields a controllable account of a linguistic-relativity effect in LLMs. We add human validation on the exact multilingual items (ambiguity judgments and default-frame resolutions), not only a language-level index, and hard negative controls (patching non-frame examples, and frame-unambiguous and non-spatial items) to bound collateral damage. Falsifiable core: if identical ambiguous scenes do not disagree across query languages, or if a located frame-register cannot be flipped while preserving spatial content, the query-language-default account is rejected.
Experiments:
Common setup (applies to every experiment below): models are Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B (decoder-only, ~7-8B parameters), base weights frozen throughout. Probes are L2-regularized logistic-regression classifiers on cached hidden states (60/20/20 train/validation/test by scene, 3 seeds {0,1,2}); interpretations elicited under greedy decoding via multiple-choice over frame-consistent answers. Steering and activation patching modify activations at inference with no weight updates. "pp" = percentage points; "frame of reference" (FoR) = the coordinate system for projective terms - relative (speaker viewpoint), intrinsic (object's own sides), or absolute (cardinal). Dataset (FRAME-SPACE, constructed): scenes with an observer, a landmark object with clear intrinsic sides (car/person/house), and a target. Each scene yields (a) FRAME-AMBIGUOUS descriptions using projective terms ("left", "in front of", "behind", "beyond") whose truth flips across relative/intrinsic/absolute frames, with a question whose correct answer differs by frame; and (b) FRAME-FORCING variants adding explicit cues ("from where you are standing" -> relative; "the car's own front" -> intrinsic; "to the north of" -> absolute). We build ~200 scenes x these variants x 12+ languages spanning RELATIVE-default (English, Dutch, German, Japanese), INTRINSIC/mixed (Spanish, Mandarin, Hausa), and ABSOLUTE/cardinal-favoring (Tamil, Balinese, constructed Guugu-Yimithirr-style items, a cardinal-heavy register). Native speakers validate each language's canonical default frame (kept above 0.7 agreement) and a per-language frame-conventionalization index (how obligatory/preferred one frame is). Fewer than an exhaustive set because each scene needs frame-controlled construction and native validation.

Experiment 1 (H-b - the query language sets a default frame that resolves ambiguous scenes differently): Tests whether the identical ambiguous scene is interpreted according to the query language's default, and whether that default overrides an explicit conflicting cue. Data: FRAME-AMBIGUOUS items (default test) and FRAME-FORCING items whose explicit cue conflicts with the query language's default (override test). Systems compared: per-language interpretation; query-in-English (relative anchor); translate-to-English-first. Decisive metric: frame-override rate = fraction of conflicting-cue items where the output follows the query-language default rather than the explicit cue; secondary: per-language frame-choice distribution and cross-language disagreement rate on identical ambiguous scenes. Convincing result: cross-language disagreement on identical ambiguous scenes exceeds 15 pp AND override rate differs across language types by >=15 pp (strongly-conventionalized languages override more), averaged over models. Indecision band: disagreement or override differences of 5-15 pp are reported per language rather than as a global claim. Negative result: <5 pp cross-language disagreement means the query language does not set a default frame and claim (b) fails.

Experiment 2 (H-a - an abstract, language-agnostic spatial-relation representation distinct from the resolved frame): Tests whether the underspecified projective relation is shared across languages while the resolved frame is what varies. Data: hidden states on ambiguous items. One probe decodes the underspecified relation (e.g. "left-type"), another decodes the resolved frame; a relation probe trained on one language is applied to others (transfer). Systems compared: relation probe, frame probe, label-shuffled control. Decisive metric: cross-language relation-probe transfer accuracy minus control; secondary: the relation-vs-frame dissociation (relation transfers, resolved frame is language-dependent). Convincing result: relation transfer >=15 pp above control while the resolved-frame probe shows language-dependent structure, supporting a shared relation with a variable frame. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above control is reported as partial sharing. Negative result: relation transfer within 5 pp of control means no shared abstract relation, weakening claim (a). Decodability is not use; Exp. 3 supplies causal evidence.

Experiment 3 (H-c - a compact, separable, causally-manipulable frame-register): Tests whether a small component carries the resolved frame and can be flipped without changing the scene/relation. Data: identical ambiguous items run under context forcing RELATIVE vs ABSOLUTE (or intrinsic) interpretation, yielding different answers. Activation patching transfers mid-layer components from one run into the other. Systems compared: patch at candidate components vs random-component control; overlap of the recovered frame direction with language-identity and prior absolute-geolocation directions (separability check). Decisive metric: frame-flip rate (answer switches frame) minus control, with scene/relation content preserved; secondary: cosine overlap of the frame direction with language-identity and geolocation directions (should be low). Convincing result: flip rate >=15 pp above control with content preserved AND frame-direction overlap with language/geolocation directions <0.3 cosine (separable register). Indecision band: 5-15 pp flip, or overlap 0.3-0.5, indicates a diffuse/entangled register; reported as such. Negative result: <=5 pp flip means the frame is not causally locatable and claim (c) fails.

Experiment 4 (H-d - override strength tracks frame-conventionalization, not resource level): Tests the dissociation between conventionalization and resource. Data: per-language frame-override rate and default-strength vs the frame-conventionalization index and a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy); key contrast a lower-resource strongly-absolute language vs a higher-resource mixed language. Decisive metric: partial Spearman of override rate with conventionalization controlling for resource, and with resource controlling for conventionalization. Convincing result: partial correlation with conventionalization >=0.4 (95% CI excluding 0) while the partial with resource includes 0, and the low-resource-absolute language imposes its frame more than the high-resource-mixed one. Indecision band: conventionalization correlation 0.2-0.4, or overlapping partial CIs, is reported as suggestive only. Negative result: override tracks resource (|rho| >=0.4) not conventionalization, refuting claim (d)'s scaling half.

Experiment 5 (H-d - training-free repair/induction by steering the frame direction): Tests whether steering the frame-register repairs mis-framed interpretations and induces non-default frames. Data: mis-framed items (repair); items where a non-default frame was not chosen (induction); a frame-UNambiguous spatial control set (should have no flippable register) and non-spatial items (specificity). Frame direction = mean activation difference between relative-forced and absolute/intrinsic-forced runs, pooled across languages. Systems compared: frame steering vs explicit frame-instruction prompting vs translate-first. Decisive metric: repair rate (fraction correctly re-framed under explicit context) minus baseline, and induction rate on non-default frames; secondary: interpretation accuracy, fluency (perplexity), specificity (non-spatial and frame-unambiguous items unchanged). Convincing result: repair and induction rates >=15 pp over baseline with specificity change <=5 pp and fluency within 10% of baseline. Indecision band: 5-15 pp effects, or specificity change 5-10 pp, indicate a weak/leaky intervention. Negative result: <5 pp effect means the frame direction is not functionally causal, refuting the steerability half of claim (d). Ablations (secondary): layer sweep; probe transfer across models; model scale. Reported metrics throughout: frame-choice distribution, cross-language disagreement, frame-override rate, relation vs frame probe accuracy and transfer, causal flip/repair/induction rates, content preservation, Spearman with conventionalization vs resource, fluency, specificity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Annotating each language's default frame and building a conventionalization index is subjective and some languages are mixed; we ground labels in the established typology literature, use multiple native-speaker annotators, restrict to high-agreement items, and report robustness to index operationalization. 2. Probe decodability of an abstract relation/frame may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal patching flip (Exp. 3) and steering repair/induction (Exp. 5) to establish functional relevance. 3. Frame preference could be confounded with translation artifacts of projective terms across languages; the frame-forcing and override conditions and native-speaker validation isolate the default from mere translation. 4. Strong models may collapse to a single (English-relative) frame regardless of query language, weakening cross-language variation; even documenting this near-universal English-relative default and its resistance to explicit cues is a valuable linguistic-relativity finding, and multiple models/languages give power. 5. Constructed items for very-low-resource absolute languages (e.g., Guugu Yimithirr) may have thin coverage, confounding frame-imposition with ignorance; we include higher-resource absolute/cardinal registers (Tamil, cardinal-heavy phrasing) and control with same-scene items. 6. Tokenization of projective/cardinal terms varies across scripts; we use pooled-span or last-token representations and report tokenization statistics. 7. Steering may trade frame correctness for fluency; we report both. 8. Findings may be model-specific; three model families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: latent_language_suppression
Title: The Ghost in the Machine Translation: Automatic Co-activation and Active Suppression of Non-target Languages in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Like the bilingual brain, multilingual LLMs automatically co-activate the dominant language's answer as a latent competitor during monolingual generation, and must *actively suppress* it in late layers. The specific, falsifiable phenomenon we claim (and which distinguishes this from generic language-direction steering) is a dynamic trajectory: the dominant-language competitor answer is boosted in mid layers, then actively pushed DOWN in late layers (a within-run rank reversal, not mere absence), and *leakage* (code-switching / wrong-language output) occurs when this late suppression fails. We define 'co-activation' as the dominant-language answer being decodable above an unrelated-language baseline while the surface output is verified target-language, and 'active suppression' as a causal signature: the competitor's logit rank rises then falls across layers AND ablating an identified late-layer component raises both the competitor logit and the leakage rate above matched random-component ablation. We hypothesize (a) such dominant-language co-activation, (b) an identifiable late-layer suppression mechanism whose ablation induces leakage, and (c) that co-activation strength and suppression failure scale with typological/script distance from the dominant language.
Related Work: Interpretability work frames LLMs as computing in a language-agnostic concept space (Semantic Hub 2024) and 'transitioning' to the target language in final layers, with failures at this transition causing inconsistency (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025). These works model the dominant language as an intermediate *pivot* that is translated away, and non-target languages as simply absent. A growing line of language-steering and sparse-feature-steering work (language-direction steering 2024-2025; SAE language features 2025) shows one can ADD a direction to change output language, but treats language as a static, additively-steerable attribute; none exhibits or requires a dynamic boost-then-suppress trajectory, and none shows that a mechanism actively damps a competitor whose ablation causes leakage. Cross-lingual knowledge-conflict work (CLEAR 2026) studies conflict between explicit external evidence, not internal automatic co-activation. Cognitive neuroscience (Language Conflict in the Bilingual Brain 2008; RLD & Bilingual Control 2019) shows non-target languages are automatically co-activated and must be actively inhibited, with cost scaling with relative language distance. Our delta over the steering literature is precise: we do not merely steer language, we test whether the model already runs an *interference-control* loop (boost -> active late suppression -> leakage on failure) and localize the suppressing component causally. We therefore soften any 'first ever' language and claim specifically the first test and causal localization of an active-suppression (not additive-steering) account of cross-lingual leakage.
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer questions in many languages, and interpretability work describes an English-centric internal pipeline that is 'translated away' before output; the language-steering literature shows output language can be shifted by adding a direction. We propose a different, cognitively-inspired and more dynamic lens: the dominant language is not passively absent but *automatically co-activated* as a latent competitor that is boosted in mid layers and must be *actively suppressed* in late layers to produce fluent monolingual text. This is materially different from generic language steering: the intervention target is an existing suppression loop, not an additive attribute. We test three claims with explicit falsifiable definitions. First, during verified target-language generation, the dominant-language answer token remains decodable above an unrelated-language baseline (co-activation). Second, an identifiable late-layer mechanism actively damps the competitor: its logit rank rises then falls, and ablating specific heads/directions raises the competitor logit and induces leakage above matched random ablation (active suppression). Third, co-activation strength and suppression failure scale with typological and script distance from the dominant language. We operationalize a per-item Suppression Cost (logit-rank the competitor is pushed down over late layers) and a Leakage Rate (wrong-language output). We first quantify leakage prevalence across Llama-3, Aya-23, and Qwen2 and language groups to show it is not a niche curiosity. So what: if active suppression is real, the practical levers change from generic language steering to monitoring the suppression signal as a leakage early-warning diagnostic, adding a suppression-strengthening training objective, and inference-time amplification of the suppression direction to reduce code-switching in low-resource languages with no retraining. Experiments span multilingual factual QA (mLAMA/BMLAMA) and translation-free generation across 20+ languages, and disambiguate whether the competitor is the dominant or the typologically nearest high-resource language. This bridges cognitive theories of bilingual control with mechanistic interpretability and yields concrete diagnostics and a training-free fix.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Tasks: multilingual factual QA (mLAMA + BMLAMA, existing) subsampled to 2,000 short-answer items, plus 1,000 open-ended target-language generation prompts (constructed), each with a known dominant-language (English) reference answer token. Languages: 20+ spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families; English is the dominant language. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, all weights frozen; greedy decoding, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds. Every output is passed through an automatic language-identifier (human spot-checks on 5%) so co-activation is measured only while the surface output is verified target-language. Probe protocol (fixed in advance): language-ID probes are L2 logistic regressions trained on a held-out language-labeled split, with train/dev/test disjoint by ITEM and validated by cross-language transfer accuracy before use, so decodability cannot arise from item-level label leakage. Two quantities recur: Suppression Cost = the drop in the dominant-language competitor answer's logit RANK from its peak-activation layer to the output layer; Leakage Rate = fraction of outputs that switch wholly or partly into the dominant language. Prevalence pre-study: before the mechanistic experiments we report Leakage Rate per model and per language group (script/family/resource) to establish scope. Circuit-vs-diffuse criterion (pre-registered): the suppression is called a 'circuit' only if <=5% of heads (or a single direction) account for >=50% of the leakage-induction effect; otherwise it is reported as diffuse/direction-based.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- automatic co-activation of the dominant-language answer): tests claim (a). Data/model as Setup. Method: at each layer apply logit-lens and the trained linear probes to detect the dominant-language (English) answer token while the output is confirmed target-language. Decisive metric: layer-wise decodability of the English answer, contrasted against two baselines -- decodability of an UNRELATED third-language answer and of a random token (chance). Convincing result: English-answer decodability exceeds the unrelated-language baseline by >=15 percentage points (pp) in mid-to-late layers across most languages -- co-activation is specific to the dominant language, not a generic shared-concept effect. Indecision band: 5-15 pp above the unrelated-language baseline = weak co-activation; <5 pp = no dominant-specific co-activation and (a) is refuted. Negative result (English answer no more decodable than an unrelated language) means apparent co-activation is just the shared concept space, refuting (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- an identifiable late-layer suppression mechanism, with strong causal controls): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup, frozen, activation patching and attention-head attribution. Method: (1) track the competitor logit rank across late layers to compute Suppression Cost and verify the competitor is actively pushed DOWN after a peak (the rank-reversal signature), not merely never boosted; (2) localise the suppressing components via head/MLP attribution and patching at MULTIPLE layers, ablate them, and measure the rise in competitor logit and change in Leakage Rate; (3) recover a suppression direction (mean activation difference between clean and leakage-prone runs) and AMPLIFY it, testing the reverse effect. Causal controls: matched random-component ablation, a norm-matched random-direction steer, a matched-logit control (a same-magnitude non-suppression edit), and counterfactual language swaps; the identified effect must exceed all of these. Decisive metric: increase in Leakage Rate when the identified components are ablated, relative to random-component ablation. Convincing result: ablating the identified components raises Leakage Rate by >=20 pp over random-component ablation and raises the competitor logit, the pre-registered circuit criterion is met, AND amplifying the recovered direction reduces baseline Leakage Rate -- a bidirectionally functional suppression mechanism. Indecision band: leakage increase of 8-20 pp over random = diffuse/partial suppression (reported as direction-based); <8 pp, or no active push-down (Suppression Cost approximately 0), or effects matched by the control edits = no identifiable active suppression and (b) is refuted. Negative result (ablation matches random, or no active push-down) refutes the suppression-mechanism claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- co-activation and suppression failure scale with distance, disentangled from confounds): tests claim (c). Data: per-language co-activation strength (Experiment 1), Suppression Cost, and Leakage Rate (Experiment 2). Predictors: lang2vec typological distance, a binary same-script indicator, and a data-frequency proxy (pretraining token share) entered together in a multivariate model, since these three are confounded; we report each predictor's unique contribution. Decisive metric: partial Spearman / standardized coefficients for typological distance, script, and frequency, with bootstrap CIs. Convincing result: distance (and/or script) retains |effect| corresponding to Spearman >=0.5 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.2 for BOTH co-activation and Leakage Rate after controlling for frequency. Indecision band: 0.2-0.5 = weak scaling (suggestive); <0.2, or the effect fully absorbed by frequency, = no distinct distance/script scaling and that half of (c) is refuted. Negative result (no distance relationship) refutes the dose-response claim.

Experiment 4 (H1/H2 -- is the competitor the DOMINANT or the typologically NEAREST high-resource language): the key novel disambiguation, ensuring Experiment 3's distance is not confounded and testing the 'typically English' qualifier -- a question additive-steering papers never pose. Data: target languages each paired with the dominant language (English) AND their typologically nearest high-resource language (e.g. Spanish for Catalan, Hindi for Marathi). Model as Setup. Method: repeat the Experiment 1 co-activation probe and the Experiment 2 Suppression Cost for both candidate competitors. Decisive metric: per target language, dominant-competitor co-activation/Suppression Cost minus nearest-competitor co-activation/Suppression Cost. Convincing result: the dominant language shows higher co-activation and Suppression Cost than the nearest high-resource language by >=10 pp for the majority of target languages, supporting 'typically English'. Indecision band: the two within 5-10 pp = dual competitor (co-activation of both); nearest > dominant = the competitor is the nearest high-resource language, qualifying (a). Negative result (nearest dominates) replaces the English-centric reading with a nearest-language account -- an informative correction rather than a null.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The 'competitor' might be decodable simply because the concept space is shared, not because of genuine co-activation of a specific language's token; we control by comparing dominant-language decodability against unrelated languages and by requiring the dynamic rank-reversal and causal ablation signatures rather than mere presence. 2. Logit-lens/probe decodability can reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the causal ablation (leakage induction above matched controls) to confirm functional relevance. 3. Suppression may be diffuse rather than localized; the pre-registered circuit-vs-diffuse criterion forces an honest fallback to a direction-based account. 4. Leakage may be rare in strong models, limiting power; the prevalence pre-study quantifies this, and we include low-resource languages and adversarial prompts to elicit it. 5. Typological distance, script, and data frequency are confounded; Experiment 3's multivariate analysis reports each predictor's unique contribution. 6. Whether the target is the dominant or nearest high-resource language is a genuine ambiguity Experiment 4 is designed to resolve. 7. Findings may vary across model families; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: concreteness_transfer_inversion
Title: The Concreteness Inversion: Why LLMs Share Abstract Concepts Across Languages Better Than Concrete Ones, Opposite to the Bilingual Brain
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs functionally transfer ABSTRACT concepts across languages better than CONCRETE ones, an inversion of the human bilingual pattern. The novelty is mechanism-level: not that a concreteness effect exists in multilingual LLMs (embedding-geometry work already reports this), but that it holds at the level of CAUSAL, functional cross-lingual transfer inside a running decoder. We hypothesize (a) the inversion appears in functional transfer (word translation / factual recall), not just static embedding geometry; (b) it is driven by concrete concepts being represented more language-specifically in the shared concept space, so activation-patching a concrete concept from language A into a language-B prompt transfers less reliably than an abstract one; and (c) it is driven by grounding-deprivation rather than raw training frequency, dissociable by holding corpus frequency fixed. Pre-registered frequency-vs-grounding distinction: under frequency-matched pairs the negative concreteness slope must persist AND an imageability/visual-grounding score must add explanatory variance beyond concreteness and frequency; if the slope collapses under frequency matching, the effect is frequency-driven.
Related Work: Embedding-geometry work finds abstract concepts align more linearly across languages than concrete ones in LLMs, attributing it to frequency (Concept Space Alignment in Multilingual LLMs / Peng & Søgaard 2024; On the Geometry of Concreteness 2022; Predicting Concreteness Across Languages 2018). Our sharp delta over Peng & Søgaard 2024: they measure STATIC embedding similarity and cannot show (i) that the asymmetry drives functional per-item transfer success, (ii) that activation-patching a concrete vs abstract concept representation causally transfers less across languages, or (iii) a frequency-vs-grounding dissociation under matched frequency -- all of which require intervening in a running model, not comparing embeddings. Multimodal work shows visual grounding especially helps concrete words (Leverage Points in Modality Shifts 2023; Word Representation Learning in Multimodal Transformers 2021). Causal concept-space work shows language-agnostic concept representations manipulable by patching, with output-language resolved before concept (Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; When Meanings Meet 2026). Human bilingual evidence is split and we treat it carefully: BEHAVIORAL psycholinguistics (translation-priming concreteness effects 2023) is the more robust anchor for a human concrete>abstract sharing pattern, while the neuroimaging claim (Concreteness Shapes Semantic Representations in Bilingual Brains 2025) is more contested; we frame the human-vs-LLM inversion primarily against the behavioral literature and flag the neuroimaging comparison as suggestive. We contribute the causal, functional reframing and the frequency-vs-grounding dissociation.
Abstract: In the bilingual brain, concrete concepts appear to be shared more across languages than abstract ones: 'apple' overlaps cross-linguistically while 'justice' is more language-dependent. Multilingual LLMs surprisingly show the reverse in embedding geometry, but this has only been observed as static similarity and attributed to training frequency. We ask whether LLMs exhibit a genuine, CAUSAL concreteness inversion at the level of functional cross-lingual concept transfer, and why -- our contribution is mechanism-level, not the mere existence of a concreteness effect. We anchor the human comparison on the more robust behavioral psycholinguistic pattern and treat the contested neuroimaging result as suggestive. We first establish the phenomenon behaviorally on ONE primary task family (cross-lingual word translation), treating factual recall as a robustness check, using validated concreteness norms and pre-registered statistical tests with confidence intervals and multiple-comparison control. We then move inside the model: using activation patching with a specified protocol (mid-layer concept representation over the concept span, injected from a source-language prompt into a target-language prompt, success = correct target concept AND correct output language), we test whether concrete concepts transfer less faithfully than abstract ones. Our central claim is that concrete concepts occupy a more language-specific region of the shared space. Finally we dissociate frequency from grounding-deprivation -- operationalized as reliance on perceptual, language-specific referent detail that a text-only model must approximate, indexed by imageability norms and multimodal-embedding shift -- by matching pairs on corpus frequency and testing whether the inversion persists and whether grounding adds variance. Controls address tokenization, polysemy, morphology, script, length, and semantic-neighborhood confounds, with random-pair negative controls. If null, the widely-cited geometry-based concreteness claim is challenged. The result informs multilingual QA, translation, and cross-lingual retrieval, where concrete-term queries may transfer worst. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 12+ languages; a multimodal LLM comparison is noted as a stronger grounding test.
Experiments:
Setup (shared). Stimuli: ~600 concepts spanning the full concreteness range from validated norms (Brysbaert concreteness ratings, existing) with cross-lingually verified translation equivalents (bilingual dictionaries / MUSE, native-speaker-verified), plus a factual-QA subset (mLAMA/BMLAMA facts varying in subject/object concreteness) used as a ROBUSTNESS check, not the primary claim. Rendered across 12 languages spanning Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic/CJK/Devanagari and 4+ families (scope: the inversion is expected wherever a shared concept space and text-only grounding hold, i.e. broadly across current decoder LLMs, which motivates the multi-family design). Per-concept corpus frequency (public pretraining-proxy corpus), length, polysemy count, and morphological-complexity flags recorded for control. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen. Concept tokens localized via last-token-of-concept or pooled-span (tokenization statistics reported). Statistics: primary hypotheses tested with pre-registered regressions reporting effect sizes and 95% CIs, with Benjamini-Hochberg control across languages/models; decisive 'thresholds' below are the pre-registered effect-size targets, not post-hoc cutoffs.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a functional concreteness inversion in the PRIMARY task, word translation): Task: cross-lingual word translation (source -> target); per-concept transfer success recorded. Decisive metric: the regression slope of transfer accuracy on concreteness, controlling corpus frequency, length, and polysemy. Convincing result: a significantly NEGATIVE slope (abstract transfers better), CI excluding 0, stable across the three models, and compared against the reported positive human behavioral slope. Robustness: repeat on the factual-recall subset. Indecision band: CI includes 0 or |slope| within +/-0.02 accuracy per concreteness unit = null (reported as an informative challenge to the geometry claim); a POSITIVE slope means LLMs match humans, refuting H1.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- concrete concepts are more language-specific, causal; specified patching protocol): (a) extract per-language mid-layer concept directions/probes and measure cross-lingual alignment (cosine of matched-concept directions and probe-transfer, plus CKA) as a function of concreteness; (b) core causal test with a fully specified protocol -- at the pre-selected best mid-layer (chosen by a held-out layer sweep on dev concepts), extract the concept representation over the concept span from a source-language prompt, inject it into a target-language prompt, success = correct target-language translation/answer AND preserved output language (>=95%). Controls: random-pair patch (mismatched concept) and same-language patch as null baselines. Decisive metric: the slope of patched transfer fidelity on concreteness. Convincing result: patched transfer fidelity DECREASES with concreteness (significant negative slope, CI excluding 0), cross-lingual concept-direction alignment lower for concrete than abstract by >=0.1 cosine, output language preserved, above null baselines. Indecision band: fidelity-slope CI including 0, or alignment gap 0.03-0.1 = weak; <0.03 or nulls matching = refutes H2 (behavioral inversion not backed by shared-space mechanism). This experiment, not the embedding geometry, is what distinguishes us from Peng & Søgaard 2024.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- grounding-deprivation, not frequency; pre-registered dissociation with ablations): Data: (a) frequency-MATCHED concrete/abstract pairs (matched within a corpus-frequency band); (b) an imageability/visual-grounding score (imageability norms; availability of image-text pairs; multimodal-embedding shift magnitude) as an operational index of grounding-deprivation. Additional within-model ablations isolating the driver: frequency-only match, length-only match, semantic-neighborhood match, and random-pair negative controls. Model: re-run Exp. 1 behavioral transfer, Exp. 2 probe alignment, and Exp. 2 patching on the matched pairs. Decisive metric: the concreteness slope on transfer under frequency matching, and the added R^2 of the grounding score beyond concreteness and frequency. Convincing result (pre-registered): the negative concreteness slope persists under frequency matching (retains >=50% of unmatched magnitude, CI excluding 0) AND grounding adds R^2 >=0.03 beyond concreteness+frequency. Indecision band: matched slope retains 20-50% = mixed frequency/grounding account; retains <20% (inversion collapses under matching) = frequency-driven, refuting H3. Optional stronger test noted for submission-readiness: repeat the transfer/patching on a multimodal (grounded) LLM to test whether grounding closes the concrete-transfer gap.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. The inversion may be an embedding-geometry artifact not surviving at the functional-transfer level; a null behavioral transfer result is an informative, publishable challenge to the geometry-based claim. 2. Probe alignment and geometric similarity are correlational; the activation-patching causal test (Exp. 2, with random-pair/same-language null baselines and the output-language specificity check) promotes the finding to a mechanism, and we keep geometry, probe, patching, and behavioral evidence explicitly distinct in the narrative rather than conflating them. 3. Concreteness, frequency, and length are correlated; the frequency-matched pairs plus frequency-only/length-only/semantic-neighborhood ablations (Exp. 3) are the crucial dissociation. 4. Cross-lingual concreteness norms and translation equivalents are noisy, especially for abstract/polysemous words; we use validated norms, native-verified equivalents, restrict to high-agreement items, and flag polysemy/morphology as controls. 5. Tokenization/script differences complicate concept localization and patching; we use last-token/pooled-span representations and report tokenization statistics. 6. The human comparison uses published behavioral slopes (robust) and contested neuroimaging (suggestive only); we frame the inversion primarily against behavioral psycholinguistics and do not overclaim a clean neural inversion. 7. Grounding-deprivation is inferred from imageability/multimodal proxies, not a grounded model; the multimodal-LLM comparison is the stronger test and is noted. 8. We narrow the primary claim to word translation and treat factual recall as robustness to avoid over-broad claims. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: tense_grammaticalization_gap
Title: When the Grammar Is Silent: How Multilingual LLMs Represent Time in Tenseless vs. Tensed Languages
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic 'reference-time' representation -- the abstract past/present/future location of the described situation -- that is operationally DISTINCT from surface tense-morphology (which verb form appears). The two come apart even in tensed languages (e.g. English present-for-future 'the train leaves tomorrow', historical present 'in 1500 Luther writes...', backshifted reported speech), and existing tense-localization work probes only the surface form, never this abstract situation time. We hypothesize (a) for tensed languages the model can lazily read reference time off surface tense features, while for tenseless/aspect-only languages (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba) it must infer reference time from lexical/pragmatic context via a slower, later-layer, more error-prone circuit; (b) this yields a measurable 'grammaticalization gap' in robustness and localization that tracks whether a language grammatically marks tense, NOT its resource level; and (c) the abstract reference-time direction is shared across languages, so it can be read from a tensed language and injected to improve temporal inference in a tenseless one. The cross-lingual steering/localization are tools; the core contributions are the reference-time-vs-surface-tense dissociation and the grammaticalization-gap mechanism.
Related Work: Prior probing work shows tense is easy to decode in morphologically-marked languages (French) but hard in Chinese, attributing the drop to memorization vs abstraction (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021), and that transformers encode aspect features like telicity/duration (About Time 2022; Verbal Aspect 2024). Recent interpretability shows grammatical concepts (number, gender, tense) share cross-lingual feature directions (Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), that tense/aspect are steerable orthogonal directions (Steering Tense and Aspect / TenseLoC 2025), and that LLMs encode linear time and 'temporal heads' for factual dates (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Temporal Heads 2025). Claim-by-claim contrast: TenseLoC localizes and steers SURFACE tense features (which morphology is produced) -- we target the abstract SENTENCE-INTERNAL reference time, which is present even when no tense morphology exists and can diverge from surface tense within tensed languages; Latent Grammatical Concepts shows a shared surface-tense direction across languages -- we test whether the abstract reference-time variable (not the surface feature) is shared, and whether tenseless languages recruit a distinct later circuit. Neither tests a tensed donor repairing temporal inference in a tenseless target. We reframe the classic French-vs-Chinese gap as a mechanistic grammaticalization-gap phenomenon; the dataset and the mechanism are the contributions, cross-lingual steering is a tool.
Abstract: Some languages grammatically mark when an event happened (English 'walked' vs 'walks'); others, like Chinese, Indonesian, and Yoruba, are largely tenseless and leave temporal location to be inferred from adverbs, aspect markers, and pragmatics. Yet any comprehending model must recover the same abstract reference time -- and even in tensed languages, surface tense and reference time diverge (present-for-future, historical present, backshifting). We operationally distinguish surface tense morphology (which verb form appears) from abstract reference time (the situation's past/present/future location) and ask how multilingual LLMs represent the latter, and whether the mechanism differs when grammar is silent. Using parallel sentences whose reference time is fixed by context across tensed and tenseless languages -- plus native-authored non-parallel items to rule out translation artifacts -- we train linear probes and locate the layers and components that encode reference time in each. We predict a 'grammaticalization gap': in tensed languages reference time is decodable early and localizes with surface-tense features, whereas in tenseless languages it emerges only in later layers via a distinct, more error-prone circuit, and this gap tracks whether a language marks tense rather than its resource level (low-resource tensed Swahili patterns with English; high-resource tenseless Chinese with Indonesian). We test whether the abstract reference-time direction is shared by extracting it from a tensed donor and steering it into a tenseless-language forward pass, measuring actual temporal-reasoning task behavior (event ordering, when-questions, temporal NLI), not merely probe confidence. So what: if the account holds, cross-lingual temporal QA, legal/medical timeline extraction, cross-lingual information extraction, and temporal NLI in tenseless languages are systematically weaker for a structural, not resource, reason -- so multilingual evaluation and alignment should test temporal inference by tense typology, and the typology-vs-resource dissociation matters for equitable model development. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B and 12+ languages of both types.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed, ~1,200 items -- scaled up for cross-lingual mechanistic power): parallel minimal-pair sentences whose abstract reference time (past/present/future) is fixed either by an explicit temporal adverbial ('yesterday'/'now'/'tomorrow') or in a BARE-CONTEXT / DISCOURSE-CUE version (no adverbial and no lexical shortcut; reference time inferable only from multi-sentence discourse), plus items where surface tense and reference time DIVERGE within tensed languages (present-for-future, historical present, backshifted reported speech). A separate NATIVE-AUTHORED non-parallel subset per language rules out translation artifacts. Rendered in 12 languages split into TENSED (English, Spanish, Russian, Swahili [low-resource but tensed], Hindi) and TENSELESS/aspect-only (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba, Thai, Vietnamese). Each item carries two separate labels -- surface tense-morphology and abstract reference time -- with a documented annotation protocol: reference time is labeled by >=3 native-speaker annotators using written criteria (the temporal location the discourse asserts, independent of verb form), inter-annotator agreement reported, and items below an agreement threshold discarded. Templates are counterbalanced and paraphrased, with cue-swapped adversarial variants, so probes cannot exploit fixed lexical semantics. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; linear probes (3 seeds, held-out validation); verb-token or clause-final representations; tokenisation statistics reported. Emergence layer = first layer at which a probe exceeds 90% accuracy (or its peak), reported as a fraction of model depth; we report robustness to alternative emergence definitions (75% threshold, area-under-the-layerwise-curve) and justify the metric.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- a distinct, later, error-prone reference-time circuit when grammar is silent): tests that abstract reference time is separable from surface tense and, in tenseless languages, emerges later via a distinct circuit whose weakness predicts errors. Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) two-target probing -- separate per-layer probes for surface tense morphology and for abstract reference time, per language, recording emergence layers, evaluated including on the surface-vs-reference divergence items (where a reference-time probe must disagree with a surface-tense probe); (b) circuit localisation -- activation patching / attention-head attribution find the components carrying reference time in tensed vs tenseless languages, with Jaccard overlap and whether tenseless languages recruit additional later components tied to adverbial/context tokens; (c) behavioural link -- on a temporal-inference TASK (order two events / answer a when-question), test that low reference-time probe confidence in tenseless bare-context items predicts task errors, distinguishing evidence for a shared representation from evidence for functionally-used circuitry via patching. Decisive metric: the reference-time emergence-layer difference (tenseless minus tensed) and the tensed-vs-tenseless circuit Jaccard overlap, with the behavioural task-error link alongside. Convincing result: in tensed languages reference time is decodable early and its probe tracks the surface-tense probe (except on divergence items, where they dissociate); in tenseless languages it emerges >=15% of model depth LATER, dissociates from surface tense, its circuit overlaps the tensed circuit at Jaccard <=0.4 while recruiting later adverbial-tied components, and low probe confidence predicts behavioural task error at Spearman >=0.3. Indecision band: emergence delay 5-15% of depth or Jaccard 0.4-0.6 = weak/partial (reported as such); delay <5% with Jaccard >0.6 = no distinct circuit and H1 is refuted. Negative result (reference time decoded identically and via the same circuit in both types) refutes the grammaticalisation-gap mechanism.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- the gap tracks whether a language marks tense, not its resource level): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup. Method: define the grammaticalisation gap per language = reference-time emergence delay plus the bare-context robustness drop (fall in probe accuracy from adverbial to discourse-only context). Predictors entered together: a binary 'grammatically marks tense' typology indicator vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / mLAMA accuracy). Decisive metric: partial Spearman of the gap with the typology indicator vs the resource proxy, bootstrap CIs, with the crucial contrast of low-resource tensed Swahili vs high-resource tenseless Chinese. Convincing result: |Spearman with typology| >=0.5 and exceeds |Spearman with resource| by >=0.2, with Swahili patterning with the tensed languages and Chinese with the tenseless ones. Indecision band: within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed account; typology not stronger, or gap <0.05 = the typology claim is refuted. Negative result (the gap tracks resource) reassigns it to resource scarcity.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- a shared reference-time direction that transfers and improves temporal inference by injection): tests claim (c), reporting task behavior and stating the intervention as a mechanistic demonstration whose generalization is explicitly tested. Data: bare-context temporal-inference items where the model errs in tenseless languages (diagnosis set) and a DISJOINT held-out set (to test generalization beyond the curated errors), plus perfect-aspect temporal-NLI items. Model: extract the abstract reference-time direction (mean activation difference past vs future) from a TENSED donor language; (a) test cross-lingual decodability by applying the donor probe to a tenseless language; (b) steer the donor-derived direction into the tenseless-language forward pass. Negative controls: random directions, unrelated grammatical directions (e.g. number/gender), a within-language null direction, and donor languages with mismatched scripts/tokenization -- all must fail to improve inference. Systems compared: donor-direction steering vs same-language steering vs translate-to-English. Decisive metric: temporal-inference/NLI TASK accuracy gain in the tenseless language on the held-out set, then fluency (perplexity) and specificity, with donor-probe transfer accuracy reported first. Convincing result: the donor probe transfers within 10 pp of in-language accuracy AND steering raises tenseless temporal-inference accuracy by >=5 points on the held-out set without harming fluency (<5% perplexity increase), matching or beating same-language steering and exceeding all negative controls. Indecision band: transfer 10-25 pp below in-language, or a 2-5 point gain = partial sharing/repair; transfer near chance, <2 point gain, or gains not exceeding the negative controls = the direction is not shared/functional and H3 is refuted. Negative result (no transfer, or gains only on the curated errors and not the held-out set) refutes the shared-direction and causal-improvement claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1. Probe decodability may reflect the readout basis rather than a used representation; we require the Exp.-1 patching (functional circuitry, not just decodable representation), the behavioural task-error link, and the Exp.-3 held-out task-accuracy gains with negative controls. 2. Separating abstract reference time from surface tense is hard where they coincide; the tenseless languages, the bare-context/discourse condition, and the within-tensed-language divergence items are the crucial dissociating cases. 3. Ground-truth reference time in bare-context items can be genuinely ambiguous; we restrict to items with high native-annotator agreement under a written protocol. 4. Probes might exploit lexical semantics; counterbalanced templates, paraphrases, cue-swapped adversarial items, and native-authored non-parallel data guard against this and against translation artifacts. 5. Emergence-layer thresholds are arbitrary in isolation; we justify the metric and report robustness to alternatives. 6. Some models may route everything through English tense; showing this via the shared-direction transfer is itself informative. 7. The typology-vs-resource dissociation hinges on chosen languages; we report robustness to alternatives. 8. The repair is presented as a mechanistic demonstration whose generalization is tested on a held-out set, not overclaimed as a deployed fix. 9. Findings may be model-specific; three families address but do not exhaust generality.

Name: honorific_register_binding
Title: Who Am I Talking To? A Causal Study of How Multilingual LLMs Represent Social Register and Bind It to Honorific Grammar
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs build a shared, language-agnostic representation of the speaker-addressee social relationship (relative status/formality), stored separately from surface honorific morphology; the CONTRIBUTION is not this shared direction (which prior formality work already suggests) but the late-layer BINDING mechanism that reads register off it onto obligatory honorific grammar, and the LAZY-INHERITANCE failure of that binding. We hypothesize (a) an abstract social-register variable decodable across languages including register-lax ones; (b) that honorific errors in obligatory-honorific languages arise from a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the register implied by the input/query language rather than re-inferring it from context; and (c)—the primary empirical novelty—that this inheritance bias tracks how strongly a language grammaticalizes register (obligatory verb honorifics > T-V pronouns > lexical-only), operationally defined by a register-grammaticalisation-strength index, and NOT its resource level, and is causally repairable by steering the shared register direction at the binding layer.
Related Work: Prior work studies politeness behaviorally and stylistically (TyDiP 2022; Comparing Styles across Languages 2023; Should We Respect LLMs? 2024), probes function words/negation in monolingual BERT-era models (Negation Scope 2020; Function Words 2022), and—closest to us—recovers steerable formality/register features with sparse autoencoders and steering vectors (SAE-formality and style-steering work 2024-2025). Interpretability work shows LLMs share cross-lingual concept and grammatical-concept directions (Semantic Hub 2024; Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) and decode into the target language in late layers. Direct contrast with the SAE-formality work: it recovers and steers a formality/register FEATURE as an output style, but does not explain how that variable is BOUND onto obligatory honorific morphology at generation time, nor why models produce input-language-inherited register ERRORS in obligatory-honorific languages, nor whether the failure scales with grammaticalisation strength vs resource level. We therefore do not claim discovering a register direction; we claim the binding mechanism and the lazy-inheritance failure, and the grammaticalisation-vs-resource dissociation, as the novelty. We treat honorification/T-V typology as a controlled probe and give causal (patching + steering) evidence for a late-layer register-to-morphology binding step, avoiding any 'first complete account' framing.
Abstract: Languages encode the speaker-addressee relationship very differently: Japanese and Korean obligatorily mark honorification through verb morphology, Romance/Slavic/German languages force a T-V (informal/formal 'you') choice, and English leaves register to lexical and pragmatic cues. A competent multilingual model must recover the same abstract relationship and, when the target language demands it, commit to a grammatical register. So what: when a model binds the wrong register, a Japanese or Korean assistant addresses an elder or customer with casual verb endings (or a stranger with over-familiar forms), a concrete, face-threatening deployment failure in translation, chatbots, and assistant localization. We ask how multilingual LLMs represent this social-register variable and, our focus, how they BIND it onto honorific grammar. We distinguish an abstract, language-agnostic social-register variable from the surface honorific/T-V morphology that realizes it. Prior formality-steering work already suggests the former exists; our contribution is the late-layer binding step and its lazy-inheritance failure. Using parallel dialogues whose social relationship is fixed by context across register-marking and register-lax languages, we localize where register is bound to grammar and test three claims: (1) the abstract register direction is decodable across languages including English; (2) honorific errors stem from a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the register implied by the query/input language; and (3)—the primary empirical novelty—this inheritance bias tracks a register-grammaticalisation-strength index, not resource level (register-lax high-resource English vs register-heavy lower-resource Korean). We causally test binding via activation patching with strong controls and repair errors by steering the shared register direction, comparing against explicit-context-reasoning and translate-then-generate baselines. We also test whether the binding mechanism generalizes to other pragmatic bindings. Experiments span Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, and Qwen2-7B across 10+ languages, with pre-registered confirmatory criteria separated from exploratory analyses.
Experiments:
Setup (shared across all experiments). Stimuli (constructed): parallel dialogue/instruction items whose speaker-addressee social relationship is unambiguously fixed by context (a student writing to a professor = high formality vs texting a close friend = low formality; power, status, intimacy varied), ~500 base items each with a bare-context variant (relationship inferable only from lexical cues) and an explicit-context variant. Rendered in 10+ languages spanning three register-grammar types: OBLIGATORY-HONORIFIC (Japanese, Korean), T-V DISTINCTION (Spanish, French, German, Russian, Hindi), REGISTER-LAX (English, Chinese, Indonesian). The correct target register per item is native-speaker validated, and each language gets a register-grammaticalisation-strength index, operationally defined as an ordinal scale: obligatory verb-honorific morphology (3) > obligatory T-V pronoun choice (2) > lexical-only optional marking (1). Register labels and the annotation protocol are documented; bare-context items are labeled by >=3 native annotators with an inter-annotator-agreement threshold, and sub-threshold items discarded. Probe target is stated explicitly per analysis: we separately probe (i) the INTENDED register (context-mandated label), (ii) the REALIZED output register (from the generated text), and (iii) the latent model state, and never conflate them. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2-7B, frozen; greedy, temperature 0, 3 paraphrase seeds; verb-final or reply-final token representations; obligatory-honorific, T-V, and lexical cases analysed separately; tokenisation reported. Confirmatory hypotheses and thresholds below are pre-registered; additional analyses are labeled exploratory.

Experiment 1 (H1 -- an abstract, cross-lingual social-register variable distinct from surface morphology): tests claim (a) as groundwork for the binding claim. Data/model as Setup. Method: train per-layer linear probes to decode the intended social register (formal/informal, or ordinal level) from mid-layer hidden states on held-out items; test decodability in register-lax languages (English/Chinese) and cross-lingual transfer (train one language, test others); contrast with a surface-morphology probe (which honorific/T-V form appears) to establish the abstract-vs-surface dissociation. Decisive metric: cross-lingual register-probe transfer accuracy, plus register decodability in register-lax languages. Convincing result: register decodable above chance in register-lax languages and the register probe transfers cross-lingually within 10 pp of in-language accuracy, while the surface-morphology probe does NOT transfer. Indecision band: transfer 10-25 pp below in-language = partially shared; transfer >25 pp below, or register-lax decodability at chance = the register variable is not abstract/shared and (a) is refuted. Negative result (register decodable only where grammatically marked) refutes the shared-representation groundwork.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- honorific errors are a late-layer binding failure that lazily inherits the input-language register: the core mechanism): tests claim (b). Data/model as Setup, activation patching. Method: (a) lazy-inheritance test -- hold the target generation language fixed (e.g. Japanese) but vary the language/framing of the context (English formal framing vs Japanese informal context, etc.) and measure how often the output register matches the INPUT-language-implied register rather than the context-mandated register; (b) localise the binding step -- run the identical item under context forcing FORMAL vs INFORMAL and activation-patch late-layer components from the formal run into the informal run to find the minimal set whose patching flips the produced register while message content is preserved; localize the binding LAYER by patching across layers and identify where the register-to-morphology mapping is committed, explicitly testing whether the effect is a late-layer binding vs a still-later token-level selection by patching pre- vs post-final-token positions. Strong controls: random-component patching, layer-shuffled patching, a same-language but wrong-context control, and a morphology-only baseline (patching surface-form features alone), all of which must produce smaller/qualitatively different effects. Decisive metric: the late-layer register-flip rate under patching (content preserved) and the lazy-inheritance rate. Convincing result: a compact late-layer set flips the produced register in >=50% of items with content preserved (>=95%), exceeding all controls, AND the inheritance rate is >=20 pp higher when generating an obligatory-honorific language from a register-lax input than in matched controls. Indecision band: flip rate 25-50% = diffuse binding; inheritance excess 8-20 pp = weak lazy inheritance (both partial); flip rate <25% or inheritance excess <8 pp = no binding-failure mechanism and (b) is refuted. Negative result (register recomputed from context regardless of input language, no locatable binding step) refutes the lazy-inheritance account.

Experiment 3 (H3 -- inheritance scales with grammaticalisation and is causally repairable: the primary empirical novelty): tests claim (c). Data/model as Setup. Method: (a) dose-response -- correlate register-error and inheritance rate with the grammaticalisation-strength index vs a resource-level proxy (pretraining share / benchmark accuracy), entered together, with the crucial contrast of register-lax high-resource English vs register-heavy lower-resource Korean; (b) steering repair -- extract a shared social-register direction (mean activation difference formal vs informal, pooled across languages) at the binding layer, steer mis-registered items toward the correct register, and in bare context steer to INDUCE the wrong register. Systems compared: steering vs an explicit register-instruction prompt, vs explicit-context-reasoning prompting, vs translate-context-first. Decisive metric: partial Spearman(inheritance/error, grammaticalisation strength) vs Spearman(., resource proxy), then repair rate and induction rate, with content preservation, fluency (perplexity), and specificity. Convincing result: |partial Spearman with grammaticalisation| >=0.5 exceeding resource by >=0.2 (English patterning register-lax despite high resource, Korean register-heavy despite lower resource), AND steering repairs >=40% of mis-registered items and induces the wrong register in >=40% of bare-context items with content preserved and fluency unharmed, matching or beating the prompting baselines. Indecision band: correlations within 0.05-0.2 of each other = mixed account; repair/induction 20-40% = partial; correlations not stronger for grammaticalisation, or repair/induction <20% = H3 is refuted. Negative result (inheritance tracks resource, or steering neither repairs nor induces) refutes the scaling and causal-repair claims. Exploratory: whether the same binding-layer mechanism generalizes to another pragmatic binding (e.g. speaker-stance/evidentiality marking), and error analysis of degenerate polite-default behavior and of languages where morphology and register are tightly coupled.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1.
